en: Chapter One:
When the night of Brahmā had passed and the Lotus-born was awakened,
Viṣṇu, desiring to create living beings, perceived that the earth was submerged by the waters.
Delighting in aquatic sports, as in the auspicious times of old at the beginning of the kalpas,
he assumed the form of a boar and lifted up the earth.
The Vedas are his feet, the sacrificial posts are his fangs, the rituals are his mouth, and the fire-altars are his face;
Agni is his tongue, the Darbha grass is his hair, Brahmā is his head, and he is possessed of great ascetic power.

The divine one has day and night for his eyes, the Vedāṅgas and the Śruti for his ornaments, clarified butter for his nose, the sacrificial ladle for his beak, and the sound of the Sāmaveda for his great voice. ||4||
Consisting of the truth of the Dharma, glorious, honored by his successive strides, consisting of expiation, steadfast, with knees like those of a beast, he is the great bull. ||5||
The Udgātṛ priest is his intestines; the oblation is his characteristic mark; the seeds and medicinal herbs are his great fruit;
the wind is his inner self; the mantra is his buttocks; and Soma is his blood. (6)
The altar was his shoulder, the fragrance of the oblation was his scent, and he possessed the great momentum of offerings to gods and ancestors;
the eastern hall was his body, he was radiant, and he was endowed with various initiations.
The yogin has the *dakṣiṇā* as his heart; he is all-pervading and consists of the Great Mantra;
he is beautiful with the *upākarma* as his lips and adorned with the *pravargya* as his whorls. ||8||

He whose path of movement consists of various meters, who sits upon the secret Upanishads as his seat, and who is accompanied by his consort Chāyā, is indeed as lofty as the peak of a jewel-mountain. ||9||
The Lord, having entered the single ocean, beheld the earth— bounded by the sea and containing its mountains, groves, and forests—
submerged in the waters of that single ocean.
Having lifted it up with the tip of his tusk out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds,
the primordial God, the great yogin, fashioned the earth anew.
Thus, in ancient times, having become the Sacrificial Boar and desiring the welfare of all beings, the divine Earth was lifted up by him from the midst of the waters. 12.
Having extracted them and placed them in their own steady locations,
Madhusūdana distributed the waters contained therein according to their respective places.
And those born of the ocean were in the oceans, those of the rivers in the rivers,
those of the ponds in the ponds, and those born of lakes in the lakes.
He created the seven netherworlds (pātālas) as well as the seven worlds (lokas),
and the various locations for the continents (dvīpas) and the oceans.
The guardians of the quarters, the world-protectors, the rivers, mountains, and trees;
the sages who know all dharmas, the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs, and the gods and asuras.
Piśācas, uragas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, and humans;
cattle, birds, wild animals, and the fourfold assembly of beings; as well as clouds, rainbows, lightning, and various kinds of sacrifices. (17)
Thus the Blessed Lord Varāha, having created this world with all its moving and non-moving beings, departed for that destination of the worlds which is unknown. ||18||
When Janārdana, the god of gods, had departed for an unknown destination, the Earth reflected: "What support will there be for me? (19)
"I shall go and ask Kaśyapa; he will tell me without doubt, for that great sage is constantly concerned for my welfare. (20)
Having thus made her resolve, the goddess, assuming the form of a woman, went to see Kaśyapa; and Kaśyapa beheld her.
Her eyes were like the petals of a blue lotus, her face resembled the autumnal moon,
her hair was adorned with swarms of bees, and she was radiant and auspicious, with lips as red as the bandhujīva flower.
She had very white, fine teeth, a beautiful nose, and arched eyebrows;
she possessed a neck like a conch shell, joined thighs, and full, rounded hips and thighs.
Her two breasts shone—symmetrical, full, and closely set; resembling the frontal lobes of a noble elephant and possessing the luster of refined gold.
Her arms were as tender as lotus stalks, her hands like young sprouts;
her thighs resembled golden pillars, and her knees were well-concealed and closely set.
Her shanks were hairless and perfectly symmetrical, her feet exceedingly beautiful, and her hips and waist were firm like those of a lion cub. (26)
Her copper-colored nails were endowed with radiance, her form was captivating to all, and with her glances she made every direction appear as if filled with blue lotuses. ||27||
The goddess was making the quarters free from darkness with her radiance;
she was clad in very white, fine garments and adorned with the finest jewels.
With her footsteps she made the earth appear as if strewn with lotuses;
endowed with beauty and youth, she stood before him with humble demeanor. (29)
Seeing her approach and having honored her, Kaśyapa said to that woman of beautiful hips: "O lady of excellent limbs, what is in your heart has been understood by me."
"O large-eyed one, bear this in mind; go, O Goddess, to Janārdana.
He will tell you everything regarding how your steadfastness shall come to pass. (31)
O fair-faced one, O lovely-limbed one, I have learned through the power of meditative concentration and by his grace that he dwells in the Ocean of Milk for your sake.
Having been addressed in this manner, the Earth then paid homage to Kaśyapa and departed for the Ocean of Milk, the sea of Keśava, to behold him.
She beheld that ocean of nectar, enchanting as the rays of the moon,
agitated by hundreds of waves produced by the turbulence of the wind.
Resembling a hundred Himalayas, it was like another circle of the earth, as if calling out to the ground with its moving hands of waves. (35)
By those very rays, it was as if white radiance were being incessantly bestowed upon the moon;
with all impurities entirely gone, it was as if by the Hari residing within.
Therefore, [one should worship] him who maintains a very white and powerful body,
the pale bird who is accessible and dwells in the lower world.
Rich with sapphire-like dark-red [fruits], it was like a sky turned upside down, completely covered by a multitude of jewels produced from its rows of fruit. (38)
Indeed, seeing that [lake] there, which was exceedingly vast in its expanse like the slough of the serpent Śeṣa, one beheld the abode of Keśava situated in its center.
Upon that [bed], he beheld Madhusūdana reclining on his side, his dimensions indescribable and endowed with inconceivable supernatural power.
His lotus-face was difficult to distinguish from the rays of the jewels on the hoods of the serpent Śeṣa;
it resembled a hundred moons and possessed a splendor equal to a hundred suns. ||41||
He is clothed in yellow garments, Akṣobhya, adorned with all kinds of jewels, resplendent with a crown the color of the sun and with two earrings. ||42||
His pair of feet were being massaged by the auspicious palms of Lakṣmī,
and he was being attended on all sides by personified weapons.
Seeing that lotus-eyed Madhusūdana, she prostrated herself before him;
having knelt upon the ground, she addressed him in this manner.
O Lord Viṣṇu, I who had gone to the depths of the netherworld have been uplifted by you and established in my own place out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds. 45.
"In this matter, O Lord of Gods, what support will there be for me now?
Having been addressed thus by the Goddess, the God spoke these words: 46.
O Earth, the virtuous who are devoted solely to the scriptures and endowed with the conduct of their respective castes and stages of life will support you; upon them your burden has been placed. (47)
Thus addressed, Vasumatī spoke to the God of gods:
"O son of Vāsava, [tell me] the duties of the social classes and the stages of life. (48)
I wish to hear from you, for you are my supreme refuge;
salutations to you, O God, Lord of gods, destroyer of the hosts of the enemies of the gods.
O Nārāyaṇa, Lord of the World, wielder of the conch, discus, and mace;
O Padmanābha, Hṛṣīkeśa, possessed of great strength and prowess! ||50||
O you who transcend the senses, O most difficult to cross over, O God who wields the Śārṅga bow, O Varāha, O Bhīma, O Govinda, O Ancient One, O Supreme Person! 51.
O golden-haired one, O all-seeing one, O embodiment of sacrifice, O stainless one!
O Knower of the Field, O Lord of the worlds, O you who recline upon the ocean of waters! 52.
O Mantra, whose vehicle is the mantra, inconceivable one, whose body is the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences, you who are the cause of the creation and destruction of this entire world! 53.
O Dharma, O Knower of Dharma, O Limb of Dharma, O Source of Dharma, O Bestower of Boons!
O Viṣvaksena, O Nectar, O Sky, O Slayer of Madhu and Kaiṭabha! ||54||
O Great One, nourisher of the great, unconquerable, bestower of fearlessness upon all beings;
O most excellent, sinless one, cloud-like creator of the world! ||55||
O nourisher of the waters, O abode, O support of consciousness, O inactive one;
O seven-headed teacher of the sacrifice, O Pradhāna, O Supreme Person! 56.
O Lord of the eternal syllable, O most subtle Master, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, O Vāmana!
You are the refuge of all the gods; you are the refuge of those who discourse on Brahman.
O Supreme Person, you are the goal of those who have known what is to be known;
O Lord of the World, I have taken refuge in you, the eternal Master of Speech. 58.
Subrahmaṇya, the unassailable, the one whose army is wealth, the bestower of wealth;
endowed with the power of great yoga, the son of Pṛśni, who maintains the radiant flame.
To the high-souled Vāsudeva, the lotus-eyed, the infallible,
the god who is the teacher of gods and asuras, the all-pervading Lord, the Great Sovereign of all beings.
To him who has one horn, four arms, and is the cause of the causes of the world—
O Blessed One, tell me the eternal duties of the four castes.
[He spoke of] those [duties] connected with the conduct of the stages of life (āśrama), together with their secret doctrines and their summaries.
Thus addressed by the Earth, the Lord of Gods spoke to the Earth: 62.
Listen, O Goddess Earth, to the eternal duties of the four castes,
together with the conduct of the stages of life, along with their secret doctrines and essential summaries.
But for those virtuous ones who shall uphold you as their supreme refuge,
sit down, O lady of beautiful thighs, upon this excellent golden seat.
Seated comfortably, understand the duties as I proclaim them;
at that time, the Earth, seated comfortably, heard the Vaiṣṇava duties.
Thus ends the first chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Two.

The four social classes (*varṇas*) are the Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and the Śūdra. (1) Of these, the first three are the twice-born (*dvijāti*). (2) For them, there is the collection of rites accompanied by sacred formulas (*mantra*), beginning with the impregnation rite (*niṣeka*) and ending with the funeral rites at the cemetery (*śmaśāna*). (3) Their duties (*dharma*) are as follows: (4) for the Brāhmaṇa, teaching; (5) for the Kṣatriya, constant readiness with weapons; (6) for the Vaiśya, tending cattle; (7) for the Śūdra, service to the twice-born. (8) For the twice-born, [the duties] are sacrificing and studying. (9) Now, their means of livelihood (*vṛtti*): (10) for the Brāhmaṇa, officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and receiving gifts; (11) for the Kṣatriya, protecting the earth; (12) for the Vaiśya, agriculture, cattle-rearing, trade, money-lending, and raising livestock; (13) for the Śūdra, all manual crafts. (14) In times of distress, one may follow the livelihood of the next lower class. (15)
Forbearance, truthfulness, self-restraint, purity, charity, control of the senses, non-violence, service to the guru, visiting sacred fords, and compassion. ||16||
Uprightness, freedom from greed, worship of the gods and Brahmins, and absence of malice—this is said to be the common dharma. (17)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Three.

Now, the duties of a king (*rājadharma*). 1. Protecting the subjects. 2. Establishing the social classes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) in their respective duties. 3. A king should settle in a region that is dry, suitable for cattle, and endowed with all kinds of crops. 4. It should also be a place where Vaiśyas and Śūdras predominate. 5. Therein, he should take refuge in one of the following types of fortresses: a desert, a marsh, a water-fort, a tree-fort, or a mountain-fort. 6. Residing there, he should appoint village overseers (*grāmādhipa*). 7. Overseers of ten villages (*daśādhyakṣa*). 8. Overseers of a hundred villages (*śatādhyakṣa*). 9. And overseers of an entire district (*deśādhyakṣa*). 10. The village overseer should remedy the faults of the village. 11. If he is unable, he should report them to the overseer of ten villages. 12. If he too is unable, [he reports] to the overseer of a hundred. 13. If he too is unable, [he reports] to the district overseer. 14. The district overseer must eradicate the fault by every means possible. 15. He should appoint trustworthy persons over mines, salt-works, toll-stations, ferries, and elephant forests. 16. Righteous men for religious duties. 17. Skilled men for financial affairs. 18. Brave men for military operations. 19. Fierce men for fierce tasks. 20. Eunuchs for the protection of women. 21. From the subjects, he should collect a sixth part of the grain as tax once a year. 22. And likewise from all other crops. 23. Two percent on cattle and gold, and likewise on clothes. 24. An eighth part on meat, honey, clarified butter, medicinal herbs, perfumes, flowers, fruits, roots, juices, vegetables, leaves, skins, earthenware, stone vessels, and bamboo articles. 25. He should not levy taxes from Brāhmaṇas; for they are the source of the king’s merit-based revenue. 26. The king receives a sixth part of both the good and evil deeds of all his subjects. 27. From goods produced in his own country, he should take a tenth part as toll (*śulka*). 28. And from goods from foreign countries, a twentieth part. 29. One who evades a toll station incurs the forfeiture of his entire property. 30. Artisans and those who live by manual labor should perform one day of work for the king every month. 31. The constituent elements of the state (*prakṛti*) are: the sovereign, the ministers, the fort, the treasury, the army, the kingdom, and allies. 32. He should execute those who corrupt these elements. 33. He should have spies as his eyes throughout his own kingdom and the kingdoms of others. 34. He should honor the virtuous. 35. And he should punish the wicked. 36. Toward enemies, friends, neutrals, and mediators, he should employ conciliation, bribery, sowing dissension, and force as appropriate and at the right time. 37. And he should resort to peace, war, marching, halting, seeking shelter, or duplicity according to the occasion. 38. He should set out on a military expedition in the month of Caitra or Mārgaśīrṣa. 39. Or when the enemy is in distress. 40. Upon acquiring a foreign territory, he should not abolish the laws of that country. 41. When attacked by an enemy, he should protect his kingdom with all his soul. 42. For kings, there is no duty equal to sacrificing one's body in battle. 43. Those who are killed while protecting cows, Brāhmaṇas, the king, friends, wealth, wives, or their own lives, attain the heavenly world. 44. And likewise for the sake of preventing the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*). 45. Upon capturing a foreign city, the king should install a member of that family on the throne. 46. He should not exterminate the royal lineage. 47. Except in the case of a family that has no noble lineage. 48. He should avoid addiction to hunting, gambling, women, and drinking. 49. And to verbal and physical violence. 50. He should not engage in the corruption of wealth. 51. He should not cut off the sources of revenue. 52. He should not shower gifts upon unworthy recipients. 53. He should take everything from the mines. 54. Having found a hidden treasure, he should give half to Brāhmaṇas. 55. The second half he should deposit in the treasury. 56. A Brāhmaṇa who finds a treasure may take it all. 57. A Kṣatriya should give a fourth part to the king, a fourth part to Brāhmaṇas, and keep half for himself. 58. A Vaiśya should give a fourth part to the king, a fourth part to Brāhmaṇas, and keep half. 59. A Śūdra, having acquired a treasure, should divide it into twelve parts: five parts to the king, five parts to Brāhmaṇas, and two parts for himself. 60. If a treasure is discovered without being reported, the king may confiscate it all. 61. From a treasure buried by oneself, everyone except a Brāhmaṇa should give a twelfth part to the king. 62. One who claims a treasure buried by another to be his own should be fined an amount equal to its value. 63. He should protect the property of children, the helpless, and women. 64. Having recovered property stolen by thieves, he should restore it all to the owners of all castes. 65. If he cannot recover it, he should pay it from his own treasury. 66. He should pacify divine calamities through propitiatory rites and auspicious ceremonies. 67. And he should ward off attacks from enemy armies by constant readiness with weapons. 68. He should choose a family priest (*purohita*) who is well-versed in the Vedas, the Epics, and the Law-books (*dharmaśāstra*), of noble birth, free from physical defects, and ascetic. 69. And he should appoint pure, honest, attentive, and capable assistants for all matters. 70. He himself should oversee legal proceedings (*vyavahāra*) together with learned Brāhmaṇas. 71. Or he may appoint a Brāhmaṇa to preside over the court of justice. 72. The members of the assembly (*sabhāsada*) should be endowed with noble birth, good conduct, and Vedic learning, impartial toward friend and foe, and incorruptible by litigants through desire, anger, fear, or greed. 73. In all matters, the king should be dependent on his astrologer. 74. He should constantly worship the gods and Brāhmaṇas. 75. He should serve the elderly. 76. And he should perform sacrifices. 77. No Brāhmaṇa in his kingdom should suffer from hunger. 78. Nor should anyone else who is devoted to righteous deeds. 79. He should grant land to Brāhmaṇas. 80. To those to whom he grants land, he should provide a document—written on cloth or a copper plate—detailing their lineage, the extent of the land, and the conditions of the grant, and marked with his own seal, for the information of future kings. 81. He should not confiscate land previously granted by another. 82. He should always bestow gifts upon Brāhmaṇas. 83. But he should protect himself from all sides. 84. He should be pleasant to behold. 85. He should carry antidotes against poison and spells. 86. He should not consume anything untested. 87. He should speak with a smile. 88. He should not frown even toward those condemned to death. 89. He should inflict punishment on those deserving of it in proportion to the offense. 90. He should administer justice properly. 91. He should not forgive anyone for a second offense. 92. He should maintain his own duty (*svadharma*); for kings, there is no one who is exempt from punishment. 93. Thus ends the section on the duties of a king.
Where the dark-complexioned, red-eyed Rod of Punishment moves about fearlessly, there the subjects flourish, provided that the leader perceives rightly. (95)
He should conduct himself with justice within his own kingdom, be severe in punishment toward enemies, straightforward toward friends, and endowed with patience toward Brahmins. (96)
For a king who conducts himself in this manner, even if he lives by gleaning grains from the field, his fame shall spread throughout the world like a drop of oil upon the water. (97)
The king who finds happiness in the happiness of his subjects and who is pained by their suffering is endowed with fame in this world and is glorified in heaven after death. (98)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Four.

The particle of dust found in a sunbeam passing through a lattice window is known as a *trasareṇu* (1). Eight of those make a *likṣā* (2). Three of those make a *rājasarṣapa* (3). Three of those make a *gaurasarṣapa* (4). Six of those make a *yava* (barley grain) (5). Three of those make a *kṛṣṇala* (6). Five of those make a *māṣaka* (7). Twelve of those make half an *akṣa* (8). Half an *akṣa*, together with four *māṣakas*, is a *suvarṇa* (9). Four *suvarṇas* make a *niṣka* (10). Two *kṛṣṇalas* of equal weight make a silver *māṣaka* (11). Sixteen of those make a *dharaṇa* (12). A copper coin weighing one *karṣa* is a *kārṣāpaṇa* (13).
Two hundred and fifty paṇas are declared to be the first amercement; five hundred should be known as the middle, and one thousand as the highest. ||14||
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Five.

Now, those who have committed mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*), with the exception of Brāhmaṇas, are to be executed. (1) No corporal punishment shall be inflicted upon a Brāhmaṇa. (2) A Brāhmaṇa should be banished from his own country after having been branded on the forehead. (3) And for the crime of killing a Brāhmaṇa, one should place the image of a headless man on his forehead. (4) For drinking liquor, the sign of a tavern flag. (5) For theft, the footprint of a dog. (6) For violating the Guru’s bed, the female organ. (7) In other cases of capital offenses as well, one should banish the offender while he remains whole in body and possesses all his property. (8) The king shall put to death those who forge royal edicts. (9) And those who forge written documents. (10) Those who administer poison, arsonists, violent robbers, and those who kill women, children, or men. (11) And those who steal more than ten *kumbhas* of grain. (12) Or more than a hundred units of goods measured by weight. (13) And those of low birth who covet the kingdom. (14) And those who destroy embankments. (15) And those who provide shelter or food to violent robbers. (16) Except when the king is unable to deal with them. (17) A woman whose husband is impotent and one who violates him. (18) If a person of lower caste commits an offense against one of higher caste with a particular limb, that very limb of his shall be cut off. (19) One who sits on the same seat [with a superior] shall be branded on the hip and banished. (20) One who spits [on a superior] shall be deprived of both lips. (21) One who breaks wind [against a superior] shall be deprived of the anus. (22) One who reviles [a superior] shall be deprived of the tongue. (23) If one out of pride gives religious instruction [to a superior], the king shall pour boiling oil into his mouth. (24) And if one mentions [a superior's] name or caste with malice, a ten-finger-long spike shall be driven into his tongue. (25) One who speaks falsely regarding sacred learning, country, caste, or occupation shall be fined two hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. (26) Even one who speaks the truth regarding those who are blind, lame, and so forth, shall be fined two *kārṣāpaṇas*. (27) One who slanders his teachers shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. (28) When an accusation of a sin causing loss of caste (*patanīya*) is made against another, the highest fine (*uttamasāhasa*) shall be imposed. (29) If the accusation involves a minor offense (*upapātaka*), the middle fine (*madhyamasāhasa*) shall be imposed. (30) The same applies to slandering those learned in the three Vedas (*traividyavṛddha*). (31) And also to castes and guilds (*jātipūga*). (32) For slandering a village or a district, the first fine (*prathamasāhasa*) shall be imposed. (33) For slandering one who is physically deformed, the first fine shall be imposed. (33) But for slandering [one's] mother, the highest fine shall be imposed. (34) For reviling someone of equal caste, one shall be fined twelve *paṇas*. (35) For reviling someone of lower caste, six *paṇas*. (36) For reviling someone of higher caste at the appropriate time, the fine shall be of that same measure. (37) Or three *kārṣāpaṇas*. (38) The same applies to speaking harsh words. (39) An adulterer, if he approaches a woman of equal caste, shall be fined the highest fine. (40) If he approaches a woman of lower caste, the middle fine. (41) And the same for approaching a cow. (42) If he approaches a woman of the lowest caste (*antyajāti*), he is to be executed. (43) And for approaching domestic animals, he shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. (44) And the same for giving away a girl without disclosing her defects. (45) And he shall maintain her. (46) But one who says a girl is defective when she is not shall be fined the highest fine. (47) One who kills an elephant, a horse, a camel, or a cow shall be deprived of one hand and one foot. (48) One who sells forbidden meat shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. (49) One who kills domestic animals shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. (50) And he shall pay the value of the animal to its owner. (51) One who kills wild animals shall be fined fifty *kārṣāpaṇas*. (52) One who kills birds or fish shall be fined ten *kārṣāpaṇas*. (53) One who destroys insects shall be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa*. (54) One who cuts down a fruit-bearing tree shall be fined the highest fine. (55) One who cuts down a flowering tree shall be fined the middle fine. (56) One who cuts down creepers, shrubs, or climbing plants shall be fined one hundred *kārṣāpaṇas*. (57) One who cuts grass shall be fined one *kārṣāpaṇa*. (58) And all these offenders shall also pay the value of the produce to the owners. (59) One who threatens with the hand shall be fined ten *kārṣāpaṇas*. (60) With the foot, twenty *kārṣāpaṇas*. (61) With a wooden stick, the first fine. (62) With a stone, the middle fine. (63) With a weapon, the highest fine. (64) One who pulls out hair, clothes, or hands, or plucks out a finger, shall be fined ten *paṇas*. (65) One who causes pain without drawing blood shall be fined thirty-two *paṇas*. (66) If blood flows, sixty-four *paṇas*. (67) For breaking a hand, foot, or tooth, or for cutting off an ear or nose, the middle fine shall be imposed. (68) And the same for obstructing movement, eating, or speech. (69) For breaking an eye, the neck, an arm, a thigh, or a shoulder, the highest fine shall be imposed. (70) The king shall not release for life from prison one who destroys both eyes of another. (71) Or he may inflict a similar injury upon him. (72) When many people strike one person, the fine for each shall be double that which has been stated. (73) The same applies to those standing nearby who do not run to the aid of one crying out. (74) All those who cause injury to a person shall pay the expenses for his recovery. (75) And the same for those who injure domestic animals. (76) One who steals an ox, a horse, a camel, or an elephant shall be deprived of one hand and one foot. (77) One who steals a goat or a sheep shall be deprived of one hand. (78) One who steals grain shall be fined eleven times its value. (79) And the same for one who steals standing crops. (80) One who steals gold, silver, or clothing exceeding fifty [in value] shall be deprived of a hand. (81) If it is less than that, he shall be fined eleven times its value. (82) One who steals thread, cotton, cow-dung, curds, milk, buttermilk, molasses, grass, salt, earth, ashes, fish, birds, oil, meat, clarified butter, honey, bamboo vessels, clay vessels, or iron vessels shall be fined twice their value. (83) And the same for cooked food. (84) For stealing flowers, green vegetables, shrubs, creepers, or climbing plants, five *kṛṣṇalas*. (85) And the same for leafy vegetables, roots
A man may eat for a year whatever fruit happens to be available;
whether that earth be only the size of a cow-hide, or small, or even vast—[it all matters not]. (184)
When two men dispute over a pledge that has been deposited with them, the one whose possession is established by usage has the stronger claim, provided it was made without force. (185)
But when property has been properly enjoyed for a long time with possession accompanied by title, the possessor acquires it; that may never be taken away from him. 186.

Whatever property was enjoyed by the father in accordance with the practice of enjoyment and according to dharma—when he has died, no objection can be raised against that, for it was acquired by him through such enjoyment. ||187||
But if land has been enjoyed by three persons in due order according to the law, even in the absence of documentary evidence, a fourth person may acquire it there. ||188||
In the killing of those with claws, those with horns, those with fangs, or assassins, as well as elephants, horses, and others, the killer incurs no fault. (189)
Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or a learned Brahmin, one should indeed kill an approaching assassin without hesitation. (190)
No fault whatsoever attaches to the slayer for killing an assassin, whether done openly or in secret; in such a case, it is fury that meets fury.
One who raises a sword, poison, or fire; likewise one who holds a curse ready in hand;
one who kills by means of Atharvan rites; and a slanderer among kings.

And one who violates his wife—these seven are indeed assassins (ātatāyin); others say that those who seize one's reputation or livelihood, as well as those who take away one's dharma or wealth, are also such. (193)
I have described to you in brief this method of punishment for all offenses, which otherwise would be excessively detailed. (194)
Regarding other offenses as well, having ascertained the caste, wealth, and age [of the offender], the king shall determine the punishment after consulting with Brahmins. (195)
One who releases a person deserving of punishment shall incur a fine double that of the offense;
and one who, though appointed, inflicts punishment upon those who do not deserve it, is the lowest of men. (196)
That king in whose city there is no thief, no adulterer, no speaker of evil words, and no perpetrator of violence or one who strikes with impunity, shares the world of Śakra.
Thus ends the fifth chapter, on Punishment, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Six.

Now, the creditor shall recover from the debtor the wealth as it was lent. (1) Two, three, four, or five percent per month, according to the order of the castes. (2) Or, all castes may pay the interest as agreed upon by themselves. (3) Even if not previously stipulated, [interest] shall be paid at the end of the year as prescribed. (4) There is no interest on the use of a pledge. (5) The creditor shall restore the pledge if it is lost, except in cases of damage caused by fate or the king. (6) This applies even when the final interest has been reached. (7) An immovable pledge shall not be forfeited except by specific agreement. (8) That immovable property which was given solely for the purpose of securing the repayment of the debt shall be restored once the debt has been repaid. (9) Interest ceases to accrue beyond this point if the creditor does not accept the wealth being offered. (10) The maximum interest on gold is double the principal. (11) On cloth, it is triple. (12) On grain, it is quadruple. (13) On liquids, it is eightfold. (14) For female slaves and cattle, the offspring constitutes the interest. (15) For yeast, cotton, thread, leather, armor, weapons, bricks, and charcoal, the interest is inexhaustible. (16) For items not mentioned, the interest is double. (17) One recovering the lent wealth by any means whatsoever shall not be subject to reproach by the king. (18) If the debtor, while being pursued for recovery, approaches the king, he shall be fined an amount equal to the debt. (19) If the creditor goes to the king, the debtor, having been proven in court, shall pay to the king a fine equal to one-tenth of the wealth. (20) And the creditor, having recovered the wealth, shall pay a twentieth part to the king. (21) One who denies the whole debt shall pay the whole, even if proven only in part. (22) There are three means of proof for such a case: a written document, witnesses, and an ordeal. (23) What was received in the presence of witnesses must be returned in the presence of witnesses. (24) When the entry of the debt has been made into the document, the creditor shall cause the document to be rewritten. (25) In the case of partial payment or the absence of the document, the creditor shall provide a receipt written in his own hand. (26) If the debtor is dead, has become an ascetic, or has been abroad for twenty years, the debt shall be paid by his sons or grandsons. (27) Beyond that, they need not pay if they do not wish to. (28) Whether there is a son or no son, the heir to the estate shall pay the debt. (29) In the case of one who has no wealth, the husband of the woman shall pay. (30) A wife is not liable for a debt contracted by her husband or son. (31) Nor are a husband or son liable for a debt contracted by the wife. (32) A father is not liable for a debt contracted by his son. (33) He among undivided kinsmen who remains in the household shall pay the debt contracted by them. (34) A debt incurred by a father belongs to the undivided brothers. (35) Divided brothers shall each pay a share proportionate to their respective inheritance. (36) The husband shall pay the debts of a cowherd, a vintner, an actor, a washerman, a hunter, or a woman. (37) What is admitted by word of mouth need not be paid. (38) Nor need be paid what was contracted for the sake of another's family. (39)
He who, having previously taken a loan on equal terms with the agreement that he would repay it the next day, does not pay it later out of greed, shall incur interest for that very day. ||40||
Suretyship is prescribed for appearance, for testimony, and for payment;
however, in the case of the first two failing, the debt must be paid by the sons of the other [the surety for payment]. (41)

If there are many sureties, they shall pay the debt according to the agreement; however, if no specific share has been assigned among them, the payment shall be made according to the will of the creditor.
Whatever amount the surety may pay when pressured by the creditor, the debtor ought to pay that same amount doubled to the surety. (43)
Thus ends the sixth chapter, concerning debts, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seven.

Now, a document is of three kinds: [1] witnessed by the king, [2] with witnesses, and [3] without witnesses. [2] A document executed in the royal court by a scribe appointed by him, and marked with the hand-signature of its presiding officer, is "witnessed by the king. [3] One written anywhere by anyone, and marked with the hand-signatures of witnesses, is "with witnesses. [4] One written in one's own hand is "without witnesses. [5] That which is produced under duress is not authoritative. [6] And all those executed through fraud are likewise invalid. [7] Even a document with witnesses is invalid if it is marked by a witness who has performed a censurable act or is otherwise corrupt. [8] And so too is that which is written by a scribe of such a character. [9] Furthermore, a document executed by a woman, a child, one who is not independent, one who is intoxicated, insane, terrified, or afflicted is invalid. [10] Only a document that is not contrary to local custom, which clearly states the authorized characteristics [of the parties], and whose sequence and letters are uncorrupted, is authoritative. [11] Thus ends the section on documents.
One should clear up a doubtful document by means of its colors, the marks made therein, the readings, and logical arguments, using counter-evidence that corresponds to those very arguments.
Wherever the debtor, the creditor, the witness, or even the scribe dies, there that document shall be validated by their own signatures.
Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eight.

Now, those who are not witnesses: [1] Kings, Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*), renunciants (*pravrajita*), gamblers, thieves, those dependent on others, women, children, violent persons, the very aged, the intoxicated, the insane, the accused, the outcastes (*patita*), those afflicted by hunger or thirst, those in distress, those blinded by passion, [2] enemies, friends, relatives, those engaged in forbidden acts, those whose faults have been observed, and accomplices; [3] and one who, though not designated as a witness, comes forward and speaks. [4] A single person may also be a witness. [5] In cases of theft, violence, verbal or physical assault, and adultery, witnesses need not be examined. [6] Now, regarding witnesses: [7] Those of noble birth, endowed with good conduct and wealth, performers of sacrifices, ascetics, those with sons, knowers of the Dharma, students, truthful, and elders learned in the three Vedas. [8] However, even a single person endowed with the aforementioned qualities, if approved by both parties, may serve. [9] When two parties are disputing, the witnesses of that party which has the prior claim (*pūrvavāda*) should be questioned. [10] Where, due to the nature of the matter, the priority belongs to the defendant, there the witnesses of the respondent (*prativādin*) should also be questioned. [11] If the designated witness is dead or has gone abroad, those who heard what was said by him are the authority. [12] A witness is so called because of having seen or heard something in person. [13] Witnesses are purified by truth. [14] But where there is the execution of members of the [first] four castes (*varṇa*), they are purified by falsehood. [15] To purify himself from that, a twice-born man (*dvija*) should offer oblations into the fire with the *Kūṣmāṇḍī* verses. [16] And a Śūdra should give for one day the fodder of ten cows. [17] One should recognize a false witness by a change in natural disposition, a loss of facial color, or incoherent speech. [18] Having summoned the witnesses at sunrise, he should question them after they have taken an oath. [19] He should ask a Brāhmaṇa, "Speak! [20] A Kṣatriya, "Speak the truth! [21] A Vaiśya, "By means of cattle, seed, and gold! [22] And a Śūdra, "By all sins! [23] And he should cause the witnesses to hear this: [24] "Those worlds which belong to great sinners and those which belong to minor sinners, those belong also to false witnesses. [25] Furthermore, there is the loss of merit performed between birth and death. [26] By truth the sun shines. [27] By truth the moon gleams. [28] By truth the wind blows. [29] By truth the earth supports [all]. [30] By truth the waters remain steady. [31] And the sky by truth. [32] By truth the fire [burns]. [33] By truth the gods [exist]. [34] By truth the sacrifices [are established]. [35]
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale;
indeed, truth alone outweighed a thousand horse-sacrifices. (36)
For those who, though knowing the truth, remain silent and sit by as witnesses, [are likewise at fault].
They are equal to false witnesses in their sin, and likewise in their punishment.
In this manner, the king should question the witnesses according to the order of their castes. ||38||
He whose witnesses declare his claim to be true shall be the victor;
he who speaks otherwise shall certainly suffer defeat. (39)

In a conflict between witnesses, O Lord of Men, the king should accept the majority; when they are equal in number, he should accept those distinguished by their virtues; and when there is a conflict between those equally virtuous, he should accept the best among the twice-born.
In whatever legal dispute a false witness should speak untruth, that very matter shall be reversed; even if it has been completed, it shall be as if uncompleted. (41)
Thus ends the eighth chapter, on witnesses, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Nine.

Now, the procedure for the ordeal (*samayakriyā*). [1] In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, it may be administered at will. [2] In cases of deposits, gold, and theft, the value of the object shall determine the ordeal. [3] In all such matters involving wealth, one should calculate the value in gold. [4] In that regard, for a debt of less than one *kṛṣṇala*, one should cause a Śūdra to swear by holding blades of *dūrvā* grass. [5] For less than two *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding sesame seeds. [6] For less than three *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding silver. [7] For less than four *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding gold. [8] For less than five *kṛṣṇalas*, by holding earth taken from a furrow. [9] For a debt of half a *suvarṇa* or more, the Śūdra must undergo the ordeal of the sacred water-pot (*kośa*). [10] Beyond that, according to the circumstances, one of the ordeals of the balance, fire, water, or poison shall be used. [11] When the amount in dispute is double, the same procedure for the ordeal as prescribed applies to a Vaiśya. [12] When it is triple, to a Kṣatriya. [13] When it is quadruple, to a Brāhmaṇa. [14] One should not administer the ordeal of the sacred water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa. [15] Except when it is for the purpose of establishing a formal agreement for future times. [16] In place of the water-pot ordeal, one should cause a Brāhmaṇa to swear by holding earth taken from a furrow. [17] If a person has been previously seen to be guilty of a crime, even in a small matter, one should cause him to undergo one of the divine ordeals. [18] But if he is known to be virtuous and of good character, even in a great matter, he should not be subjected to them. [19] The plaintiff shall pay the fee for the head-ordeal (the fee for the performance of the ordeal). [20] And the defendant shall undergo the ordeal. [21] In cases of treason against the king and acts of violence, it may be administered even without the payment of the fee. [22] The balance ordeal should be given to women, Brāhmaṇas, the infirm, the incapacitated, and the sick. [23] And that [balance] should not be used when the wind is blowing. [24] Fire should not be administered to lepers, the incapacitated, or blacksmiths. [25] Nor during autumn or summer. [26] Poison should not be administered to lepers, those of bilious temperament, or Brāhmaṇas. [27] Nor during the rainy season. [28] Water should not be administered to those afflicted by phlegmatic diseases, the timid, those suffering from asthma or cough, those who live by water, or during the winter and early spring. [29-30] The ordeal of the sacred water-pot should not be administered to atheists. [31] Nor in a region afflicted by disease or pestilence. [32]
Having summoned one who has fasted since sunrise and bathed with his clothes on, he should cause all the ordeals to be performed in the presence of the gods and Brahmins. (33)
Thus ends the ninth chapter, on the section concerning conventions, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Ten.

Now, the balance (*dhaṭa*): [It shall be] four cubits high and two cubits wide. (2) Therein, a scale made from a solid wood, five cubits long, with a sling on each side, [shall be used]. (3) Any one among merchants, goldsmiths, or brazier-makers shall maintain it. (4) And there, he shall place a man in one sling and a counterweight, such as a stone, in the second. (5) Having ensured that the counterweight and the man are held equally balanced and having marked them clearly, he shall cause the man to descend. (6) He shall take hold of the balance according to the established rule, as shall the keeper of the scale. (7–8)
Whatever worlds are ordained for the slayer of a Brahmin, and whatever worlds for a false witness—those same worlds belong to the one who holds the scales while bearing false weight. (9)
By the words of this Dharma discourse, you are called the "Balance" (dhaṭa).
You alone, O Balance, know those things which human beings do not understand. (10)
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, is being weighed against you;
therefore, you ought to save him from this doubt in accordance with dharma. (11)
Then he should place that man back onto the scale once more;
if, when weighed, he increases [in weight], then he is pure according to the law.
In the event of the rope breaking or the axle snapping, one should place the man back on the scale once more;
thus, through this doubt-free knowledge, a definitive conclusion is reached. ||13||
Thus ends the tenth chapter, concerning the ordeal of the balance, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eleven.

Now, regarding the fire ordeal: ||1|| One should prepare seven circles with a distance between them of sixteen finger-breadths each. ||2|| Then, one facing east with both arms extended, one should place seven *aśvattha* leaves in the hands. ||3|| These, together with the two hands, should be bound with a cord. ||4|| Then, one should place therein an iron ball, glowing with the color of fire, weighing fifty palas and being perfectly round. ||5|| Taking it up, one should walk through the circles, placing the foot neither too quickly nor too slowly. ||6|| Then, having passed the seventh circle, one should drop the iron ball upon the ground. ||7||
If he should be burnt anywhere, one should designate him as impure;
but that man who is not burnt in any way whatsoever shall be pure. (8)
If one should cause [the metal] to fall out of fear, or if it is burnt and cannot be discerned, he must have that metal brought back again because the covenant has not been purified. (9)
At the very beginning, one should observe his hands as they handle crushed grains;
then, having consecrated a lump of iron with mantras, one should place it upon his hands.
O Agni, you move within all beings like a witness;
O Agni, you alone understand those things which human beings do not know. ||11||
This man, accused in a legal proceeding, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to save him from this doubt in accordance with dharma. (12)
Thus ends the eleventh chapter, on Purification, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.

Chapter Twelve: Now, regarding the water ordeal. [The accused shall enter] into water that is free from mud, moss, wicked crocodiles, fish, leeches, and the like. (2) Therein, while another person—free from passion or hatred—holds his knees so that he does not sink below the navel, he shall enter the consecrated water. (3) At that same moment, another person shall discharge an arrow from a bow that is neither too stiff nor too soft. (4) And yet another person shall swiftly retrieve that arrow. (5)
That which is not seen in the midst of those [elements] is proclaimed to be pure;
otherwise, it would be impure upon the sight of even a single component. (6)
You move within the waters of all beings like a witness;
you alone know those waters which human beings do not know.
This man, accused in a legal dispute, is sinking into you;
therefore, you ought to rescue him from this peril according to the Dharma. (8)
Thus ends the twelfth chapter on the ordeal by water in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.

Chapter Thirteen: Now, concerning poison. (1) All poisons are not to be administered. (2) With the exception of the śārṅga poison originating from the Himālaya mountains. (3) And one should give seven grains of that [poison], soaked in clarified butter, to the accused. (4)
If the poison, free from its violent onset and exhaustion, is digested easily, then knowing it to be pure, one should release it at the end of the day. (5)
Because you are poison and because you are uneven, you are cruel toward all embodied beings;
O Poison, you alone know those things which human beings do not understand.
"This man, accused in a legal dispute, desires purification;
therefore, you ought to save him from this uncertainty in accordance with dharma. (7)
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter, on the ordeal by poison, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Fourteen:

Now, the ordeal by sacred libation (kośa). [1] Having worshipped fierce deities, one shall drink three handfuls of water from their bathing-vessel. [2] Facing the deity, one shall declare: "This was not done by me. [3]
Within two weeks, or even three weeks, he will see [the consequences]:
either illness, fire, the death of a kinsman, or perhaps a royal affliction.
One should recognize that as impure, and likewise pure in the opposite case;
a righteous king should honor the person found pure in matters concerning divine ordeals.
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, concerning the ordeal by sacred libation, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Fifteen.

Now, there are twelve kinds of sons. 1. The first is the *aurasa* (legitimate) son, begotten by oneself upon one’s own wedded wife. 2. The second is the *kṣetraja* (field-born) son, begotten upon the wedded wife by a *sapiṇḍa* or by a man of a higher caste who has been authorized [to do so]. 3. The third is the son of an appointed daughter (*putrikāputra*). 4. She is called an *appointed daughter* whom her father gives away with the stipulation, "The son born of her shall be my son. 5. Even one not formally given away according to the rite of appointment is considered an *appointed daughter* if she has no brother. 6. The fourth is the *paunarbhava* (son of a remarried woman). 7. A *punarbhū* (remarried woman) is one who, being previously unmarried (*akṣatā*), undergoes the marriage ceremony again. 8. Furthermore, one who was previously married to another, even if not formally remarried, is also a *punarbhū*. 9. The fifth is the *kānīna* (maiden-born) son. 10. He is begotten by a man upon an unmarried girl in her father’s house. 11. And he belongs to the man who takes her hand in marriage (*pāṇigrāha*). 12. The sixth is the son secretly born in the house. 13. He belongs to him whose wife gave birth to him. 14. The seventh is the *sahoḍha* (son received with the bride). 15. He is the son of a woman who is married while already pregnant. 16. And he belongs to the man who took her hand in marriage. 17. The eighth is the *dattaka* (adopted son). 18. And he belongs to the one to whom he is given by his mother and father. 19. The ninth is the *krīta* (bought) son. 20. And he belongs to the one by whom he was bought. 21. The tenth is the *svayamupagata* (self-offered) son. 22. And he belongs to the one to whom he has offered himself. 23. The eleventh is the *apaviddha* (cast-off) son. 24. He is one abandoned by his father and mother. 25. And he belongs to the one who takes him in. 26. The twelfth is the son begotten on any woman whatsoever. 27. Among these, each preceding one is superior to the next. 28. That very one is the heir to the inheritance. 29. And he shall maintain the others. 30. He should provide the sacramental rites for unmarried daughters in accordance with his own wealth. 31. But those who are outcasts (*patita*), impotent (*klība*), incurably diseased, or deformed are not entitled to a share of the inheritance. 32. They must be maintained by those who take the inheritance. 33. Only their legitimate sons (*aurasa*) are entitled to a share of the inheritance. 34. But not the son of an outcast. 35. However, if the act causing loss of caste was committed unintentionally, sons born subsequently are entitled to a share. 36. Those born of women in the inverse order of castes (*pratiloma*) are not entitled to a share. 37. Their sons are likewise not entitled to a share of the grandfather's property. 38. They must be maintained by those who take the inheritance. 39. Whoever takes the inheritance is the one who offers the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*). 40. Even among women married to different men, the son of one is the son of all. 41. And this applies to brothers born of the same father. 42. A son shall offer the funeral cake even if he does not receive a portion of the paternal estate. 43. [End of Section 1]
Because a son protects his father from the hell named Put, he was therefore called "putra" by the Self-Existent One himself. (44)
In this son, the father pays off his debt and attains immortality, provided that he beholds the face of his born son while the son is still living. (45)
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains infinity;
and through the grandson of a son, one reaches the realm of the Sun. (46) In this world, no distinction exists between a son and a daughter’s son;
for the daughter’s son delivers one who has no son, just like a son. (47)
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter, concerning the specific types of sons, in the Dharmaśāstra of Viṣṇu.
Chapter Sixteen.

Sons born of women of the same caste as their fathers are of that same caste. (1) Sons born of women in the direct order of castes (anuloma) take the caste of their mothers. (2) Sons born of women in the inverse order of castes (pratiloma) are despised by the noble. (3) Among them, the son of a Vaiśya woman by a Śūdra is an Āyogava. (4) The Pulkasa and the Māgadha are the sons of a Kṣatriya woman by a Vaiśya and a Śūdra respectively. (5) The Caṇḍāla, the Vaidehaka, and the Sūta are the sons of a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, and a Kṣatriya respectively. (6) The mixed castes resulting from further intermixture are innumerable. (7) The profession of the Āyogavas is entering the arena (to perform as wrestlers or actors). (8) The profession of the Pulkasas is hunting. (9) The profession of the Māgadhas is the composition of panegyrics. (10) The profession of the Caṇḍālas is executing those condemned to death. (11) The protection of women and making a living thereby is the profession of the Vaidehakas. (12) The profession of the Sūtas is charioteering of horses. (13) The specific rule for the Caṇḍālas is that they must live outside the village and wear the clothes of the dead. (14) For all these castes, marriage is with women of their own caste. (15) And they shall inherit the property of their own fathers. (16)
These castes resulting from intermixture, as indicated by their fathers and mothers, are to be known—whether they are concealed or manifest—by their own respective actions. ||17||

The unconditioned sacrifice of one’s body for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, and the protection of women and children, is the cause of purification for those of the outer castes. (18)
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter, concerning the duties of those born of mixed castes, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventeen.

If a father divides his property among his sons, he may do so according to his own will regarding wealth acquired by himself. (1) But in the case of ancestral property, the ownership of the father and the son is equal. (2) Those who have been divided from their father shall give a share to one born after the partition. (3) The wealth of a sonless man goes to his wife. (4) In her absence, it goes to his daughters. (5) In their absence, it goes to his father. (6) In his absence, it goes to his mother. (7) In her absence, it goes to his brothers. (8) In their absence, it goes to his brother’s sons. (9) In their absence, it goes to his paternal kinsmen (*bandhu*). (10) In their absence, it goes to his *sakulyas* (distant agnates). (11) In their absence, it goes to his fellow students. (12) In their absence, with the exception of the property of a Brāhmaṇa, it goes to the King. (13) The property of a Brāhmaṇa belongs only to other Brāhmaṇas. (14) The wealth of a forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) shall be taken by his preceptor. (15) Or by his pupil. (16)
But a reunited coparcener shall give and take the share of one who was reunited; likewise, a uterine brother [shall do so] for a uterine brother, both for one born and for one deceased. (17)

What is given by the father, mother, son, or brother; what is received before the nuptial fire; what is given upon supersession; what is given by a kinsman; the bride-price; and what is given subsequently—these constitute the woman’s property (strīdhana). (18) In the case of the four forms of marriage beginning with the Brāhma, if she dies without offspring, that property belongs to her husband. (19) In the remaining [forms of marriage], the father shall take it. (20) In all cases, however, whatever wealth she has acquired after bearing children goes to the daughter. (21)
Whatever ornaments may have been worn by women while their husband was alive, the heirs shall not divide them; those who do so fall from their caste.
But for those who have many fathers, the allotment of shares is according to the father;
whatever paternal inheritance belongs to one, he shall take that, and not another. (23)
Thus ends the seventeenth chapter, concerning the division of inheritance, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eighteen.

If a Brāhmaṇa should have sons from wives of the four castes, they shall divide the paternal inheritance into ten parts. Of these, the son of the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take four shares; the son of the Kṣatriyā wife, three; the son of the Vaiśyā wife, two shares; and the son of the Śūdrā wife, one. (1–5) Now, if there should be three sons of a Brāhmaṇa, excluding the son of the Śūdrā wife, they shall then divide that wealth into nine parts. They shall take the shares assigned according to the order of the castes, consisting of four, three, and two parts respectively. (6–7) Excluding the Vaiśyā, from the wealth divided into eight parts, they shall take four, three, and one share respectively. (8) Excluding the Kṣatriyā, from the wealth divided into seven parts, they shall take four, two, and one. (9) Excluding the Brāhmaṇī, from the wealth divided into six parts, they shall take three, two, and one. (10) This same division applies to the sons of a Kṣatriya born of Kṣatriyā, Vaiśyā, and Śūdrā wives. (11) Now, if a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya, then from the wealth divided into seven parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares and the Rājanya (Kṣatriya) three. (12–13) If a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Vaiśya, then from the wealth divided into six parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares and the Vaiśya two. (14–15) If a Brāhmaṇa should have two sons, a Brāhmaṇa and a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into five parts. The Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares and the Śūdra one. (16–18) If a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya, then they shall divide that wealth into five parts. The Kṣatriya shall take three shares and the Vaiśya two. (19–21) If a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya should have two sons, a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into four parts. The Kṣatriya shall take three shares and the Śūdra one. (22–24) If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya should have two sons, a Vaiśya and a Śūdra, then they shall divide that wealth into three parts. The Vaiśya shall take two shares and the Śūdra one. (25–27) If a Brāhmaṇa has only one son, whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, that son takes the entire estate. (28) For a Kṣatriya, it is the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya sons. (29) For a Vaiśya, it is the Vaiśya son. (30) For a Śūdra, it is the Śūdra son. (31) But for the twice-born, a Śūdra who is the only son inherits half. (32) The fate of the property of one who dies without a son is the same as that of the second half in this case. (33) Mothers receive a share corresponding to the share of their sons. (34) So too do unmarried daughters. (35) Sons of the same caste shall take equal shares. (36) To the eldest, they shall give an excellent additional portion (*uddhāra*). (37) If there should be two sons of a Brāhmaṇī wife and one son of a Śūdrā wife, then from the property divided into nine parts, the two Brāhmaṇī sons shall take eight shares and the Śūdrā son one. (38) Now, if there should be two sons of a Śūdrā wife and one son of a Brāhmaṇī wife, then from the property divided into six parts, the Brāhmaṇa shall take four shares and the two Śūdrā sons two shares. (39) In this manner, the allotment of shares is determined in other cases as well. (40)
If those who were divided while living together should divide again, the division in that case shall be equal; there, the right of primogeniture does not exist. (41)
That which has been acquired through one's own labor without depleting the paternal estate, being obtained by one's own effort—that one is not obliged to give away unless one so desires. //42//
But when one recovers ancestral property that was previously unobtained, he need not share it with his sons if he so desires, as it was acquired by himself. (43)
Clothing, vehicles, ornaments, prepared food, water, women, the management of property and security, and books are not to be divided. (44)
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter, on the Partition of Inheritance, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Nineteen.

One should not have a deceased twice-born man carried out by a Śūdra (1). Nor a Śūdra by a twice-born man (2). Sons should carry out their father and mother (3), but Śūdras should not carry out even a twice-born father (4). Those Brāhmaṇas who carry out a Brāhmaṇa who is without a protector partake of the heavenly world (5). Having carried out the deceased relative and performed the cremation, they should approach the funeral pyre from the left and perform an immersion in water while still wearing their clothes (6). Having offered the water libation for the deceased, they should offer a single rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) upon *kuśa* grass (7). Having changed their garments, bitten neem leaves, and placed their footprints upon a stone at the doorway, they should enter the house (8). They should also throw unbroken grains (*akṣata*) into the fire (9). On the fourth day, they should perform the collection of the bones (10). And these should be cast into the waters of the Gaṅgā (11).
For as many thousands of years as the number of bones of a person remain in the waters of the Gaṅgā, for that long he dwells in the heavenly world. ||12||

For as long as the period of impurity lasts, they shall offer water and funeral cakes (piṇḍa) for the deceased. (13) They shall subsist on food that is purchased or obtained [unasked]. (14) And they shall abstain from eating meat. (15) They shall sleep on the bare ground. (16) And they shall sleep separately. (17) Having gone out of the village at the end of the period of impurity, having had their hair and beards shaved, having bathed with a paste of sesame or a paste of mustard seeds, and having changed their clothes, they shall enter the house. (18) There, having performed a rite of pacification, they shall perform the worship of the Brahmins. (19) The gods are the invisible gods; the Brahmins are the visible gods. (20) By the Brahmins, the worlds are sustained. (21)
By the grace of the brahmins, the deities abide in heaven;
the word spoken by a brahmin never becomes false anywhere.
Whatever the Brahmins, being most satisfied, declare,
that the deities welcome;
when they are satisfied, [the deities] are constantly satisfied.
The gods who are beyond perception [are superior] to the gods who are perceptible. ||23||
Those of undaunted spirit should offer consolation to those afflicted by suffering who have lost their kinsmen;
O Earth, I shall describe to you the words with which they should do so.
I [uttered] those words which were pleasing to the mind.
Thus ends the nineteenth chapter, concerning the removal of the deceased, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Twenty.

That which is the northern course (of the sun) is day for the gods; the southern course is night. A year is a day and night [for Brahmā]. Thirty such [days] make a month. Twelve months make a year. Twelve hundred divine years constitute the Kali Yuga. Twice that is the Dvāpara Yuga. Thrice that is the Tretā Yuga. Four times that is the Kṛta Yuga. Twelve thousand divine years constitute a cycle of four Yugas (Caturyuga). Seventy-one cycles of four Yugas make a Manvantara. One thousand cycles of four Yugas make a Kalpa. And that is one day of Pitāmaha (Brahmā). His night is of equal duration. By calculating months and years according to such days and nights, the lifespan of the entire Brahmā is one hundred years. A single day of Puruṣa is delimited by the lifespan of Brahmā. At its conclusion is a Mahākalpa. His night is of exactly the same duration. There is no counting the number of past days and nights of Puruṣa, nor of those yet to come, because time is without beginning or end.
Thus, in this supportless time that flows on incessantly, I do not perceive any such thing that might have a permanent stability. (22)
The grains of sand in the Ganges and the showers of rain when Indra pours them down can be counted in this world, but the number of past Grandfathers cannot.
In every eon, fourteen lords of the gods perish,
as do the fourteen Manus who are the foremost in all the worlds.
Many thousands of Indras and millions of lords of the Daityas have perished here through time; what then can be said of mere mortals? (25)
And many royal sages, endowed with all virtues, as well as divine and brahminical sages, have passed away in the course of time. ||26||
Even those who are capable of being the cause of creation and destruction in this world are led away by time; for time is indeed difficult to overcome.
Overwhelmed by time, every living being is led to the next world; since a creature subsists on the path of karma, what cause for lamentation is there in that? (28)
For one who is born, death is certain; for one who has died, birth is certain.
Since this matter is unavoidable, there is no help to be found in this world. (29)
Since grieving people do not benefit the deceased here in this world, one should not grieve; rather, the funeral rites for him should be performed according to one's ability.
For one who departs with both good deeds and evil deeds as his two companions, what need has he for kinsmen, whether they grieve or not? (31)
While the period of impurity for his kinsmen lasts, the deceased finds no rest;
therefore, he approaches precisely those who offer the funeral cakes and water. (32)
One who has died remains a *preta* until the *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite is performed;
offer food along with a water-pot to him who has gone to the world of the *pretas*.
When one has gone to the world of the ancestors, he eats food at the śrāddha that is equal to nectar;
therefore, offer the śrāddha for him who has gone to the world of the ancestors. (34)
Whether in the state of a deity, in a place of torment, in the animal realm, or likewise in the human state, one receives the śrāddha offered by one's own kinsmen. (35)
When a śrāddha is performed, nourishment for both the deceased and the performer of the śrāddha is certain.
Therefore, having abandoned useless grief, one should always perform the śrāddha. (36)
Only this much should always be done for the deceased by his kinsmen; a man should not help the dead by grieving, which is of benefit only to himself. (37)
Seeing that the world is without refuge and that even one's kinsmen die,
O men, always choose the Dharma alone as your companion.
Even when a man has died, his kinsmen are unable to follow him;
for, with the exception of the wife, the path to Yama diverges for everyone. (39)
Dharma alone follows him wherever he may go;
indeed, in this essence-less triple world, practice Dharma without delay! (40)
One should do tomorrow's work today, and the afternoon's task in the forenoon;
for death does not wait to see whether one's work is finished or unfinished. 41.
Death seizes and departs with one who is attached to fields, shops, and houses, and whose mind is directed elsewhere, just as a she-wolf seizes a lamb. (42)
Time has no one dear to it, nor is there anyone it hates;
when the karma that sustains life is exhausted, it forcibly carries away the person.
One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows;
but one whose time has arrived does not live, even if merely touched by the tip of a blade of kusha grass. 44.
Neither medicines, nor mantras, nor fire-offerings, nor even recitations can protect a human being who is overtaken by death or even by old age. (45)
For even with hundreds of remedies, one cannot avert a future misfortune that is destined to come; what lamentation can there be in such a case? (46)
Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows, so too does the fruit of past actions unfailingly find its doer. 47.
Beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, O Bhārata, and unmanifest again in their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this? (48)
Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it attain another body; the wise man is not deluded by this. 49.
Just as a person here takes up a garment after discarding one previously worn, so too does the embodied soul, bound by its karma, take up a new body. (50)
Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it;
water does not moisten it, nor does the wind dry it. (51)
This [Self] is indestructible, it cannot be burned, it cannot be moistened, and it cannot be dried away;
it is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient.
This Self is said to be unmanifest, unthinkable, and unchangeable;
therefore, having known it thus, you ought not to grieve.
Thus ends the twentieth chapter, on the Instruction for the Welfare [of Others], in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Twenty-One.

Then, upon the passing of the period of impurity, having bathed well, having thoroughly washed his hands and feet, and having sipped water (performed *ācamana*), he should feed Brāhmaṇas of such a kind as himself, facing north, according to his ability, after honoring them with perfumes, garlands, garments, ornaments, and so forth. (1) In the *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, one should modify the mantras by using the singular number. (2) Near the remains of the food, one should offer a single *piṇḍa* (rice ball) using the name and *gotra* of the deceased. (3) When the Brāhmaṇas have eaten and have been honored with sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and when the water for the inexhaustible offering has been given with the name and *gotra* of the deceased, one should make three trenches—four finger-breadths wide, that deep, and that much apart, each one span long. (4) Having established three fires near the trenches and strewn grass around them, one should offer three oblations into each fire. (5) "To Soma, accompanied by the ancestors, Svadhā! Adoration! (6) "To Agni, the bearer of the *kavya*, Svadhā! Adoration! (7) "To Yama, the descendant of Aṅgiras, Svadhā! Adoration! (8) And in these three places, one should perform the offering of the *piṇḍas* as before. (9) Having filled the three trenches with rice, curd, ghee, honey, and meat, one should mutter: "This is for you. (10) One should perform this in the same manner every month on the anniversary of the death. (11) At the end of the year, one should feed Brāhmaṇas, beginning with those representing the gods, for the deceased, his father, his grandfather, and his great-grandfather. (12) In this case, one should perform the preparation of the fire (*agnaukaraṇa*), the invocation (*āvāhana*), and the offering of water for the feet (*pādya*). (13) With the mantra "May the earth unite you" and "The common [ancestors]...", one should join the vessel of the deceased with the three vessels of the ancestors. (14) Near the remains of the food, one should prepare four *piṇḍas*. (15) After the Brāhmaṇas have sipped water and have been given their sacrificial fees, one should follow them and bid them farewell. (16) Then, one should place the *piṇḍa* of the deceased into the three *piṇḍas*, just as one did with the water from the vessel for the feet. (17) The same applies even in the vicinity of the three trenches. (18) The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite should be performed on the twelfth day after performing the monthly *śrāddhas*, or on the thirteenth day. (19) For Śūdras, it is performed on the twelfth day, excluding the recitation of mantras. (20) If an intercalary month (*adhimāsa*) occurs within the year, one should increase the day for the purpose of the monthly rites by one. (21)
The sapindikarana rite for women should be performed in this same manner;
likewise, one should perform the śrāddha annually for as long as one lives.
For one whose *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* has been performed before the completion of a year,
one should also give food along with a water-pot to a twice-born man for the duration of a year.
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter, concerning the Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa rite, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Twenty-Two.

1. For a Brāhmaṇa, there is impurity for ten days upon the birth or death of a *sapiṇḍa*. 2. For a Kṣatriya, it is twelve days. 3. For a Vaiśya, it is fifteen days. 4. For a Śūdra, it is one month. 5. And *sapiṇḍa*-relationship ceases with the seventh person (in the genealogy). 6. During a period of impurity, the performance of fire-offerings (*homa*), giving, receiving gifts, and Vedic study are suspended. 7. One should not eat the food of anyone during their period of impurity. 8. If one eats the food even once while a Brāhmaṇa or others are in a state of impurity, he remains impure for as long as they are. 9. Upon the cessation of the impurity, he should perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). 10. A twice-born man who has eaten during the impurity of a person of his own caste, having gone to a flowing river and submerged therein, should mutter the *Aghamarṣaṇa* verse three times and, having emerged, mutter the *Gāyatrī* eight thousand times. 11. But a Brāhmaṇa, having eaten during the impurity of a Kṣatriya, becomes pure by fasting for this same period and performing the aforementioned rite. 12. And a Kṣatriya [becomes pure] during the impurity of a Vaiśya in the same manner. 13. A Brāhmaṇa, having eaten during the impurity of a Vaiśya, shall fast for three nights. 14. A Kṣatriya, having eaten during the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Vaiśya, having eaten during the impurity of a Kṣatriya, shall go to a flowing river and mutter five hundred *Gāyatrīs*. 15. And a Vaiśya, having eaten during the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, shall mutter eight hundred *Gāyatrīs*. 16. A twice-born man, having eaten during the impurity of a Śūdra, shall perform the *Prājāpatya* penance. 17. And a Śūdra, having eaten during the impurity of a twice-born man, shall perform a ritual bath. 18. A Śūdra, having eaten during the impurity of another Śūdra, shall bathe and drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). 19. For wives and male slaves born in the direct order of castes, the impurity is equal to that of their master. 20. When the master is deceased, they shall observe their own respective periods of impurity. 21. For those of lower castes, in the case of *sapiṇḍas* of higher castes, purification occurs at the end of the impurity of the latter. 22. For a Brāhmaṇa, in the case of *sapiṇḍas* who are Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras, the impurity lasts six nights, three nights, and one night respectively. 23. For a Kṣatriya, in the case of Vaiśyas and Śūdras, it lasts six nights and three nights respectively. 24. For a Vaiśya, in the case of a Śūdra, it lasts six nights. 25. In the case of a miscarriage, the impurity lasts for a number of days and nights equal to the months of pregnancy. 27. If a child dies before the eruption of teeth, purification is immediate. 28. For such a child, there is neither cremation nor the offering of water. 29. But if the teeth have erupted, yet the tonsure (*cūḍā*) has not been performed, purification is after one day and night. 30. But if the tonsure has been performed, yet the other sacraments (*saṃskāra*) have not been completed, it is after three nights. 31. Beyond that, it is according to the time prescribed for each caste. 32. For women, marriage is the sacrament. 33. In the case of women who have undergone the sacrament of marriage, there is no impurity on the paternal side. 34. If their birth or death occurs in the father's house, then there is impurity for one night or three nights. 35. If another birth occurs during the midst of an impurity caused by a birth, then purification occurs at the end of the first impurity. 36. If it occurs when only a portion of the night remains, purification is after two days. 37. If it occurs at dawn, purification is after three days. 38. The same rule applies to the death of a relative during an impurity caused by a death. 39. One living in a distant land, hearing of a birth or death while the period of impurity still remains, shall become pure by the remainder of that period. 40. Even if the period of impurity has passed, if it is within a year, purification is after one night. 41. Beyond that, purification is by a ritual bath. 42. Upon the death of a teacher (*ācārya*) or a maternal grandfather, purification is after three nights.
When sons born of other men have been born or have died, and when wives who previously belonged to others have given birth or have died; ||43||

Upon the death of the wife of a teacher (*ācārya*), a son, a sub-teacher (*upādhyāya*), a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, a mother-in-law, a brother-in-law, or a fellow student, if they have passed away, one is impure for one night. (44) The same applies upon the death of the king of one’s own country. (45) And also when a person who is not a *sapinda* relative has died in one’s own house. (46) There is no period of impurity for those who die by leaping from a precipice (*bhṛgu*), by fire, by fasting (*anāśaka*), by water, in battle, by lightning, or killed by the king. (47) There is no impurity for kings while engaged in royal duties. (48) There is no impurity for those observing a vow (*vratin*) while in the state of that vow. (49) There is no impurity for those performing a sacrificial session (*sattra*) while in that session. (50) There is no impurity for artisans while engaged in their craft. (51) There is no impurity for those executing the king’s orders, provided it is by his will. (52) There is no impurity during the consecration of a deity or a wedding, provided the preparations were made beforehand. (53) There is no impurity during a national upheaval. (54) Nor even in times of dire distress. (55) Those who commit suicide and outcasts (*patita*) do not partake in the period of impurity or the water libations. (56) When an outcast dies, a female slave should, on the day of death, overturn a pot with her foot. (57) He who cuts the rope of one who has died by hanging becomes pure through the *taptakṛcchra* penance. (58) The same applies to the one who performs the funeral rites (*saṃskartṛ*) for those who have committed suicide. (59) And also for the one who sheds tears for them. (60) For every deceased person, after shedding tears together with their relatives, one becomes pure by bathing. (61) If the collection of bones (*asthisaṃcaya*) has not yet been performed, one becomes pure by bathing with one's clothes on. (62) A twice-born man (*dvija*), having followed the corpse of a *śūdra*, should go to a river and mutter the *gāyatrī* mantra eight thousand times. (63) In the case of the corpse of a twice-born man, he should mutter it eight hundred times. (64) A *śūdra*, having followed the corpse, should perform a bath. (65) All social classes (*varṇa*) should perform a bath upon coming into contact with the smoke of a funeral pyre. (66) [One should bathe] after sexual intercourse, shaving, a bad dream, blood reaching the throat, vomiting, or purging. (67) And also when a shave (*śmaśrukarma*) has been performed. (68) And having touched one who has touched a corpse, a menstruating woman, a *caṇḍāla*, or a sacrificial post (*yūpa*).
