(69) And having touched the carcass of a five-toed animal—excluding those fit for consumption—or its bone, if it still contains fat. (70) In all these cases of bathing, one must not wear the previous garment without washing it. (71) A menstruating woman becomes pure by bathing on the fourth day. (72) A menstruating woman, having touched another menstruating woman of a lower caste, shall not eat until she is purified. (73) Having touched one of the same caste or of a higher caste, she may eat after bathing. (74) One should sip water (*ācamana*) after sneezing, sleeping, eating, desiring to eat or study, drinking, bathing, spitting, changing clothes, walking on a public road, voiding urine or feces, or touching the bone of a five-toed animal or its fat. (75) And also after conversing with a *caṇḍāla* or a barbarian (*mleccha*). (76) If one is defiled below the navel or on the arms by bodily excretions, liquor, or intoxicants, one becomes pure by washing that limb with earth and water. (77) If defiled elsewhere, one becomes pure by washing that limb with earth and water and then bathing. (78) But if defiled in the eyes, one becomes pure by fasting, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). (79) And also if defiled by the lips. (80)
Fat, semen, blood, marrow, urine, feces, earwax, nasal mucus, nails, phlegm, tears, and rheum of the eyes—these twelve are the impurities of human beings. 81.
Gauḍī, paiṣṭī, and mādhvī are to be known as the three kinds of liquor;
just as one is so are all—none of them should be drunk by the twice-born.
Mādhūka, ikṣu-ṭāṅka, kaula, dates, jackfruit, grape juice, honey-wine (madhvīka), maireya, and that produced from coconut; ||83||
These ten intoxicants are impure for a Brāhmaṇa;
however, a Kṣatriya and a Vaiśya do not incur sin by touching them.
A disciple, however, should perform the funeral rites (pitṛmedha) for his deceased guru;
he becomes pure there after ten nights together with those who partake of the food for the deceased. ||85||
Having carried out the funeral rites for one's own teacher, sub-teacher, father, mother, or guru who has passed away, the one observing the vow is not deprived of his vow. (86)
One who has been initiated shall not offer water libations until the completion of his vow;
but once it is completed, having offered the water libation, he becomes pure after three nights alone. ||87||
Knowledge, austerity, fire, food, earth, mind, water, smearing [with clay], wind, ritual action, the sun, and time are the agents that purify embodied beings. (88)
Of all forms of purity, purity in purpose is declared to be supreme;
for he who is pure in purpose is truly pure, not he who is purified by clay and water. (89)
The wise are purified by patience; those who have committed forbidden acts by giving;
those whose sins are concealed by silent recitation; and those most learned in the Vedas by austerity. (90)

That which requires cleansing is purified by earth and water; a river is purified by its current; a woman whose mind is defiled is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born are purified by renunciation. 91.
The limbs are purified by water; the mind is purified by truth;
the elemental self is purified by knowledge and austerity; and the intellect is purified by wisdom. ||92||
This determination regarding the purification of the body has been declared to you;
now hear the determination regarding the purification of various kinds of objects.
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter, on the determination of impurity, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Twenty-Three.

That which is defiled by bodily impurities, by *surā* liquor, or by intoxicants (*madya*) is considered "extremely defiled" (*atyantopahata*). (1) All vessels made of metal that are extremely defiled are purified by being cast into fire. (2) Those made of gems, stone, or lotus-fiber are purified by burying them in the earth for seven nights. (3) Those made of horn, ivory, or bone are purified by planing. (4) One should discard those made of wood or clay. (5) In the case of a garment that is extremely defiled, if it cannot be separated from the stain even after washing, one should cut it out. (6) Gold, silver, lotus-fiber, and gemstone vessels that are free from stains are purified with water. (7) The same applies to stone cups (*camasa*) and sacrificial ladles (*graha*). (8) Sacrificial pots (*caru*), large ladles (*sruc*), and small spoons (*sruva*) are purified with hot water. (9) In the performance of a sacrifice, sacrificial vessels are purified by wiping them with the hand. (10) The wooden sword (*sphya*), winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), cart, pestle, and mortar are purified by sprinkling. (11) The same applies to beds, vehicles, and seats. (12) And to many grains, skins, ropes, woven cloth, split bamboo, thread, cotton, and garments. (13–14) And to vegetables, roots, fruits, and flowers. (15) And to grass, wood, and straw. (16) For these, when they are small in quantity, purification is by washing. (17–18) Silk and woolen cloth are purified with alkaline salt (*ūṣa*). (19) Blankets (*kutapa*) are purified with *ariṣṭaka* seeds. (20) Fine linen (*aṃśupaṭṭa*) is purified with *bilva* fruits. (21) Linen cloth (*kṣauma*) is purified with white mustard seeds. (22) The same applies to items made of horn, bone, or ivory. (23) Deer-hair blankets are purified with *padmākṣa* seeds. (24) Vessels made of copper, brass, tin, and lead are purified with acidic water. (25) Bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and iron are purified with ashes. (26) Wooden articles are purified by planing. (27) Items produced from fruit are purified with cow-hair brushes. (28) Solid objects are purified by sprinkling. (29) Liquid substances are purified by skimming. (30) When large quantities of sugarcane products such as molasses and the like are stored in a house and become defiled, they are purified by placing a fire at the doorway. (31) The same applies to all honey and salt. (32) Earthenware is purified by baking again. (33) For deities whose purification has been performed according to the rules for the materials, purification is further achieved by re-consecrating them. (34) Regarding uncooked food, one should discard only that portion which is defiled and perform threshing and washing on the remainder. (35) Cooked food exceeding one *droṇa* in measure does not become spoiled even if defiled. (36) Having removed the defiled portion of that food, one should sprinkle water over it consecrated with the *Gāyatrī* mantra, and show it to a dog and to fire. (37)
Food that has been pecked by birds, smelled by a cow, blown upon,
sneezed at, or defiled by hair or insects is purified by the scattering of earth over it.
As long as the odor and the stain caused by it do not depart from an object smeared with impurity, so long must earth and water be applied to all types of substances. (39)
The goat and the horse are pure by their mouths; neither the cow nor those born of humans are impure;
and roads are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the wind. (40)
The mud and water in a street that have been touched by outcastes, dogs, or crows are purified by the wind alone, as are structures built of baked bricks.
Furthermore, for all living beings, one should always untiringly perform purification with earth and water whenever they are excessively defiled. 42.
Water found on the ground is pure if it quenches the thirst of a cow;
likewise, water situated on a stone is pure provided it is not contaminated by impurities.
From a well containing a dead five-toed animal or one that is otherwise utterly defiled, one should draw out all the water; the remainder should be purified with a weapon.
One should perform the kindling of fire in a well constructed with baked bricks;
thereafter, one should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in a well produced from fresh water.
O Earth, in the case of small, stagnant reservoirs, purification is said to be like that of a well; however, there is no defilement in large ones.
The gods have ordained three purifiers for Brahmins: that which is unseen, that which is washed with water, and that which is commended by word. (47)
The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise that has been displayed for sale; likewise, almsfood offered by a Brāhmaṇa and all mines are pure. 48.
The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall; a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game.
The meat of an animal killed by dogs is proclaimed to be pure;
so too is that of one killed by other carnivorous beasts, or by Cāṇḍālas and other such outcasts or bandits.
One should declare those apertures which are above the navel to be pure;
those below are impure, as are the excretions that have fallen from the body. (51)
Flies, droplets, shadows, a cow, a horse, the rays of the sun,
dust, the earth, wind, fire, and a cat are always pure.
The principal [limbs] do not become defiled by food remnants; nor do droplets that fall upon the body [cause impurity];
nor do the beard hairs that enter the mouth, nor what is caught between the teeth. (53)
The drops that touch the feet of one who is providing water for rinsing to others should be known as equal to those on the ground; one does not become impure because of them. //54//
If one who holds a substance in his hand is somehow touched by something defiled by food remnants,
he shall attain purity by sipping water (ācamana) without first setting that substance down.
A house [is purified] by sweeping and smearing; a book, by sprinkling;
and [the ground] by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling, and scraping. (56)
The earth is purified by burning or else by the dwelling of cows;
cows are purifying and auspicious, and upon cows the worlds are established. (57)
Cows extend the sacrifice; cows are the destroyers of all evil.
[They provide] cow-urine, cow-dung, milk, clarified butter, curd, and gorocanā.
This sixfold [rite] is supremely auspicious for cows at all times;
the water from the horns of cows is meritorious and destroys all sins. (59)
Scratching the bodies of cows indeed destroys all impurities;
by giving mouthfuls of fodder to cows, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
For the Gaṅgā dwells here in the footprint of cows;
likewise, nourishment is increased in their dust,
prosperity in their dried dung, and dharma in bowing before them.
And one should constantly pay homage to them. ||61||
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter, on Purification, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Twenty-Four.

Now, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives according to the order of the castes: [one of each]. (1) A Kṣatriya may have three. (2) A Vaiśya two. (3) A Śūdra one. (4) When taking a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*) as a subsequent marriage, the hand should be taken in marriage. (5) When taking a wife of a different caste (*asavarṇā*), a Kṣatriya maiden should take hold of an arrow. (6) A Vaiśya maiden should take hold of a goad. (7) A Śūdra maiden should take hold of the end of a garment’s fringe. (8) One should not take as a wife a woman who belongs to the same *gotra* or the same *pravara*. (9) [This applies] up to the fifth generation on the mother’s side and up to the seventh on the father’s side. (10) One should not marry a woman of low family. (11) Nor one who is diseased. (12) Nor one with extra limbs. (13) Nor one deficient in limbs. (14) Nor one who is excessively reddish-brown. (15) Nor one who is talkative. (16) Now, there are eight forms of marriage: (17) the Brāhma, the Daiva, the Ārṣa, the Prājāpatya, the Gāndharva, the Āsura, the Rākṣasa, and the Paiśāca. (18) The Brāhma marriage consists of giving a daughter to a virtuous man after inviting him. (19) The Daiva marriage consists of giving her to an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*) at a sacrifice. (20) The Ārṣa marriage consists of taking a pair of cattle (*gomithuna*) in exchange. (21) The Prājāpatya marriage consists of giving her away after requesting it. (22) The Gāndharva marriage is the union of two who desire each other, without the consent of the mother and father. (23) The Āsura marriage consists of buying her. (24) The Rākṣasa marriage consists of seizing her by force in battle. (25) The Paiśāca marriage consists of approaching her while she is asleep or intoxicated. (26) Of these, the first four are lawful. (27) The Gāndharva is also lawful for Kṣatriyas. (28) The son of a Brāhma marriage purifies twenty-one generations. (29) The son of a Daiva marriage, fourteen. (30) The son of an Ārṣa marriage, seven. (31) The son of a Prājāpatya marriage, six. (32) The father, the grandfather, the brother, a kinsman (*sakulya*), the maternal grandfather, and the mother are those who may give a daughter in marriage. (38) In the absence of each preceding one, each succeeding one, provided he is of sound mind, shall do so. (39)
Having thus observed three menstrual periods, a maiden may perform her *svayaṃvara* (self-choice of a husband);
but once three periods have passed, she always has the power to dispose of herself.
A maiden who sees her menses while still in her father's house and remains unconsecrated by marriage is to be known as a *vṛṣalī*; one who carries her off does not incur sin. (41)
Thus ends the twenty-fourth chapter, on Marriage, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Twenty-five.

Now, the duties of women: 1. Observing the same vows and conduct as her husband. 2. Worshipping her mother-in-law, father-in-law, elders, deities, and guests. 3. Keeping household utensils well-cleaned and polished. 4. Not being stingy with expenditures. 5. Keeping household vessels well-concealed and secure. 6. Having no interest in root-cultivation (or base occupations). 7. Being devoted to auspicious customs and conduct. 8. Refraining from personal adornment when her husband is away on a journey. 9. Avoiding visiting the houses of others. 10. Not lingering at doorways or windows. 11. Remaining dependent in all her actions. 12. Being subject to the authority of her father, husband, or son during childhood, youth, and old age respectively. 13. Practicing celibacy or ascending the funeral pyre after her husband’s death. 14. Or [following him] by ascending the funeral pyre.
For women there is no separate sacrifice, no vow, nor even a fast; by serving her husband, however, she is exalted in heaven. (15)
If a woman observes a fast or a vow while her husband is still living, she takes away her husband’s life-span and goes to hell. (16)
When her husband has died, a virtuous woman who remains established in celibacy goes to heaven even if she is childless, just like those who practice lifelong celibacy. ||17||
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter on the Duties of Women in the Dharmaśāstra of Viṣṇu.
Chapter Twenty-Six:

When many wives of the same caste (savarṇā) are present, he should perform religious duties together with the eldest alone. (1) And when they are of mixed castes, he may do so even with the youngest, provided she is of the same caste as himself. (2) In the absence of a wife of the same caste, however, he may do so with one of the next lower caste in times of distress. (3) But a twice-born man must never do so with a Śūdra woman. (4)
A Śūdra wife for a twice-born man can never serve the purpose of dharma;
she is declared to be for the sake of pleasure alone for him who is blinded by passion. (5)
Twice-born men who, out of delusion, marry women of low birth quickly lead their families, along with their descendants, to the status of Śūdras.
But for one whose rites for the gods, ancestors, and guests are dominated by that [wealth], neither the ancestors nor the gods eat [the offerings]; he does not go to heaven. (7)
Thus ends the twenty-sixth chapter, the Section on the Determination of Dharma, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Twenty-Seven.

The *niṣeka* rite is performed when the pregnancy becomes manifest. (1) The *puṃsavana* rite is performed before the fetus moves. (2) The *sīmantonnayana* rite is performed in the sixth or eighth month. (3) Upon the birth of the boy, the *jātakarma* rite is performed. (4) When the period of impurity has passed, the naming ceremony (*nāmadheya*) is performed. (5) For a Brāhmaṇa, the name should be auspicious; (6) for a Kṣatriya, it should be associated with power; (7) for a Vaiśya, it should be associated with wealth; (8) for a Śūdra, it should be contemptible. (9) In the fourth month, the child is shown the sun (*ādityadarśana*). (10) In the sixth month, the first feeding of solid food (*annaprāśana*) is performed. (11) In the third year, the tonsure (*cūḍākaraṇa*) is performed. (12) These same rites are performed for girls, but without mantras. (13) For them, however, the marriage ceremony is performed with mantras. (14) The initiation (*upanayana*) for a Brāhmaṇa is in the eighth year from conception; (15) for a King (Kṣatriya), in the eleventh year from conception; (16) for a Vaiśya, in the twelfth year from conception. (17) Their girdles (*mauñjī*) are made of Muñja grass, bowstring, and Balbaja grass, respectively. (18) Their sacred threads (*upavīta*) and garments are made of cotton, hemp, and wool, respectively. (19) Their skins are those of the black antelope, the tiger, and the goat, respectively. (20) Their staffs are made of Palāśa, Khadira, and Udumbara wood, respectively. (21) They should reach the hairline, the forehead, and the shoulder region, respectively. (22) All of them should be straight and have their bark intact. (23–24) The begging of alms begins with the word "Bhavat" at the beginning, middle, and end of the request, respectively. (25)
The Sāvitrī does not expire for a Brāhmaṇa until the sixteenth year;
for a Kṣatriya until the twenty-second; and for a Vaiśya until the twenty-fourth. (26)
Beyond this point, all three of these, if not consecrated at the proper time, become fallen from the Sāvitrī, outcastes (vrātyas), and despised by the noble ones. ||27||
Whatever skin, whatever sacred thread, and whatever girdle is prescribed for each,
and whatever staff and whatever garment— each of these is also [to be maintained] during his religious observances.
Having thrown the girdle, the skin, the staff, the sacrificial thread,
and the water-pot into the water when they are ruined, he should take others with the appropriate mantras.
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, on the sacraments, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Twenty-Eight.

Now follows the residence of the religious student (*brahmacārin*) in the teacher’s household. (1) He shall perform the worship of the two twilights. (2) He shall recite the prayers during the morning twilight while standing, and during the evening twilight while sitting. (3) At both times, he shall bathe and perform the fire-ritual. (4) He shall immerse himself in water like a staff. (5) He shall study when summoned [by the teacher]. (6) He shall practice what is pleasing and beneficial to the teacher. (7) He shall wear a girdle, a staff, an antelope skin, and a sacred thread. (8) He shall go for alms among virtuous people, except within the teacher’s own household. (9) He shall consume the alms-food only after being permitted by the teacher. (10) He shall avoid salt, fermented sour liquids, stale food, dancing, singing, women, honey, meat, collyrium, food-leavings, injury to living beings, and vulgar speech. (11) He shall sleep on the ground. (12) He shall rise before the teacher and go to bed after him. (13) Having performed the twilight worship, he shall offer salutation to the teacher. (14) With hands crossed, he shall touch the teacher’s feet. (15) The right foot with the right hand, and the other with the other. (16) At the end of the salutation, he shall announce his own name, ending with the word "bhoḥ. (17) He shall not speak to the teacher while standing, sitting, lying down, eating, or facing away. (18) He shall speak to one who is sitting while standing; to one who is standing while approaching; to one who is coming toward him while going out to meet him; and to one who is running while running behind him. (19) To one who is facing away, he shall face him. (20) To one who is at a distance, he shall approach him closely. (21) To one who is lying down, he shall bow down. (22) Within the range of the teacher’s vision, he shall not sit as he pleases. (23) Nor shall he utter the teacher’s name alone [without the title]. (24) He shall not mimic the teacher’s gait, gestures, speech, and so forth. (25) He shall not stay where there is censure or slander of the teacher. (26) He shall not share the same seat with the teacher, except on a stone slab, a wooden plank, or in a boat. (28) When the teacher’s teacher is present, he shall behave toward him as toward his own teacher. (29) Unless directed by the teacher, he shall not offer salutation to his own teachers. (30) Toward the teacher’s son who is a child, of equal age, or an instructor, he shall behave as toward the teacher. (31) He shall not wash his feet. (32) He shall not eat the leftovers. (33) In this manner, he shall master one Veda, two Vedas, or all the Vedas. (34) Thereafter, he shall study the Vedāṅgas. (35) But he who, having not studied the Vedas, exerts effort elsewhere, along with his progeny, sinks to the status of a Śūdra. (36) Birth occurs first from the mother, and the second at the tying of the girdle (*mauñjībandhana*). (37) In that [second birth], the Sāvitrī verse becomes his mother, and the teacher becomes his father. (38) By this very fact, these [twice-born] attain the status of the twice-born. (39) Before the tying of the girdle, a twice-born person is equal to a Śūdra. (40) A religious student should be either shaven-headed or wear matted hair. (41) After mastering the Veda, being permitted by the teacher and having given him a gift, he shall perform the ceremonial bath (*snāna*). (42) Or, he may spend the remainder of his life in the teacher’s household itself. (43) If the teacher dies there, he shall behave toward the teacher’s son as toward the teacher. (44) Or toward the teacher’s wife, or toward a woman of the same caste (*savarṇā*). (45) In the absence of these, he shall remain a lifelong student (*naiṣṭhika-brahmacārin*), devoted to the service of the sacred fire. (46)
The Brahmin who thus practices the life of celibacy without sloth goes to the highest station and is not born here again. ||47||
Those who know the Dharma and proclaim the Veda say that for a twice-born man established in a vow, the emission of semen through lust constitutes a transgression of his vow. 48.
When this offense has been committed, having worn the skin of a donkey,
he shall go for alms at seven houses, proclaiming his own deed.
Subsisting on alms obtained from them only once a day, and performing ablutions at the three periods of the day, he becomes purified in one year. //50//
If a twice-born student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) involuntarily emits semen during sleep, he shall bathe, worship the sun, and then mutter three times the verse beginning with "punar mām. (51)
If, while not being ill, he fails to go out for alms and fails to kindle the sacred fire for seven nights, he shall perform the penance of an *avakīrṇin*.
If the sun should rise while he is sleeping out of his own volition,
or if it should set while he is unaware of it, he shall fast for the day while muttering prayers.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter on the Student (*brahmacārin*) in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra. Chapter Twenty-nine:

One who, having performed the initiation (*upanayana*), instructs him in the observances (*vrata*) and teaches him the Veda, one should know him as the *ācārya*. [1] But he who teaches him for a fee, whether the entire Veda or a single portion, one should know him as the *upādhyāya*. [2] He who performs the ritual acts at his sacrifice is the *ṛtvij* (officiant). [3] One should not officiate at a sacrifice for someone who has not been examined. [4] One should not teach him. [5] One should not initiate him. [6]
He who speaks unrighteously and he who asks unrighteously—one of these two perishes or incurs enmity. (7)
Where neither righteousness nor wealth is found, nor even a corresponding desire to serve, there knowledge should not be sown, just as a good seed is not sown in saline soil. (8)
Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin and said:
"Guard me; I am your treasure. [Do not give me] to one who is censorious, nor to one who is not upright, nor to one who is unrestrained."
Do not say "Vīryavatī" to me; may I be so. ||9||
Teach it only to one whom you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with the practice of celibacy—
one who would never deceive you in any way whatsoever.
O Brahmin, speak of me to him as the guardian of the treasure.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, concerning the Guru, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Thirty.

Having performed the *upākarma* (the ritual commencement of Vedic study) on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa or Prauṣṭhapada, he should study for four and a half months. (1) Then he should perform their *utsarga* (the ritual conclusion) outside [the village]. (2) Between the *utsarga* and the *upākarma*, he should engage in the study of the Vedāṅgas. (3) He should not study for a day and night on the fourteenth, fifteenth, and eighth days of the lunar fortnight; (4) nor during the transition between seasons, nor during eclipses, nor during periods of impurity (*sūtaka*); (5) nor during Indra’s departure (*indraprayāṇa*); (6) nor when a violent wind blows; (7) nor during unseasonable rain, lightning, or thunder; (8) nor during earthquakes, the fall of meteors, or the burning of the quarters; (9) nor while there is a corpse within the village; (10) nor during the clash of weapons; (11) nor when there is the howling of dogs, jackals, or donkeys; (12) nor during the sound of musical instruments; (13) nor in the presence of a Śūdra or an outcast (*patita*); (14) nor in temples, cemeteries, crossroads, or on main roads; (15) nor in the water; (16) nor with his feet placed upon a seat; (17) nor while riding an elephant, horse, camel, or boat; (18) nor after vomiting; (19) nor after purging; (20) nor while suffering from indigestion; (21) nor when passing between five-toed animals; (22) nor during the misfortune of a king, a learned Brahmin (*śrotriya*), a cow, or a Brāhmaṇa; (23) nor at the time of the *upākarma*; (24) nor at the time of the *utsarga*; (25) nor while the sound of the Sāman chants is present, [during which] the Ṛg and Yajus verses [are not to be studied]; (26) nor having studied during the latter part of the night, should he go to sleep. (27) Even if he is diligent, he should avoid studying on the days forbidden for study (*anadhyāya*). (28) For what is studied on forbidden days yields no fruit either in this world or the next. (29) Through such study, there is a loss of the lifespan of both teacher and pupil. (30) Therefore, except on forbidden days, the teacher who desires the world of Brahmā should sow knowledge in the "fields" of worthy pupils. (31) At the beginning and end of the study of the Veda, the pupil must clasp the feet of the teacher. (32) And the syllable *praṇava* (Om) must be uttered. (33) In that regard, by whatever Ṛg verses he studies, thereby the ancestors are satisfied with clarified butter (*ājya*); (34) by whatever Yajus formulas, with honey; (35) by whatever Sāmans, with milk; (36) and by whatever Atharvan [verses], with meat; (37) and by whatever Purāṇas, Itihāsas, Vedāṅgas, and Dharmaśāstras he studies, by those he is satisfied with food. (38) If one acquires knowledge and lives by it in this world, yet does not share it, that knowledge shall yield no fruit for him in the next world. (39) And he who destroys the fame of others through his learning [is likewise punished]. (40) One should not acquire knowledge from another who is studying without permission. (41) Taking knowledge thus constitutes theft of the Veda (*brahmasteya*) and leads to hell. (42)
Whether it be worldly, Vedic, or even spiritual knowledge, one should never bear malice toward the person from whom that knowledge is received. (43)
Between the father who gives birth and the father who imparts the Veda, the father who gives the Veda is the more venerable;
for the birth through the Veda is eternal for a Brahmin, both after death and in this world. 44.
One should understand that the birth which occurs here from a womb is merely the production of this being by its mother and father through their mutual desire. //45//
But that birth which the teacher, having mastered the Vedas, produces for him according to rule with the Sāvitrī—*that* is real, *that* is ageless and immortal. (46)
One who fills one's ears with that which is not false,
bringing about freedom from suffering and bestowing the deathless—
him one should regard as both father and mother.
Knowing what he has done for him, one should not bear him malice.
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter, on the occasions when study is forbidden, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.

Chapter Thirty-One: There are three persons who are exceedingly venerable to a man: the mother, the father, and the teacher. (1–2) One must always be intent on serving them. (3) Whatever they may say, that one should do. (4) One should act for their pleasure and welfare. (5) Without being permitted by them, one should not do anything at all. (6)
These indeed are the three Vedas; these indeed are the three gods;
these indeed are the three worlds; these indeed are the three fires. ||7||
The father is the Gārhapatya fire, the mother is the Dakṣiṇa fire, and the teacher is the Āhavanīya fire. ||8||
All dharmas are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual actions are fruitless. (9)
By devotion to one's mother one attains this world; by devotion to one's father, the middle world; but by service to one's teacher, one reaches the world of Brahmā. ||10||
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, concerning the Teacher, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Thirty-Two.

A king, an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a learned scholar (*śrotriya*), one who prohibits unrighteousness, a teacher (*upādhyāya*), a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, and an elder brother—these relatives are to be honored like a teacher. (1) And their wives, if they are of the same caste (*savarṇā*), [are to be honored likewise]. (2) So too are a mother’s sister, a father’s sister, and an elder sister. (3) For those who are younger than a father-in-law, a paternal uncle, a maternal uncle, or an officiating priest, the mere rising to meet them constitutes the salutation (*abhivāda*). (4) In the case of the wives of teachers belonging to a lower caste, there should be a salutation first, but not the clasping of the feet. (5) One should not perform for the wives of teachers such acts as massaging the limbs, applying collyrium, dressing the hair, or washing the feet. (6) Even if she is not a relative, the wife of another should be addressed as "sister," or as "daughter," or as "mother. (7) And one should not address one's teachers by the word "thou" (*tvam*). (8) If one uses the word "thou" in addressing them, one should fast until the end of the day, appease him, and then eat. (9) And one should not engage in contentious speech with a teacher. (10) Nor should one speak ill of him. (11) Nor should one say anything that is displeasing to him. (12)
A young wife of the guru must not be saluted by touching her feet here with one who has completed twenty years of age and understands virtues and faults.
However, on this earth, a young man should duly perform a salutation to the wives of his elders who are themselves young, saying, "I am so-and-so. (14)
Having returned from a journey abroad, one should clasp the feet of the teacher’s wives every day and offer salutations, keeping in mind the dharma of the virtuous. (15)
Wealth, kinship, age, ritual action, and learning as the fifth—these are the grounds for respect; each subsequent one is weightier than the preceding. (16)
A ten-year-old Brahmin and a hundred-year-old king— [are equal].
One should know them as father and son; however, of the two, the Brāhmaṇa is the father.
The superiority of Brahmins is by virtue of knowledge; that of Kṣatriyas, by virtue of valor;
that of Vaiśyas, by virtue of grain and wealth; and that of Śūdras alone, by virtue of birth. ||18||
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter of the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra, concerning the salutation of the guru and related instructions.

Chapter Thirty-Three: Now, a man has three most terrible enemies known as lust, anger, and greed. (1) These become especially formidable for a householder due to his attachment to possessions. (2) Overcome by these, he engages in acts of extreme sin, great sin, secondary sin, and minor sin; (3) in acts that cause loss of caste, acts that cause mixture of castes, and acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts; (4) and in acts that bring impurity, as well as miscellaneous offenses. (5)
This threefold gate of hell, which leads to one's own destruction—namely, lust, anger, and greed—one should therefore abandon these three. (6)
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter, concerning the three types of enemies, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Thirty-Four:
Sexual intercourse with one’s mother, sexual intercourse with one’s daughter, and sexual intercourse with one’s daughter-in-law are crimes of extreme gravity (atipātaka). [1]
But those who have committed heinous crimes should enter the fire;
for indeed, no other expiation for them exists in any way whatsoever. (2)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter, concerning heinous crimes, in the Dharmaśāstra of Viṣṇu.

Chapter Thirty-Five 1. Killing a Brāhmaṇa, drinking liquor, stealing the gold of a Brāhmaṇa, and violating the teacher’s wife—these are the great sins (mahāpātakas). 2. And association with those [who have committed such acts] is likewise [a great sin]. 3–4. One who associates with an outcast for one year becomes an outcast himself, as does one who shares a vehicle or a seat with him. 5. Through a matrimonial alliance or through officiating at a sacrifice for him, one becomes an outcast immediately.
These perpetrators of great sins may be purified by the horse sacrifice,
or likewise by visiting all the sacred fords on earth.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter, concerning the heinous crimes, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Thirty-Six.

The killing of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice, the killing of a woman in her menses, of a pregnant woman, of a woman of the Atri lineage, of an unknown fetus, or of one who has sought refuge—these are equal to the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. (1) Giving false testimony and the killing of a friend—these two are equal to the drinking of liquor. (2) The seizure of a Brāhmaṇa’s land and the misappropriation of a deposit are equal to the theft of gold. (3) Sexual intercourse with the wife of a paternal uncle, a maternal grandfather, a maternal uncle, a father-in-law, or a king, is equal to violating the teacher’s bed. (4) So too is sexual intercourse with a paternal aunt or a maternal aunt. (5) And so too is sexual intercourse with the wife of a learned Śrotriya, an officiating priest, a teacher, or a friend. (6) And [the same applies to] one’s own sister, a female friend, a woman of the same lineage, a woman of a higher caste, a woman of the lowest caste, a maiden, a woman in her menses, a woman who has sought refuge, a female ascetic, and a woman who has been entrusted to one’s care. (7)
But these secondary sinners, like the perpetrators of the great sins,
are purified by the horse sacrifice or by visiting sacred pilgrimage sites.
Thus ends the thirty-sixth chapter, concerning minor offenses, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Thirty-Seven.

1. False speech for the sake of self-exaltation; 2. Slander directed toward the king; 3. Insisting on falsehood toward one's teacher; 4. Censuring the Vedas; 5. Abandoning what has been studied; 6. And [abandoning] the sacred fire, father, mother, son, or wife; 7. Eating the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or eating forbidden food; 8. Stealing the property of another; 9. Adultery with the wife of another; 10. Officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom one should not officiate; 11. Living by a forbidden occupation; 12. Accepting gifts from the unworthy; 13. Killing a Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, Śūdra, or a cow; 14. Selling what ought not to be sold; 15. Being superseded in marriage by a younger brother while the elder remains unmarried; 16. Marrying before the elder brother; 17. Giving a daughter in marriage to such a younger brother; 18. And officiating at a sacrifice for him; 19. Being a Vratya (one who has lost caste through neglect of initiation); 20. Teaching for a fee; 21. Receiving instruction for a fee; 22. Supervising all types of mines; 23. Operating large-scale mechanical contrivances; 24. Destroying trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, or medicinal herbs; 25. Living off the earnings of women; 26. Engaging in malevolent magic or rites involving roots; 27. Undertaking actions solely for one's own benefit; 28. Not maintaining the sacred fires; 29. Failing to discharge the debts to the gods, the sages, and the ancestors; 30. Studying heterodox scriptures; 31. Atheism; 32. Following the profession of an actor or singer; 33. Associating with a woman who drinks liquor. These are the minor offenses (upapātakas). 34.
But those men who have committed minor offenses (upapātakin) should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance,
or they may perform the Parāka, or they should sacrifice with the Gosava.
Thus ends the thirty-seventh chapter, on Minor Offenses (*upapātaka*), in the *Dharmaśāstra* of Viṣṇu.

Chapter Thirty-eight: [Causing] Injury to a Brāhmaṇa. 1. Smelling things that should not be smelled or spirituous liquor. 2. Crookedness (deceit). 3. Engaging in sexual intercourse with animals. 4. And [intercourse] with a male. 5. These are the acts that cause loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*). 6. Thus [ends the section].
Having intentionally committed any one of those acts that cause loss of caste, one should perform the *sāṃtapana* penance; if done unintentionally, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance.
Thus ends the thirty-eighth chapter, on the Loss of Caste, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Thirty-nine:
Causing Mixture of Castes through the Killing of Domestic or Wild Animals. [1]
Having committed an act that causes confusion of castes, one should eat barley-gruel for a month,
or else perform the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra as an expiation.
Thus ends the thirty-ninth chapter, on the subject of acts that cause loss of caste, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Forty:
Accepting wealth from censurable persons, trade, living by usury, speaking untruths, and serving Śūdras—these constitute acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa).
Having committed an act that renders one unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa), one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance;
or purification may be attained through the Śītakṛcchra or the Mahāsāṃtapana.
Thus ends the fortieth chapter, concerning the acts that render one unworthy [of receiving gifts], in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Forty-One: 1.
The killing of birds, aquatic animals, and creatures born in water; 2. And of worms and insects; 3. Eating food mixed with intoxicants; 4. These are the acts that cause impurity.
For acts that cause defilement, the *taptakṛcchra* is the purifying expiation;
or else, the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* is the purifying expiation. (5)
Thus ends the forty-first chapter, concerning defiling acts, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Forty-Two:
That which has not been mentioned is miscellaneous (prakīrṇaka). ||1||
Having ascertained the gravity or lightness of a miscellaneous sin,
a wise man should always perform the penance with the approval of Brāhmaṇas.
Thus ends the forty-second chapter, the Section on Miscellaneous Topics, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Forty-Three.

Now, the hells: 1. Tāmisra; 2. Andhatāmisra; 3. Raurava; 4. Mahāraurava; 5. Kālasūtra; 6. Mahānaraka; 7. Saṃjīvana; 8. Avīci; 9. Tāpana; 10. Saṃpratāpana; 11. Saṃghātaka; 12. Kākola; 13. Kuḍmala; 14. Pūtimṛttika; 15. Lohaśaṅku; 16. Ṛcīṣa; 17. Viṣamapanthā; 18. Kūṭaśālmalī; 19. Pūyanadī; 20. Asipatravana; 21. Lohakaṇṭaka. 22. Those who have committed heinous crimes (atipātakin) without having performed expiation are cooked in these [hells] in succession for a kalpa. 24. Those who have committed great crimes (mahāpātakinaḥ) [remain] for the duration of a manvantara. 25. And those who have committed secondary crimes (anupātakinaḥ). 26. Those who have committed minor crimes (upapātakinaḥ) [remain] for four yugas. 27. Those who have caused the mixing of castes (saṃkarīkaraṇa) [remain] for a thousand years. 28. And those who have caused the loss of caste (jātibhraṃśakaraṇa). 29. And those who have rendered themselves unworthy of receiving gifts (apātrīkaraṇa). 30. And those who have committed acts that cause defilement (malinīkaraṇa). 31. And those who have committed miscellaneous sins (prakīrṇapātakin) [remain] for many series of years.
Sinful evildoers who have committed crimes, immediately after giving up their lives,
reach the path of Yama and experience terrible suffering.
Dragged here and there by the terrible messengers of Yama, they are led along a path through agonizing darkness with great difficulty. (33)
They are being devoured by dogs, jackals, carnivorous beasts, crows, herons, cranes, and the like, as well as by fire-mouthed creatures, serpents, and scorpions. (34)
Being burned by fire, pierced by thorns,
split apart by saws, and tormented by thirst.
Tormented by hunger as well as by terrible hosts of diseases,
they faint at every step from the stench of pus and blood.
Desiring the food and drink of others, they are beaten by servants with faces as terrifying as those of crows, herons, cranes, and other such birds. (37)
In some places they are boiled in oil; in some places they are beaten with pestles;
and likewise in some places they are crushed upon iron anvils and upon stone slabs. (38)
In some places they eat what has been vomited; in some, pus and blood; in some, excrement; and in others, flesh that is foul-smelling like pus and most loathsome. (39)
They remain in dreadful darknesses, and likewise in some places they are being devoured by worms with most terrible fire-like mouths.
In some places they are tormented by cold, and in others they have entered into impurity;
furthermore, in some places these most dreadful *preta*s devour one another. (41)
In some places they are driven away by smoke; likewise, in some places they hang suspended;
in some places they are struck by floods of arrows, and in others they are cut to pieces. ||42||
With their feet placed upon their throats and entwined by the coils of serpents,
they were likewise tormented by mechanical devices and dragged along by their knees.
With their backs, heads, and necks broken, and with needle-like throats, they are most dreadful;
possessing bodies as large as upper-story chambers, they are capable of enduring torment.
Thus, having experienced the consequences of their sins and being deeply afflicted by suffering, those who have committed transgressions enter the animal realm and undergo various miseries.
Thus ends the forty-third chapter, on the section concerning hells, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Forty-Four.

Now, for those of evil nature who have experienced suffering in the hells, there are births among the animal species (1). For those who have committed excessive sins, there are successively all the immobile births (2). For those who have committed great sins, there are births as worms (3). For those who have committed secondary sins, there are births as birds (4). For those who have committed minor sins, there are births as aquatic creatures (5). For those who have performed acts that cause loss of caste, there are births as water-dwellers (6). For those who have performed acts that cause mixture of castes, there are births as deer (7). For those who have performed acts that render one unworthy of receiving gifts, there are births as domestic animals (8). For those who have performed acts that cause defilement, there are births among humans as untouchables (9). Among miscellaneous sins, they become various predatory flesh-eaters (10). One who eats food that should not be eaten or forbidden food becomes a worm (11). A thief becomes a hawk (12). An adulterer becomes a ghost (13). A stealer of gems becomes a burrower (14). A stealer of grain becomes a rat (15). A stealer of bell-metal becomes a swan (16). Having stolen water, one becomes a water-fowl (17). Honey, a gadfly (18). Milk, a crow (19). A savory liquid, a dog (20). Ghee, a mongoose (21). Meat, a vulture (22). Fat, a water-crow (23). Oil, a cockroach (24). Salt, a cricket (25). Curd, a crane (26). Silk, a partridge (27). Linen, a frog (28). Cotton cloth, a curlew (29). A cow, a monitor lizard (30). Molasses, a *vālguda* (31). Perfumes, a muskrat (32). Leaf-vegetables, a peacock (33). Cooked food, a *sedhā* (34). Uncooked food, a porcupine (35). Fire, a heron (36). Household utensils, a house-lizard (37). Dyed garments, a pheasant (38). An elephant, a tortoise (39). A horse, a tiger (40). Fruits and flowers, a monkey (41). A woman, a bear (42). A vehicle, a camel (43). Cattle, a goat (44).
Having forcibly seized any kind of another's property, or having consumed an offering that has not been consecrated, a man inevitably goes to the state of an animal. (44)
Women also, by taking [the property] according to this same principle, would incur guilt;
for they become wives of these very same creatures. (45)
Thus ends the forty-fourth chapter, on the subject of castes, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Forty-Five.

Now, for those who have experienced the sufferings of hell and have emerged from the state of animals, there are these marks in human birth: 1. One who has committed a great sin (atipātakin) suffers from leprosy (*kuṣṭhin*). 2. A killer of a Brahmin (*brahmahā*) suffers from consumption (*yakṣmī*). 3. A drinker of spirituous liquor (*surāpaḥ*) has black teeth (*śyāvadantakaḥ*). 4. A stealer of gold (*suvarṇāpahārī*) has deformed nails (*kunakhī*). 5. One who violates the bed of his guru (*gurutalpagaḥ*) has bad skin (*duścarmā*). 6. A slanderer (*piśunaḥ*) has a putrid nose (*pūtināsaḥ*). 7. An informer (*sūcakaḥ*) has a foul-smelling mouth (*pūtivaktraḥ*). 8. A thief of grain (*dhānyacauraḥ*) is deficient in limbs (*aṅgahīnaḥ*). 9. A thief of mixed goods (*miśracauraḥ*) has redundant limbs (*atiriktāṅgaḥ*). 10. A stealer of food (*annāpahārī*) suffers from chronic illness (*āmayāvī*). 11. A stealer of speech (*vāgapahārakaḥ*) is mute (*mūkaḥ*). 12. A stealer of clothing (*vastrāpahārakaḥ*) is afflicted with vitiligo (*śvitrī*). 13. A stealer of horses (*aśvāpahārakaḥ*) is lame (*paṅguḥ*). 14. One who reviles gods or Brahmins (*devabrāhmaṇākrośakaḥ*) is a fool (*mūrkhaḥ*). 15. A poisoner (*garadaḥ*) has a rolling tongue (*loḍajjihvaḥ*). 16. An arsonist (*agnidaḥ*) is insane (*unmattaḥ*). 17. One who acts contrary to his guru (*guroḥ pratikūlaḥ*) suffers from epilepsy (*apasmārī*). 18. A killer of cows (*goghnas*) is blind (*andhaḥ*). 19. And so is a stealer of lamps (*dīpahartā*). 20. One who extinguishes a lamp (*dīpanirvāpakaḥ*) is one-eyed (*kāṇaḥ*). 21. A seller of tin, chowries, or lac is a washerman (*rajakaḥ*). 22. A seller of single-hoofed animals is a hunter (*mṛgavyādhaḥ*). 23. One who eats the food of a bastard (*kuṇḍāśī*) has a diseased penis (*bhagāsyaḥ*). 24. A bell-ringer is an oil-presser (*tailikaḥ*). 25. A usurer (*vārdhuṣikaḥ*) is a bee-keeper (*bhrāmarī*). 26. One who eats delicacies alone (*mṛṣṭāśy ekākī*) suffers from abdominal tumors (*vātagulmī*). 27. A breaker of agreements (*samayabhettā*) is bald (*khalvāṭaḥ*). 28. One who has broken his vow of celibacy (*avakīrṇī*) suffers from elephantiasis (*ślīpadī*). 29. One who destroys another's livelihood (*paravṛttighnaḥ*) is poor (*daridraḥ*). 30. One who causes pain to others (*parapīḍākaraḥ*) is chronically ill (*dīrgharogī*). 31.
Thus, by the particularity of their karma, they are born endowed with [physical] marks: afflicted by diseases, as well as blind, hunchbacked, lame, or one-eyed. (32)
Dwarfs, the deaf, the mute, the weak, and others as well—therefore, one should perform expiation with every effort. (33)
Thus ends the forty-fifth chapter, on the marks of sin, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.

Now follow the *kṛcchra* penances. ||1|| One should not eat for three days. ||2|| One should perform a bath three times a day (*triṣavaṇa*) every day. ||3|| At each bath, one should immerse oneself in the water three times. ||4|| While immersed, one should mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times. ||5|| During the day, one should remain standing; at night, one should remain seated. ||6–7|| At the conclusion of the rite, one should give a milch cow as a gift. ||8|| This is the *aghamarṣaṇa*. ||9|| One should eat in the evening for three days, in the morning for three days, and eat food obtained unasked for three days, and then fast for three days; this is the *prājāpatya*. ||10|| One should drink hot water for three days, hot clarified butter for three days, hot milk for three days, and fast for three days; this is the *taptakṛcchra*. ||11|| By using these same substances cold, it becomes the *śītakṛcchra*. ||12|| The *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* consists of subsisting on milk alone for twenty-one days. ||13|| The *udakakṛcchra* consists of consuming barley-meal mixed with water for a month. ||14|| The *mūlaśītakṛcchra* consists of consuming lotus stalks for a month. ||15|| The *śrīphalakṛcchra* consists of consuming *bilva* fruits for a month. ||16|| Or alternatively, by consuming lotus seeds. ||17|| The *parāka* consists of fasting for twelve days. ||18|| One should consume cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and *kuśa*-water on one day, and fast on the second day; this is the *sāṃtapana*. ||19|| When these same substances (cow’s urine, etc. are practiced daily, it is the *mahāsāṃtapana*. ||20|| When they are practiced for three days each, it is the *atisāṃtapana*. ||21|| The *tulāpuruṣa* consists of consuming oil-cake, rice-scum, buttermilk, water, and barley-meal, with a fast intervening between each. ||22|| The *parṇakṛcchra* consists of drinking water boiled with the leaves of *kuśa*, *palāśa*, *udumbara*, lotus, *śaṅkhapuṣpī*, *vaṭa*, *brāhma*, and *suvarcalā* plants, consumed daily. ||23||
One who has performed the shaving of the head should perform all these penances.
Constantly bathing at the three sessions of the day, sleeping on the ground, and having conquered his senses; ||24||
One should avoid conversing with women, Śūdras, and outcasts;
one should constantly recite purificatory texts and also offer oblations according to one's ability. (25)
Thus ends the forty-sixth chapter, on the section concerning Kṛcchra penances, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Forty-Seven.

Now, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (1) One should eat morsels according to the capacity of one's mouth. (2) One should increase those morsels in sequence as the digits of the moon wax, and decrease them as they wane; on the new moon day, one should not eat at all. This is the Cāndrāyaṇa known as *yavamadhya* ("barley-shaped"). (3) Or it may be the *pipīlikamadhyama* ("ant-shaped"). (4) That for which the new moon occurs in the middle is the *pipīlikamadhyama*. (5) That for which the full moon occurs [in the middle] is the *yavamadhya*. (6) If one eats eight morsels every day for a month, that is the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*. (7) Four morsels in the evening and four in the morning—that is the *śiśucāndrāyaṇa*. (8) If one eats three hundred minus sixty morsels in a month by any means whatsoever, that is the general *cāndrāyaṇa*. (9)
In ancient times, having performed this vow upon the earth, the stainless Seven Sages, as well as Brahmā and Rudra, attained the supreme abode. (10)
Thus ends the forty-seventh chapter, on the Cāndrāyaṇa penance, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Forty-Eight.

Now, if one should consider oneself heavy with sins committed by one's own actions, one should cook a *prasṛti* measure of barley-gruel for one's own sake. (1) One should not offer it as an oblation into the fire. (2) Nor should there be a *bali*-offering from it. (3) One should consecrate the barley-gruel while it is uncooked, while it is being cooked, and when it is fully cooked. (4) While it is being cooked, one should perform a protection rite. (5) With the mantra, "Brahman among the gods, the path of the seers," one binds *darbha* grass [around the vessel]. (6) When it is cooked, one should eat it quickly after pouring it into a bowl. (7) With the mantra, "Those gods who are born of Manu, joined with the mind, very skillful, sons of Dakṣa—may they protect us; may they help us; obeisance to them, svāhā to them," one should offer it into oneself. (8) Then, having sipped water, one should touch the navel. (9) With the mantra, "O waters, you have been bathed and drunk; you are in our bellies like barley. May you be free from disease, free from sickness, and sinless for us; O divine, immortal ones, increasers of Truth. (10) One seeking wisdom should do this for three nights. (11) A wrongdoer for six nights. (12) Having drunk it for seven nights, one purifies oneself from any one of the great sins (*mahāpātaka*). (13) By twelve nights, one drives away even the sin committed by one's ancestors. (14) By drinking it for a month, one is cleansed of all sins. (15) And likewise for twenty-one nights with barley grains freed from being trampled by cattle. (16)
You are barley; you are the king of grains; you belong to Varuṇa and are mixed with honey.
You are the cleanser of all sins, a purifier praised by the seers. ||17||
Barley is ghee, barley is honey, and barley is water or immortality;
may they purify all my evil, whatever misdeed I have committed. 18.
O barley grains, destroy the karma committed by speech, evil dreams, and ill-considered thoughts, as well as misfortune and Kālakarṇī. (19)
And that which has been licked by a dog or a pig, that which is defiled by food-leavings, and the failure to serve one's mother and father—purify all these for me with barley. (20)

The food of a group, the food of a courtesan, the food of a Śūdra, food from a funeral rite or one in a state of impurity, the food of a thief, and food from a recent funeral—purify these with barley for me. (21)

Purify for me the conduct of fools, unrighteousness, and whatever has been committed at the king's gate; the theft of gold, the state of being an *avrātya*, the officiating at a sacrifice for one unworthy to sacrifice, and the reviling of Brahmins—purify these with barley for me. (22)
Thus ends the forty-eighth chapter, on the subject of Yāvaka, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Forty-Nine.

Having fasted on the eleventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should worship the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva on the twelfth day (1). This is done with ointments, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and by satisfying the sacrificial fire and the Brahmins (2). Having performed this vow for a year, one becomes purified from sins (3). By performing it for as long as one lives, one attains Śvetadvīpa (4). By doing so on the twelfth days of both fortnights for a year, one attains the heavenly world (5). And by doing so for as long as one lives, one attains the world of Viṣṇu (6). It is exactly the same for the fifteenth days (the full and new moons) as well (7).
By attending upon Keśava, who has become Brahman on the new moon day and likewise on the full moon day— having become one with Yoga— one shall attain the Great.
That day on which the moon and Jupiter are seen together in the sky is declared by those versed in the calendar to be the "Great Full Moon" (mahatī paurṇamāsī). //9//
On that day, acts such as giving gifts and observing fasts are proclaimed to be inexhaustible;
likewise so is the twelfth lunar day of the bright fortnight when it is joined with the Śravaṇa asterism. (10)
Thus ends the forty-ninth chapter on Vows in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Fifty.

Having constructed a hut of leaves in the forest, he shall dwell there. (1) He shall bathe at the three periods of the day. (2) Proclaiming his own deed, he shall practice begging for alms in the village. (3) And he shall sleep on grass. (4) This is the Mahāvrata (Great Vow). (5) Having killed a Brāhmaṇa, he shall perform this for twelve years. (6) Or [having killed] a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice; (7) or a pregnant woman, or a woman in her courses; (8) or a woman not of the Atri lineage; (9) or a friend, or an ascetic. (10) Upon the killing of a king, he shall perform this Mahāvrata twice over. (11) It is reduced by one-quarter in the case of killing a Kṣatriya. (12) It is reduced by half in the case of killing a Vaiśya. (13) Half of that again in the case of killing a Śūdra. (14) In all these cases, he shall carry the head of a corpse as his banner. (15) Having shaved his head, he shall follow cows for one month. (16) When they sit, he shall sit; (17) when they stand, he shall stand. (18) He shall rescue them when they are exhausted. (19) And he shall protect them from dangers. (20) Without providing protection for them from cold and other hardships, he shall not provide it for himself. (21) He shall bathe with cow urine. (22) And he shall subsist on the products of the cow. (23) This is the Go-vrata (Cow-vow), which he shall perform upon the killing of a cow. (24) Having killed an elephant, he shall give five dark-colored bulls. (25) For a horse, a garment. (26) For killing a donkey, a one-year-old ox. (27) And for killing a ram or a goat. (28) For killing a camel, a *kṛṣṇala* of gold. (29) Having killed a dog, he shall fast for three nights. (30) Having killed any one of the following—mouse, cat, mongoose, frog, *ḍuṇḍubha* snake, or python—he shall fast, feed a Brāhmaṇa with *kṛsara* (rice and peas), and give an iron staff as a sacrificial fee. (31) For killing an iguana, an owl, a crow, or a blue jay, he shall fast for three nights. (32) Having killed any one of the following—swan, crane, water-hen, *madgu*, chowrie-bird, hawk, eagle, or ruddy goose—or a monkey, he shall give a cow to a Brāhmaṇa. (33) Having killed a snake, an iron hoe. (34) Having killed a eunuch, a load of straw. (35) For a boar, a jar of clarified butter. (36) For a partridge, a *droṇa* measure of sesame seeds. (37) For a parrot, a two-year-old calf. (38) For a curlew, a three-year-old calf. (39) For killing a carnivorous wild animal, he shall give a milch-cow. (40) For killing a non-carnivorous wild animal, a heifer. (41) For killing a wild animal not specifically mentioned, he shall subsist on milk for three nights. (42) For killing a bird, he shall eat only at night. (43) Or he shall give a silver *māṣaka*. (44) Having killed an aquatic creature, he shall fast. (45)
But for the killing of a thousand vertebrate beings,
or for a full cartload of boneless creatures, one should perform the penance prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra.
One should give something to a Brahmin upon killing a creature with bones;
but for killing boneless creatures, one should perform breath-control (prāṇāyāma) as a means of purification.
For cutting fruit-bearing trees, one hundred Ṛg-verses are to be recited;
likewise for shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, and flowering herbs.
For all beings born from food, those born from moisture, and those produced from fruits and flowers, the consumption of clarified butter is the complete purification. 49.
For the unauthorized plucking of cultivated plants or those grown spontaneously in the forest,
one should follow a cow for one day while subsisting on a milk-vow.
Thus ends the fiftieth chapter, on expiations, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Fifty-One

A drinker of *surā* (liquor), deprived of all desired objects, shall eat only grain-particles (*kaṇān*) for one year. (1) Upon consuming any of the impure substances or intoxicants (*madya*), one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (2) And likewise upon eating garlic, onions, leeks, or anything having their odor, as well as the meat of a village pig, a village cock, a monkey, or a cow. (3) In all these cases, at the conclusion of the penance, the twice-born (*dvija*) shall undergo the purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again. (4) In the rite of re-initiation, the shaving of the head, the girdle, the staff, the practice of begging for alms, and the vows are to be omitted. (5) Except for the hare, the porcupine, the monitor lizard, the iguana, the rhinoceros, and the tortoise, upon eating the flesh of any five-toed animal (*pañcanakha*), one shall fast for seven nights. (6) Having eaten the food of a group, a courtesan, a thief, or a singer, one should subsist on milk alone for seven nights. (7) And the food of a carpenter and of a leather-worker. (8) And that of a usurer, a miser, one initiated for a sacrifice, one bound in fetters, one accused of a crime, and a eunuch. (9) And that of an unchaste woman, a hypocrite, a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, one who eats the leavings of others, and those who eat what has been left over by such persons. (10) And that of a woman without a male protector, a goldsmith, an enemy, and one who has fallen from his caste (*patita*). (11) And that of a slanderer, a liar, and those who sell sacrifices, religious duties, or *soma*. (12) And that of an actor, a weaver, an ungrateful person, and a dyer. (13) And that of a blacksmith, a cruel man, a *Niṣāda*, a stage-player, a fletcher, and a seller of weapons. (14) And that of a dog-keeper, a distiller of liquor, an oil-presser, and a washerman. (15) And that of those who are intoxicated, angry, or diseased. (16) And that of those living in the house of a menstruating woman together with her paramour. (17) Food looked upon by a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahan*), touched by a menstruating woman, pecked at by a bird, touched by a dog, or smelled by a cow. (18) That which is intentionally touched by the foot, or that which has been sneezed upon. (19) That which is unhonored, and meat not prepared for a sacred purpose (*vṛthāmāṃsa*). (20) Except for the *pāṭhīna*, *rohit*, *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *śalka* fish, upon eating the flesh of any other fish, one shall fast for three nights. (21) And upon eating the flesh of any aquatic creature. (22) Having drunk water kept in a vessel that held *surā*, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights. (23) If it was in a vessel that held intoxicants (*madya*), one should do so for five nights. (24) A drinker of *soma* who smells the odor of a drinker of *surā* shall immerse himself in water, mutter the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times, and consume clarified butter (*ghṛta*). (25) Upon eating the flesh of a donkey, a camel, a crow, or a dog, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (26) And upon eating unknown meat or dried meat found at a slaughterhouse. (27) Upon eating the flesh of carnivorous beasts or birds, one should perform the *Taptakṛcchra* penance. (28) Upon eating the flesh of a sparrow, a water-fowl, a swan, a ruddy goose, a crane, a *rajjuvāla*, a gallinule, a parrot, a starling, a heron, a crane, a raven, or a wagtail, one shall fast for three nights. (29) And likewise upon eating the flesh of single-hoofed animals or those with two rows of teeth. (30) Except for the partridge, the grey partridge, the quail, the *vartikā*, and the peacock, upon eating the flesh of any other bird, one shall fast for a day and night. (31) Upon eating insects, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā* for one day. (32) And likewise upon eating meat from a slaughterhouse. (33) Upon eating mushrooms or fungi, one should perform the *Sāṃtapana* penance. (34) Having consumed anything stale, except for products made from barley or wheat, preparations of milk, oily foods, dry *khāṇḍava* (sweetmeats), and offerings to the gods or sacrificial oblations, one shall fast. (35) One should avoid tree-exudations that are red or produced from an impure source. (36) And the *śelu* fruit, as well as *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, cakes (*apūpa*), and fried cakes (*śaṣkulī*), even when they are divine offerings or sacrificial oblations. (37) And all milks, except for those of the cow, goat, and buffalo. (38) Even those [milks] if less than ten days old since calving. (39) And the milk of a cow that is dripping, of one in heat, or of one whose calf has died. (40) And the milk of those that eat impure things. (41) All fermented liquids (*śukta*), except for curds. (42) A student (*brahmacārin*) who eats at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*) where raw food is served shall fast for three nights. (43) And he shall dwell in water for one day. (44) Upon eating honey or meat, one should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance. (45) Upon eating the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mongoose, or a rat, one should drink *brahmasuvarcalā*. (46) Upon eating the leavings of a dog, one should fast for one day and drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). (47) Upon eating the excrement or urine of five-toed animals, one should fast for seven nights. (48) Upon eating food from a funeral feast where raw food is served, one should subsist on milk for three nights. (49) A Brāhmaṇa who eats the leavings of a Śūdra, after inducing vomiting, shall fast for seven nights. (50) Upon eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, he shall fast for five nights. (51) Upon eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya, he shall fast for three nights. (52) But upon eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, he shall fast for one day. (53) A Kṣatriya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall fast for five nights. (54) Upon eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, he shall fast for three nights. (55) A Vaiśya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall likewise do so. (56) Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, one shall fast for three nights. (57) Having eaten cooked food [from a Caṇḍāla], one shall perform the *Parāka* penance. (58)
A Brahmin must never, under any circumstances, eat unprepared animals consecrated with mantras.
But one who adheres to the eternal rule should eat [meat] that has been consecrated with mantras. 59.
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body, so many times does the slayer of animals undergo death here;
the evildoer reaps misfortune both in this world and after passing away.
Animals were created by the Self-Existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice;
sacrifice is for the prosperity of this entire world, therefore killing in a sacrifice is not killing.
The sin of a hunter seeking wealth does not become as great as that which falls upon one who eats meat in vain after death. (62)
Herbs, animals, trees, beasts, and likewise birds, having met their death for the sake of sacrifice, attain higher states once again. (63)
In the honey-mixture offering, in sacrifice, and in rites for the ancestors and the gods—only here may animals be slain, and nowhere else under any circumstances. (64)
A twice-born man who knows the true meaning of the Veda, when killing animals for these purposes,
leads both himself and the animals to the highest state.
Whether living at home, with his teacher, or in the forest, a self-possessed twice-born man should never practice violence not ordained by the Veda, even in times of distress. (66)
One should know that the violence ordained by the Veda, which is restricted to this world of moving and unmoving beings, is indeed non-violence; for from the Veda, dharma has shone forth.
He who harms harmless beings out of a desire for his own pleasure finds no happiness anywhere, neither while living nor after death. (68)
He who does not desire to inflict the affliction of bondage upon living beings, seeking the welfare of all, attains ultimate happiness. (69)
Whatever one meditates upon, whatever one does, and wherever one fixes the mind—that very thing one obtains without effort, provided one harms no living being. (70)
For meat is never produced without having caused injury to living beings, and the killing of living beings does not lead to heaven; therefore, one should abstain from meat. (71)
Having carefully considered the origin of meat and the slaughter and imprisonment of embodied beings, one should desist from the consumption of all meat. //72//
He who does not eat meat, even while disregarding the [prescribed] rule, like a *piśāca*, becomes beloved in the world and is not afflicted by diseases. (73)
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, the buyer and seller, the one who prepares the meat, the one who serves it, and the one who eats it—all these are slayers. (74)
There is no doer of unmeritorious deeds greater than he who, without having honored the ancestors and the gods, desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another. (75)
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every year for a hundred years—
And he who does not eat their flesh—the fruit of merit for these two is equal. //76//
By subsisting on pure fruits and roots, and by eating the food of sages;
One does not obtain that fruit which results from the total avoidance of meat. //77//
"He who eats my flesh here shall eat me in the next world.
The wise declare this to be the true nature of "flesh" (māṃsa). ||78||
Thus ends the fifty-first chapter, on Expiations, in the Dharmaśāstra of Viṣṇu.
Chapter Fifty-Two

One who steals gold from a king, confessing his own deed, shall offer a wooden pestle [to the king]. He becomes purified either by death or by being released. Or he may perform the *mahāvrata* penance for twelve years. The same applies to one who misappropriates a deposit. One who steals grain, cooked food, or wealth shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance for one year. For the theft of a human being, a woman, a field, a well, or a reservoir, one shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*. For the theft of articles of little value, one shall perform the *sāṃtapana*. For the theft of edible or consumable food, vehicles, beds, seats, flowers, roots, or fruits, one shall drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). For the theft of grass, wood, trees, dry food, molasses, clothing, leather, or meat, one shall fast for three nights. For the theft of gems, pearls, coral, copper, silver, iron, or bell-metal, one shall eat only grain-particles for twelve days. For the theft of cotton, silk, wool, and so forth, one shall subsist on milk for three nights. For the theft of cloven-hoofed or single-hoofed animals, one shall fast for three nights. For the theft of birds, perfumes, medicinal herbs, ropes, or wickerwork, one shall fast for one day.
Having restored by some means the property that was taken after being given,
one should then perform penance for the removal of that defilement.
Whatever a man who is unrestrained might take from others,
by that very thing he shall be deprived, wherever he is reborn.
Since both life and the desire for the Dharma are established upon wealth, one should therefore avoid harming wealth through every possible effort. (16)
He who is intent on harming living beings as well as he who is intent on harming wealth—of these two, the one intent on harming wealth attains great suffering. (17)
Thus ends the fifty-second chapter, on Expiations, in the Dharmaśāstra of Viṣṇu.
Chapter Fifty-Three.

Now, for approaching a woman who should not be approached, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance for one year in the forest, wearing bark garments, according to the procedure for the Great Vow (mahāvrata). This also applies to approaching the wife of another. For approaching a cow, one must perform the cow-vow (govrata). In the case of sexual intercourse with a male, in a non-vaginal opening, in the air, in water, during the daytime, or in a vehicle drawn by oxen, one should bathe clothed. Upon approaching a Caṇḍāla woman, one attains equality with her. If it was done unintentionally, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. For approaching an animal or a prostitute, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance. A woman who has once committed adultery should perform that same vow which applies to the man regarding another's wife.
Whatever sin a twice-born man incurs by consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night, he removes that by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [sacred texts] for three years. (9)
Thus ends the fifty-third chapter, concerning the wives of others, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Fifty-Four.

He who associates with one of evil soul shall perform the same penance as that person. (1) Having drunk water from a well from which a five-toed animal has died, or from one that is utterly defiled, a Brāhmaṇa shall fast for three nights; (2) a Kṣatriya for two days; (3) a Vaiśya for one day; (4) and a Śūdra for a single night. (5) At the conclusion of the vow, all of them shall drink the *pañcagavya*. (6) If a man fails to approach his wife during her season, except on forbidden lunar days (*parvan*), he shall fast for three nights. (8) A false witness shall perform the penance prescribed for killing a Brāhmaṇa. (9) For voiding urine or excrement in a place devoid of water, one shall bathe with one's clothes on and perform an oblation with the *mahāvyāhṛti* formulas. (10) One who is overtaken by the sun rising while he is still asleep shall bathe with his clothes on and repeat the *Sāvitrī* mantra one hundred and eight times. (11) One bitten by a dog, jackal, cat, village pig, donkey, monkey, crow, or by an unchaste woman, shall go to a river and perform sixteen breath-control exercises (*prāṇāyāma*). (12) One who neglects the Vedas or the sacred fires shall bathe at the three periods of the day, sleep on the ground, and subsist for a year on alms collected only once a day. (13) For speaking falsely regarding one's own excellence, for falsely accusing a teacher, or for slandering him, one shall subsist on milk for a month. (14) An atheist, one who lives like an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who destroys the livelihood of a Brāhmaṇa—these five shall subsist on alms for five years. (15) The younger brother who marries before his elder, the elder brother so superseded, the woman who is thus superseded, the giver of the girl in marriage, and the officiating priest shall each perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (16) A seller of living beings, land, merit, or Soma shall perform the *Taptakṛcchra* penance. (17) A seller of fresh herbs, flowers, roots, skins, bamboo, split cane, chaff, potsherds, hair, ashes, bones, milk products, oil-cakes, sesame seeds, or sesame oil shall perform the *Prājāpatya* penance. (18) A seller of phlegm, lac, beeswax, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, tin, lead, black iron, copper, or swords shall perform the *Mahāsāntapana* penance. (19) A seller of dyed cloth, dyes, gems, perfumes, molasses, honey, sugar, or wool shall fast for three nights. (20) A seller of meat, salt, lac, or milk shall perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (21) And he must undergo initiation again. (22) Having traveled on a camel or a donkey, or having bathed, slept, or eaten while naked, one shall perform three breath-control exercises. (23)
Having recited three thousand repetitions of the Sāvitrī with a concentrated mind,
and having drunk only milk for a month in a cow-pen, one is released from the sin of accepting improper gifts.

Having performed sacrifices for those unworthy of sacrificing, having performed the funeral rites for others, and having practiced malevolent magic or the Ahīna sacrifice, one removes the taint by means of three Kṛcchra penances.
Those twice-born men for whom the Sāvitrī has not been recited according to the rule, one should cause them to perform three Kṛcchra penances and then initiate them according to the rule. (26)
This same penance should be prescribed even for those twice-born men who, having engaged in forbidden acts and being excluded from the status of Brahmanas, desire to perform expiation.
When Brahmins acquire wealth through a censurable occupation, they become pure by relinquishing it, as well as by silent recitation and austerity. (28)
In the case of the omission of obligatory rites prescribed by the Vedas, and in the case of a breach of the vows of a *snātaka*, the penance is fasting. (29)

Having threatened [to strike] a Brahmin, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; for actually striking him, the *atikṛcchra*; and for drawing blood from a Brahmin, one should perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*.
One should not engage in any business with those who have committed sins until they have been purified; once they have undergone purification, a knower of dharma should not hold them in contempt.

One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who has sought refuge, or those who have killed women— even if they are pure according to the Dharma.
A child under sixteen years of age, as well as one who is eighty years old,
women, and the sick, deserve only half of the prescribed expiation.
But for the removal of sins for which no expiation has been stated, one should prescribe an expiation after considering both the capacity [of the offender] and the nature of the sin. (34)
Thus ends the fifty-fourth chapter, on miscellaneous expiations, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Fifty-five.

Now follow the secret penances (rahasya-prāyaścittas). 1. Having approached a flowing river and bathed, one who has committed the murder of a Brahmin (brahmahā) becomes purified in one month by performing sixteen breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) daily and eating sacrificial food (haviṣya) once a day. 2. At the conclusion of the rite, he should give a milch cow as a gift. 3. By means of the Aghamarṣaṇa vow, a drinker of spirituous liquor (surāpa) becomes purified. 4. By the recitation of ten thousand repetitions of the Gāyatrī, one who has stolen gold (suvarṇasteyakṛt) [is purified]. 5. One who has violated the teacher’s bed (gurutalpaga) is purified by fasting for three nights and performing the recitation and fire-oblation (japa-homa) of the Puruṣasūkta.
Just as the horse-sacrifice, the king of rituals, removes all sins,
so too does the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn remove all sins.
A twice-born man should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) for the removal of all sins;
indeed, all the sins of a twice-born man are consumed by breath control. (8)
One should recite the Gāyatrī together with the Vyāhṛtis, the Praṇava, and the Śiras three times while restraining the breath; that is called Prāṇāyāma. (9)
Prajāpati drew forth from the three Vedas the syllable *a*, the syllable *u*, and the syllable *m*, as well as the words *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*. (10)
From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out one quarter from each; that [quarter] constitutes this verse of the Sāvitrī. (11)
By muttering this syllable and this [Gāyatrī] preceded by the Vyāhṛtis during both twilights, a Brahmin becomes endowed with the merit of the Vedas. ||12||
But by practicing this triad externally a thousand times, a twice-born man is freed from even great sin within a month, just as a snake is freed from its skin.
Even one born from the womb of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya, when joined with this verse and with his own timely ritual action, attains honor among the virtuous.
The three imperishable great utterances preceded by the syllable Oṃ, together with the three-footed Gāyatrī, should be known as the mouth of Brahman. (15)
