He who studies this day after day for three years without weariness reaches the supreme Brahman, becoming like the wind and taking on the form of space.
The single syllable is the supreme Brahman; breath control is the supreme austerity;
there is nothing superior to the Sāvitrī; and truth excels silence. (17)
All Vedic rites of offering oblations and sacrifices flow away;
but the Imperishable is to be known as the Imperishable, as Brahman, and as Prajāpati. 18.
The sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the sacrifice of ritual action (vidhiyajña);
the whispered (upāṃśu) is a hundredfold, and the mental (mānasa) is declared to be a thousandfold.
The four types of cooked sacrifices (pākayajña), together with the ritual sacrifices (vidhiyajña), are all not worth even a sixteenth part of the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña). ||20||
A Brahmin shall attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt about this.
Whether he performs other rites or not, one who is friendly toward all is called a Brahmin. (21)
Thus ends the fifty-fifth chapter, on secret penances, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Fifty-Six.

Now, therefore, follow the purifiers of all the Vedas (sarvavedapavitra). By means of the recitation and the burnt offerings (homa) of these, the twice-born are purified from their sins. 1. The Aghamarṣaṇa; 2. The Devakṛta; 3. The Śuddhavatīs; 4. The Taratsamandīya; 5. The Kūṣmāṇḍyas; 6. The Pāvamānyas; 7. The Durgāsāvitrī; 8. The Abhiṣaṅgas; 9. The Padastobhas; 10. The Vyāhṛtis; 11. The Bhāruṇḍas; 12. The Candrasāman; 13. The Puruṣavrata, the Devavrata, and the Bhāsa; 14. The Abliṅgas; 15. The Bārhaspatya Vāksūkta; 16. The Gosūkta; 17. The Aśvasūkta and the Madhucchas; 18. The two Sāmans, the Aindra and the Śuddha; 19. The Śatarudriya; 20. The Atharvaśiras; 21. The Trisuparṇa; 22. The Mahāvrata; 23. The Nārāyaṇīya; 24. The Puruṣasūkta.
The three Ājyadohas, the Rathantara, the Agnivratam, the Vāmadevya, and the Bṛhat—
these, when studied, purify a person.
One who so desires shall obtain the memory of past births. ||27||
Thus ends the fifty-sixth chapter, on Purification, in the Dharmaśāstra of Viṣṇu.
Chapter Fifty-Seven.

Now, those who are unworthy of receiving sacrificial offerings: 1. The *vrātyas*; 2. The fallen (*patita*); 3. Those who are impure for three generations on both the mother’s and the father’s side; 4. All such persons are unfit to be fed and their gifts must not be accepted. 5. One should avoid even the inclination to accept gifts from those from whom one ought not to accept. 6. By accepting gifts, the spiritual luster (*brāhmya-tejas*) of Brāhmaṇas perishes. 7. He who accepts a gift without knowing the rules for accepting objects sinks into hell along with the giver. 8. But he who is capable of accepting yet refrains from accepting attains the world of the givers. 9. One should not reject fuel, water, roots, fruits, protection from fear, meat, honey, a bed, a seat, a house, flowers, curd, or vegetables when they are offered. 10.
Prajāpati considered alms that have been brought forward and offered spontaneously, even if not requested beforehand, as acceptable even from one who has performed evil deeds.
The ancestors do not eat his offerings for fifteen years,
nor does the fire carry his oblations, he who treats her with contempt.
Desiring to support his teachers and dependents, and wishing to honor the gods and guests,
he may accept gifts from all sources, but he himself should not be satisfied by that alone.
Even when capable of receiving gifts for these aforementioned purposes, one should not accept them from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy. (14)
But when the teachers have passed away, or when living at home without them,
one seeking a means of livelihood for oneself should always accept [gifts] from a virtuous person.
A partner in a business venture, a family friend, a slave, a cowherd, and a barber—among Śūdras, these are those whose food may be eaten, as well as one who offers himself [as a servant]. (16)
Thus ends the fifty-seventh chapter, on the subject of food that may and may not be eaten, in the Dharmaśāstra of Viṣṇu.
Chapter Fifty-Eight.

Now, for a householder, wealth is of three kinds: white, variegated, and black. (2) Whatever funeral rite (*aurdhvadehika*) one performs with white wealth, that he enjoys after attaining the state of a deity. (3) Whatever [he performs] with variegated wealth, that is the human state. (4) Whatever [he performs] with black wealth, that is the state of an animal. (5) That which is acquired through one’s own occupation is white for everyone. (6) That which is acquired through the occupation immediately following one’s own is variegated; and that which is acquired through an occupation separated by one degree is also indeed variegated. (7) That which is acquired through a superior occupation is black. (8)
Inheritance received in succession, a gift of affection, and property acquired together with one's wife—
all such wealth is declared to be "white" (pure) for all without distinction.
Wealth obtained through bribery or taxes, from the sale of what ought not to be sold, or received as a reward for a service rendered, is called "spotted" (śabala) wealth. ||10||
That which is acquired through gambling, theft, distress, forgery, violence, or by means of a pretext is declared to be *kṛṣṇa* (black) wealth. ||11||
Whatever a person performs with a particular kind of material substance,
he obtains a corresponding fruit both hereafter and in this world.
Thus ends the fifty-eighth chapter, on the Purification of Gifts, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
[Note: The numbering provided in the source text appears to be inconsistent with the title "Chapter Fifty-Nine."]

A householder shall perform the *pākayajñas* in the domestic fire established at marriage. (1) He shall perform the *agnihotra* every morning and evening. (2) He shall offer oblations to the deities. (3) At the times of the conjunction and opposition of the moon and sun, he shall sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa* rites. (4) At each solstice, he shall sacrifice with an animal. (5) In autumn and summer, he shall sacrifice with the *āgrayaṇa*. (6) Or, when rice and barley have ripened. (7) He who possesses food sufficient for three years or more [is exempt from these]. (8) Every year, he shall sacrifice with the *soma* rite. (9) In the absence of wealth, he shall perform the *vaiśvānarī* sacrifice. (10) He should avoid performing a sacrifice for the sake of a Śūdra. (11) Whatever wealth has been obtained or begged for the purpose of a sacrifice, he must give it all away. (12) Every morning and evening, he shall offer the *vaiśvadeva* oblation. (13) And he shall give alms to a mendicant. (14) By giving alms to a mendicant with due honor, one obtains the fruit of giving a cow. (15) In the absence of a mendicant, he shall give the first portion of food to a cow. (16) Or he may cast it into the fire. (17) Even when food is already prepared, he must not turn away a mendicant. (18) The five slaughter-houses of a householder are the mortar, the grinding stone, the hearth, the water-jar, and the household utensils. (19) To expiate for these, he shall perform the sacrifices to Brahman, the gods, the ancestors, the spirits, and men. (20) Vedic study is the sacrifice to Brahman. (21) The burnt offering is the sacrifice to the gods. (22) The libation to the ancestors is the sacrifice to the ancestors. (23) The bali-offering is the sacrifice to the spirits. (24) The honoring of guests is the sacrifice to men. (25)
He who does not offer sustenance to these five— the gods, guests, dependents, ancestors, and himself— does not truly live, even though he breathes.
The student, the ascetic, and the mendicant live by means of the householder's stage of life;
therefore, a householder should not treat these guests with contempt.
The householder alone performs sacrifice; the householder practices austerity;
and the householder gives gifts; therefore, the one in the householder stage of life is the most excellent. ||28||
Sages, ancestors, gods, living beings, and likewise guests, all have expectations from householders; therefore, the householder stage of life is the most excellent.
The constant pursuit of the three goals of life, the giving of food, the worship of the gods, the honoring of Brahmins,
the practice of Vedic study, and the libations to the ancestors.
Having done so, the householder goes to the station of Śakra. ||30||
Thus ends the fifty-ninth chapter, the section on the householder, in the Dharmaśāstra of Viṣṇu.
Chapter Sixty.

Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should void urine and feces. (1) At night one should face south; by day and during the two twilights, one should face north. (2) Not on uncovered ground; (3) not on ground ploughed by a plow; (4) not in the shade; (5) not on saline soil; (6) not on grassy ground; (7) not in a hole containing living creatures; (8) not on an anthill; (10) not on a path; (11) not on a carriage road; (12) not on what is defiled by others; (13) not in a garden; (14) not near water; (15) not on ashes; (16) not on embers; (17) not on cow-dung; (18) not in a cow-pen; (19) not in the open air; (20) not in water; (21) nor should one face the wind, fire, the sun, the moon, a woman, a teacher, or a Brahmin. (22) Nor indeed with the head uncovered. (23) Having wiped the anus with a clod of earth while holding the penis, one should rise and perform purification with water and earth drawn from [a clean spot], which removes both odor and stain. (24)
One [application] on the penis, three on the anus, likewise ten on one hand, seven on both hands, and exactly three on the feet. (25)
This is the purification for householders; it is twofold for students, threefold for forest-dwellers, and fourfold for ascetics. ||26||
Thus ends the sixtieth chapter, the Section on Purification, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Sixty-One.

Now, one should not use a tooth-stick made of *pālāśa* wood. (1) Nor one produced from *śleṣmātaka*, *ariṣṭa*, *vibhītaka*, *dhava*, or *dhanvana*. (2) Nor one produced from *kovidāra*, *śamī*, *pīlu*, *pippala*, *iṅguda*, or *guggulu*. (3) Nor one produced from *bandhūka*, *nirguṇḍī*, *śigru*, *tilvaka*, *tinduka*, or *pāribhadraka*. (4–5) Nor one produced from *āmlikā*, *mocaka*, *śalmalī*, or *śaṇa*. (6) It should not be sweet. (7) Nor sour. (8) Nor dried at the top. (9) Nor hollow. (10) Nor foul-smelling. (11) Nor slimy. (12) One should not face south or west while using it; rather, one should use it facing north or east. (13) [The wood should be] any one of the following: *vaṭa*, *asana*, *arka*, *khadira*, *karañja*, *karavīra*, *sarja*, *arimeda*, *apāmārga*, *mālatī*, *kakubha*, or *bilva*. (14) It should be astringent, bitter, or pungent. (15)
Having its thickness equal to the tip of the little finger, equipped with a brush, and twelve finger-breadths in length, one should eat the tooth-stick after breakfast, remaining silent. 16.
Having rinsed it and broken it, one should carefully discard it in a clean place.
On the new moon day (amāvāsyā), one should by no means consume a tooth-stick.
Thus ends the sixty-first chapter, concerning the brushing of the teeth, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Sixty-Two.

Now, at the root of the pupils of the twice-born, there is the *tīrtha* named Prājāpatya (1). At the base of the thumb is the Brāhma (2). At the tips of the fingers is the Daiva (3). At the base of the index finger is the Pitrya (4). Seated in a clean place, with water that is not hot from fire, free of foam, not drawn by a Śūdra or with only one hand, and not saline, he—being composed in mind and cheerful, sitting with his knees apart and facing either east or north—should perform the ritual sipping (*ācamana*) while focused on that [act] (5). Having drunk three times using the Brāhma *tīrtha* (6), he should wipe his mouth twice (7). He should touch the cavities of the head, the crown of the head, and the heart with water (8).
The twice-born classes are purified by [water] reaching the heart, the throat, and the palate respectively;
a woman and a Śūdra are purified by water touched once at the end [of the mouth]. (9)
Thus ends the sixty-second chapter, on the procedure for sipping water (ācamana), in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Sixty-Three.

Now, he may set out on a journey for the sake of *yogakṣema* (security and well-being). 1. He should not travel alone. 2. He should not travel with unrighteous persons. 3. Nor with *vṛṣalas* (outcastes or low-born people). 4. Nor with enemies. 5. Nor too early at dawn. 6. Nor in the evening. 7. Nor during the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*). 8. Nor at midday. 9. Nor where water is not available nearby. 10. Nor too hurriedly. 11. Nor in a continuous, unbroken manner. 12. Nor with vehicles that are infested by predators, diseased, or considered inauspicious. 13. Nor with those having missing limbs. 15. Nor with those having extra limbs. 16. Nor with those that are not self-controlled. 17. Nor with those having redundant limbs. 18. Without first providing fodder and water to his draft animals, he should not satisfy his own hunger and thirst. 19. He should not stand upon a crossroads. 20. Nor at night beneath a tree. 21. Nor in an empty house. 23. Nor in a slaughterhouse or a prison. 24. Nor over hair, husks, potsherds, bones, ashes, or charcoal. 25. Nor over cotton seeds. 26. He should circumambulate a crossroads clockwise. 27. So too an image of a deity. 28. And well-known trees. 29. Also fire, a Brāhmaṇa, a courtesan, a full water-jar, a mirror, an umbrella, a banner, a flag, a *śrīvṛkṣa*, a *vardhamāna*, and a *nandyāvarta*. 30. Also a palm-leaf fan, a fly-whisk, the king of elephants, a cow, curds, milk, clarified butter, honey, and white mustard. 31. Also a lute, sandalwood, weapons, fresh cow dung, fruits, flowers, fresh vegetables, yellow pigment (*gorocanā*), and sprouts of *dūrvā* grass. 32. Also a turban, ornaments, gems, gold, silver, clothing, seats, vehicles, and meat. 33. Also a water-pot, a raised mound of earth, a single bound animal, a young girl, and a fish. 34. Now, upon seeing someone intoxicated, insane, or deformed, he should turn back. 35. Also one who has vomited or purged, one with shaven hair, one with matted locks, or a dwarf. 36. Also one wearing ochre robes, a wandering ascetic, one who has fallen from grace, or one who is filthy. 37. Also oil, molasses, dried cow dung, fuel, grass, straw, ashes, and charcoal. 38. Also salt, a eunuch, liquor, a hermaphrodite, cotton, rope, fetters, or one with disheveled hair. 40. He should not step on the shadow of a deity, a Brāhmaṇa, a teacher, a brown cow, or one initiated for a sacrifice. 41. Nor on spittle, vomit, blood, feces, urine, or bathing water. 42. He should not step over a calf-cord. 43. He should not run while it is raining. 44. He should not cross a river in vain (without purpose). 45. Nor without first offering water to the deities and the ancestors. 46. He should not cross a river by swimming with his arms. 47. Nor in a leaking boat. 48. He should not stand upon a riverbank. 49. He should not look down into a well. 50. Nor should he leap over it.

The way must be yielded to the elderly, those carrying burdens, kings, those who have performed the ritual bath, women, the sick, ascetics, and those possessing a wheel; among these, O King, the one who has performed the ritual bath is to be honored even by the monarch.
Thus ends the sixty-third chapter, the Section on Conduct, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Sixty-Four.

One should not perform a bath at the water-reservoirs of others. (1) Or, in times of distress, one may do so after removing five lumps of earth. (2) One who has indigestion [should not bathe]. (3) Nor one who is ill. (4) Nor one who is naked. (5) Nor at night, except during an eclipse. (6) Nor during the two twilights. (8) One who bathes in the morning should bathe after observing the eastern direction seized by the rays of the dawn. (9) Having bathed, one should not shake one's head. (10) Nor should one wring water from one's limbs. (11) Nor should one touch oil or fat. (12) One should not wear a garment previously worn without washing it. (13) Only after bathing should one wear two garments along with a turban. (14) One should not engage in conversation with barbarians, outcastes, or those who have fallen [from their caste]. (15) One should bathe in divine pits, springs, rivers, streams, and waterfalls. (16) Water on the ground is more meritorious than drawn water; flowing water is more meritorious than that which is stagnant; river water is more meritorious than that; and the water of the Gaṅgā is more meritorious than all of these, provided it is accepted by the virtuous. (17) Having removed impurities with earth and water, and having immersed oneself in the water and sipped it, one should consecrate the bathing place (*tīrtha*) with the three verses beginning with *āpo hi ṣṭhā*, the four beginning with *hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*, and the verse *idam āpaḥ pravahata*. (18) Then, submerged in the water, one should mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn three times. (19) Or the verse *tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*. (20) Or the *drupadā* and the *Sāvitrī*. (21) Or the section beginning with *yuñjate manaḥ*. (22) Or the *Puruṣasūkta*. (23) Having bathed while still wearing wet clothes, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) to the gods and ancestors while remaining in the water. (24) And having changed one's clothes and stepped out onto the bank of the sacred site, (25) one should not wring out the bathing cloth without first performing the libation to the gods and ancestors. (26) After bathing, one should sip water according to the prescribed rule. (27) And with the *Puruṣasūkta*, one should offer flowers to the Puruṣa verse by verse. (28) And offerings of handfuls of water. (29) At the very beginning, one should perform the libation for the gods using the "divine" part of the hand. (30) Immediately thereafter, for the ancestors, using the "paternal" part. (31) First, one should perform the libation for those of one's own lineage. (32) Then for relatives and kinsmen. (33) Then for friends. (34) In this manner, one should be a regular bather. (35) Having bathed, one should mutter purifying prayers according to one's ability. (36) Especially the *Sāvitrī*. (37) Or the *Puruṣasūkta*. (38) There is nothing superior to these two. (39)
One who has bathed becomes qualified for rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors, as well as for the recitation of purifying texts and for giving gifts as enjoined by the rules. (40)
Misfortune, ill-fortune, bad dreams, and evil thoughts—these perish for one consecrated with even a mere amount of water; such is the firm conviction. (41)
One who bathes daily does not behold the suffering of the torments of Yama;
by daily bathing, even those people who are doers of evil are purified.
Thus ends the sixty-fourth chapter, on the rules for bathing, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Sixty-Five.

Then, having bathed well, with hands and feet thoroughly washed, and having sipped water according to the rules of purification (*svācānta*), one should worship the Lord Vāsudeva, who is without beginning or end, either before an image of the deity or in water, on land or in water. (1) Having offered the gift of life (*jīvādāna*) with the mantra "The breath of the two Aśvins, that [breath] for you," and having performed the invocation (*āvāhana*) with the hymn "They yoke the mind" (*yuñjate manaḥ*), one should perform prostration with the knees, the hands, and the head. (2) One should present the *arghya* offering with the three verses beginning "O Waters, you indeed... (*āpo hi ṣṭhā*). (3) With the four verses beginning "Golden-hued... (*hiraṇyavarṇāḥ*), the water for washing the feet (*pādya*). (4) With the verse "May the waters of the desert be auspicious to us... (*śaṃ na āpo dhanvanyāḥ*), the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*). (5) With the verse "These waters... (*idam āpaḥ*), the water for bathing (*snānīya*). (6) With the verse "In the chariot, in the axles... (*rathe akṣeṣu*), the unguents and ornaments. (7) With the verse "A youth, well-clothed... (*yuvā suvāsāḥ*), the garment. (8) With the verse "Flower-bearing... (*puṣpavatīḥ*), the flowers. (9) With the verse "You are the pole... (*dhūr asi*), the incense (*dhūpa*). (10) With the verse "You are splendor... (*tejo 'si*), the lamp (*dīpa*). (11) With the verse "Dadhikrāvan... (*dadhikrāvṇaḥ*), the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*). (12) With the eight verses beginning "Hiraṇyagarbha... (*hiraṇyagarbhaḥ*), the food offering (*naivedya*). (13)
The yak-tail fans, the parasol, the measure, as well as the vehicle and the seat—all that one should offer to the deities with the Sāvitra mantra alone. (14)
Having thus worshipped, one should then recite the Puruṣasūkta;
with that very [mantra], one should offer oblations of clarified butter if one desires the eternal state.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, the Section on the Rules for Worship, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Sixty-Six.

One should not perform a rite for the gods with water taken at night. (1) One should not offer an ointment except for sandalwood, saffron, agallochum, camphor, musk, and nutmeg. (2) Nor should one wear clothing dyed blue. (3) Nor should one use an ornament made of a counterfeit of gems or gold. (4) Nor [should one offer] that which is odorless. (5) Nor a flower that is pungent-smelling or foul-smelling. (6) Nor one produced from a thorny plant. (7) Even if it is produced from a thorny plant, one may offer that which is white and fragrant. (8) [One should not offer] red [flowers]. Even if they are red, one may offer those produced from saffron or those born in water. (9) For the purpose of incense, one should not use anything derived from a living being. (10) For the purpose of a lamp, one should use nothing other than clarified butter or oil. (11) For the purpose of an offering (naivedya), one should not use anything unfit for consumption. (12) Even among things fit for consumption, [one should avoid] the milk of goats and buffaloes. (13) And [one should avoid] the flesh of five-toed animals, fish, and pork. (14)
Restrained and pure, he should offer everything with his head bowed; being single-minded and cheerful, he should be free from passion and anger. ||15||
Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, concerning the five modes of worship, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Sixty-Seven.

Then, having swept around the fire, sprinkled water around it, strewn grass around it, and poured water around it, he should take the first portion from all the cooked food and offer it as an oblation: (1) To Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, Aniruddha, Puruṣa, Satya, Acyuta, and Vāsudeva; (2) To Agni, Soma, Mitra, Varuṇa, Indra, Indra and Agni, the Viśvedevas, Prajāpati, Anumati, Dhanvantari, Vāstoṣpati, and to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. (3) Thereafter, he should present the *bali* offering with the remainder of the food: (4) "To the carpenter and to the assistant carpenter. (5) On all sides, to the east of the fire: (6) "Thou art Ambā by name, thou art Dulā by name, thou art Nitatnī by name, thou art Cupuṇīkā by name, thou art Abhrayantī by name, thou art Meghayantī by name, thou art Varṣayantī by name"—thus for all [the corners]. (7) "To Nandinī, Subhagā, Sumaṅgalī, and Bhadraṃkarī"—thus on the corners, moving clockwise. (8) At the pillar and the threshold: "To Śrī Hiraṇyakeśī and to the Lords of the Forest. (9) At the door: "To Dharma and Adharma, and to Mṛtyu. (10) At the water-jar: "To Varuṇa. (11) In the mortar: "To Viṣṇu. (12) On the grinding stone: "To the Maruts. (13) Above the roof: "To King Vaiśravaṇa and to the Spirits. (14) In the eastern part: "To Indra and to Indra’s men. (15) In the southern part: "To Yama and to Yama’s men. (16) In the western part: "To Varuṇa and to Varuṇa’s men. (17) In the northern part: "To Soma and to Soma’s men. (18) In the middle: "To Brahmā and to Brahmā’s men. (19) Above: "To Ākāśa. (20) On the ground: "To the spirits that roam by day," during the day; (21) "To those that roam by night," at night. (22) Then, on *darbha* grass with its tips pointing south, he should perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) to his father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, and to his mother, grandmother, and great-grandmother, mentioning their names and *gotras*. (23) And upon the rice-balls, in order, he should present flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings. (24) Having placed a water-pot nearby, he should have a prayer for well-being recited. (25) But he should scatter [food] on the ground for dogs, crows, and outcastes. (26) And he should give alms. (27) He should exert the greatest effort in honoring guests. (28) Even in the evening, he should diligently feed a guest who has arrived. (29) He should not allow an unfed guest to dwell in his house. (30) Just as the Brāhmaṇa is the master of the social classes (*varṇas*), and just as the husband is the master of women, so is the guest the master of the householder. (31) By honoring him, one attains heaven. (32)
If a guest departs from a house with his hopes frustrated, he takes away the merit of that householder and bestows his own demerit upon him. (33)
A Brahmin staying for even a single night is considered a guest (atithi);
because he stays for a non-permanent duration, he is therefore called a guest. ||34||

One should recognize as a guest a Brahmin who has come from another village, or likewise one who has arrived from the same region, when he has presented himself at the house where the wife resides or even where the sacred fires are maintained. (35)
But if a Kṣatriya has come to the house in the manner of a guest, one may feed him as one pleases once the Brahmins have finished eating. (36)
If a Vaiśya or a Śūdra has arrived at his household as one entitled to the status of a guest,
he should feed them along with his servants, practicing benevolence.
Furthermore, he should hospitably honor his friends and others who have come to his house with affection, and together with his wife, feed them food according to his ability. (38)
One should feed these without hesitation—female residents of the household, young boys, the sick, and likewise pregnant women—before the guests themselves. (39)
But that unwise person who eats before giving to these [beings] does not realize, while eating, that he is being devoured by dogs and vultures. (40)
When the Brahmins and his own servants have indeed finished eating, the husband and wife should afterwards eat what remains. 41.
Having honored the gods, the ancestors, human beings, servants, and the household deities, the householder should thereafter eat what remains. 42.
He who cooks for his own sake eats only sin;
for it is ordained that the food of the virtuous consists of what remains from a sacrifice. 43.
A householder does not attain such worlds through Vedic study, the Agnihotra sacrifice, other sacrifices, or asceticism as he does through the honoring of guests. (44)
To a guest who has arrived, one should offer a seat and water, as well as food according to one's ability, having honored him according to the prescribed rule. (45)
By giving shelter, as well as bedding and an oil massage for the feet along with a lamp,
one obtains through each individual gift a fruit equal to that of the gift of a cow.
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, concerning the Five Great Sacrifices, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Sixty-Eight.

One should not eat during an eclipse of the moon or the sun. (1) One may eat after bathing once they have been released. (2) If they have not been released when they set, one should bathe and eat on the following day. (3) One should not eat during an eclipse of a cow or a Brahmin. (4) Nor during a calamity involving the king. (5) A traveler who maintains the *agnihotra* fire may eat when he believes the *agnihotra* has been offered. (6) He may also eat when he believes the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice has been performed. (7) And on a festival day (*parvan*), when he believes the festival rites have been completed. (8) One should not eat while suffering from indigestion. (9) Not at midnight. (10) Not at midday. (11) Not during the two twilights. (12) Not while wearing wet clothes. (13) Not while wearing only a single garment. (14) Not naked. (15) Not while standing in water. (16) Not while squatting. (17) Not while seated on a broken seat. (18) Not while lying down. (19) Not from a broken vessel. (20) Not from one's lap. (21) Not on the bare ground. (22) Not in the hand. (23) One should not eat salt directly; if someone serves it in that manner, one should not eat it. (24) One should not eat while scolding children. (25) One should not eat delicacies alone. (26) Nor food from which the oil has been extracted. (27) One should not eat parched grain by day. (28) Nor anything mixed with sesame seeds at night. (29) Nor curd-mixed barley meal (*dadhisaktu*). (30) Nor the leafy greens of the *kovidāra*, *vaṭa*, *pippala*, or hemp (*śaṇa*) trees. (31) One should not eat without having given [to others]. (32) Without having offered [into the fire]. (33) Without having moistened one's feet. (34) Nor without having moistened one's hands and face. (35) One should not take clarified butter while still impure from a previous meal. (36) One should not gaze at the moon, the sun, or the stars. (37) One should not touch one's own head. (38) One should not recite the Veda. (39) One should eat facing the east. (40) Or facing the south. (41) One should eat after praising the food. (42) With a cheerful mind, wearing a garland and anointed with unguents. (43) One should not leave no remainder of the food. (44) Except for curd, honey, clarified butter, milk, barley meal, meat paste, and boiled rice. (45)
One should not eat together with one's wife, nor in the open air, nor while standing; many should not look on at one person, nor should many eat together in one place.
One should never drink water from one's cupped hands in an empty house, a fire-chamber, or a temple; nor should one practice over-satiety in eating.
One should not eat a third meal, nor ever anything unwholesome;
one should not eat too early, nor too late, nor having already eaten in the evening, should one eat in the morning.
One should not eat food that is defiled by one's mental state, nor from a vessel defiled by one's mental state;
likewise, one should not eat while lying down, with feet raised, or while sitting with the knees bound together.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, concerning the rules and prohibitions regarding eating, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Sixty-Nine.

One should not approach a woman on the eighth, fourteenth, or fifteenth days of the lunar fortnight. (1) Nor after eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony. (2) Nor after having given [a gift] at a *śrāddha*. (3) Nor when invited to a *śrāddha*. (4) Nor while observing a vow (*vratin*). (5) Nor while initiated for a sacrifice (*dīkṣita*). (6) Nor in a temple, a cemetery, or an empty dwelling. (7) Nor at the foot of a tree. (8) Nor during the daytime. (9) Nor during the two twilights (*saṃdhyā*). (10) Nor one who is unclean (*malinā*). (11) Nor one who is unclean oneself. (12) Nor one who has anointed herself with oil. (13) Nor one who has anointed oneself with oil. (14) Nor one who is afflicted by disease. (15) Nor one who is afflicted by disease oneself. (16)
One who desires to live a long life should not approach a woman who is deficient in limbs, nor one with extra limbs, nor likewise one who is advanced in years, nor a woman who is pregnant. (17)
Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, concerning the conduct of women, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy.

One should not sleep with wet feet. (1) Not with the head toward the north or the west. (2) Not naked. (3) Not along the length of a beam. (4) Not in the open air. (5) Not on a bed made of *pālāśa* wood. (6) Not on one made of five kinds of wood. (7) Not on one made from wood broken by an elephant. (8) Not on one made from wood scorched by lightning. (9) Not on a broken one. (10) Not on one scorched by fire. (11) Not on one made from a tree watered by a jar. (12) Not in cremation grounds, empty dwellings, or temples. (13) Not in the midst of the fickle. (14) Not in the midst of women. (15) Not above grain, cattle, teachers, fire, or the gods. (16)
One should not sleep while impure from food remnants, nor during the day, nor during the two twilights, nor on ashes;
nor in an impure place, nor on moist ground, nor on the summit of a mountain.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, on the rules for sleeping, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy-One.

Now, one should not despise anyone. (1) Nor should one mock those who have missing or extra limbs, nor fools, nor those destitute of wealth. (2) One should not associate with the lowly. (3) One should not perform any action that is contrary to the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*). (4) One should wear attire appropriate to one’s age. (5) [This applies] to one’s learning, lineage, wealth, and country. (6) One should not be arrogant. (7) One should constantly study the scriptures. (8) If one has the means, one should not wear worn-out or dirty clothes. (9) One should not say "it does not exist. (10) One should not wear scentless, foul-smelling, or dyed garlands. (11) However, one may wear red lotuses. (12) One should carry a bamboo staff. (13) And a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) containing water. (14) A sacred thread (*upavīta*) made of cotton. (15) And two golden earrings. (16) One should not look at the rising sun. (17) Nor at the setting sun. Nor at the eclipsed sun. (18) Nor when it is obscured by a cloud or cloth. (19) Nor when it is reflected in a mirror, water, or similar surfaces. (20) Nor at midday. (21) Nor the face of an angry teacher. (22) Nor one’s own reflection in oil or water. (23) Nor in a dirty mirror. (24) Nor a naked woman. (25) Nor one’s own wife while she is eating. (26) Nor anyone while they are urinating. (27) Nor an elephant that has broken from its tethering post. (28) Nor should one watch a fight between bulls or other animals while standing in a dangerous position. (29) Nor a madman. (30) Nor an intoxicated person. (31) One should not throw impure things into fire. (32) Nor blood. (33) Nor poison. (34) Nor even into water. (35) One should not step over fire. (36) Nor warm one’s feet over it. (37) Nor rub oneself on *kuśa* grass. (38) Nor wash oneself in a bronze vessel (*kāṃsya*). (39) Nor touch one foot with the other. (40) Nor scratch the ground. (41) Nor be a crusher of clods of earth. (42) Nor a cutter of grass. (43) Nor bite off one's nails or hair with the teeth. (44) One should avoid gambling. (45) One should not seek the heat of the morning sun. (46) One should not wear clothing, shoes, garlands, or a sacred thread that have been worn by another. (47) One should not give counsel to a *śūdra*. (48) Nor the remains of food (*ucchiṣṭa*), nor sacrificial offerings (*haviskṛta*). (49) Nor sesame seeds. (50) Nor should one teach him the Dharma. (51) Nor religious vows (*vrata*). (52) One should not scratch one’s head or belly with both hands joined together. (53) One should not refuse curds or flowers when offered. (54) One should not remove one’s own garland. (55) One should not wake a sleeping person. (56) One should not cause a dyed object to fade. (57) One should not speak to a woman in her courses (*udakyā*). (58) Nor to barbarians (*mleccha*) or those of the lowest castes. (59) In the presence of fire, gods, Brahmins, or cows, one should keep the right arm uncovered. (60) One should not point out a cow grazing in another’s field. (61) Nor a calf while it is drinking. (62) One should not point out portents. (63) One should not dwell in a kingdom ruled by a *śūdra*. (64) Nor in a place crowded with unrighteous people. (65) Nor in a place lacking an astrologer or a physician. (66) Nor in a place afflicted by disease. (67) One should not stay long on a mountain. Nor in a place infested by snakes. (68) One should not engage in useless activities. (69) Nor in dancing or singing. (70) Nor clap the hands. (71) One should not utter vulgar speech. (72) Nor falsehood. (73) Nor what is unpleasant. (74) One should not strike anyone at their vital points. (75) One who desires to live a long life should not despise himself. (76) One should perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) for a long time. (77) One should not play with snakes or weapons. (78) One should not touch the bodily orifices (*khāni*) without a specific reason. (79) One should not raise a stick against another. (80) If one must punish someone, one should strike them for the sake of correction. (81) And that should be done with a bamboo splinter or a rope on the back. (82) One should avoid speaking ill of the gods, Brahmins, the scriptures, or great souls. (83) One should avoid wealth and pleasure that are contrary to Dharma. (84) One should also avoid even a Dharma that is detested by the world. (85) On festival days (*parvan*), one should perform propitiatory oblations (*śāntihoma*). (86) One should not cut grass. (87) One should remain adorned. (88) Thus should one be a follower of proper conduct (*ācāra*). (89)
One who desires dharma and has conquered his senses should practice that conduct which is proclaimed in the Śruti and Smṛti and which is followed by the virtuous. (90)
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct, the desired offspring;
through right conduct, inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks. (91)
Even if he lacks all auspicious marks, a man who possesses proper conduct, is full of faith, and free from envy, lives for a hundred years. (92)
Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, on Conduct, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy-Two:

One should apply oneself to self-restraint (dama). [1] And self-restraint is the non-diffusion of the senses. [2] For the self-controlled, there is both this world and the next. [3] No action whatsoever succeeds for one who lacks self-control. [4]
Self-control is the supreme purifier; self-control is the supreme auspiciousness.
Through self-control, one obtains everything that is desired by the mind. (5)
If they do not carry away that chariot— yoked with five horses, swift as thought, and following the noble path— of him who travels upon it;
Enemies do not overcome the Tathāgata. ||6||
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in immobility,
even so do all desires enter him.
He attains peace, not the seeker of desires. ||7||
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, on Punishment, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy-Three.

Now, one desiring to perform a *śrāddha* should invite the Brahmins on the day before (the first). On the second day, in the forenoon during the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) or in the afternoon during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), he should seat the Brahmins—who have bathed well and performed the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*)—upon seats covered with *kuśa* grass, according to the order of their learning and seniority. (2) Two for the gods (*daiva*), facing east; three for the ancestors (*pitrya*), facing north. (3) Or, one for each of the two groups. (4) In *ām-śrāddhas* (those using raw grain) and optional rites (*kāmya*), having offered oblations into the fire with the first pentad of verses; (5) in animal sacrifices (*paśu-śrāddha*), with the middle pentad; (6) in new-moon rites (*āmāvāsya*), with the last pentad; (7) after the *Āgrahāyaṇī* festival, and on the eighth days of the dark fortnights, with the first, middle, and last pentads respectively; (8) and likewise on the *Anvaṣṭakā* days. (9) Then, permitted by the Brahmins, he should invoke the ancestors. (10) Having performed the dismissal of the *yātudhānas* (demons) with sesame seeds while reciting the two verses beginning "May the Asuras depart," (11) and having performed the invocation with the verses "Come here, O fathers," "O Agni, bring them all," "May they come to me," and "I hide them behind mountains," he should prepare and offer water for washing the feet (*pādya*) mixed with *kuśa* grass and sesame, using the verses "Those who stand immortal" and "That which my mother [has given]. Having likewise prepared and offered the water for honor (*arghya*), and having honored the Brahmins according to his ability with ointments, garments, flowers, ornaments, incense, and lamps, he should gaze upon them with the verse "The Ādityas, Rudras, Vasus. Having said, "I shall perform the offering in the fire," and being permitted by the Brahmins, he should offer three oblations into the fire as before. (12) Having consecrated the food with the mantras "Those who are my fathers," "This is for you, O fathers," and "This sacrifice," and having poured milk or ghee over it with the verse "This is your strength, the cooked within the raw," he should present the food in whatever vessels are available—especially those made of silver—to the two facing east, starting with the words "Homage to the Viśve Devas. (13) Then, to the father, grandfather, and great-grandfather, by name and lineage, to those facing north. (14) While the Brahmins are eating, he should mutter the verses "Whatever I have done through excess," "By days and nights," and "Whatever of yours is flesh-eating. (15) He should also recite the *Itihāsas*, *Purāṇas*, and *Dharmaśāstras*. (16) Near the remains of the food, upon *darbha* grass with tips pointing south, he should place one rice-ball (*piṇḍa*) for the father with the mantra "The earth is the ladle, it is imperishable"; (17) the second rice-ball for the grandfather with "The atmosphere is the ladle, it is imperishable"; (18) the third rice-ball for the great-grandfather with "The sky is the ladle, it is imperishable. (19) He should give a cloth with the verse "Those ancestors here who have passed away"; (20) food with the verse "Give us heroes, O fathers"; (21) and he should rub his hands at the root of the *darbha* grass with the verse "O fathers, rejoice here. (22) Having sprinkled water around the rice-balls counter-clockwise with the verse "Bringing strength," he should present offerings of perfume, *arghya*, flowers, incense, lamps, food, and various edibles. (23) He should also provide a water-vessel joined with honey and sesame. (24) When the Brahmins have eaten and reached satiety, he should sprinkle the food along with the grass with the mantra "May it not be exhausted," scatter the remnants of the food before the remains, and ask, "Are you satisfied? and "Is it well-prepared? Having first given water for sipping (*ācamana*) to those facing north, then to those facing east, and having sprinkled the *śrāddha* site with the words "Well-sprinkled," he should perform everything while holding *darbha* grass in his hand. (25) Then, standing before those facing east, having circumambulated clockwise with the verse "Whatever I have done, O Rāma," and having returned, he should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) according to his ability, say "May you be pleased," and when they reply "We are pleased," he should mutter the mantra "The gods and the fathers. (26) Having given the water for inexhaustibility (*akṣayyodaka*) by name and lineage, and saying "May the Viśve Devas be gratified" to those facing east, he should then, with palms joined and mind fixed on that, with a cheerful heart, make this request: (27) "May our donors increase, as well as the Vedas and our progeny; may faith not depart from us, and may we have much to give. (28)
Then, with the words "In every battle, [may we be victorious]," he should dismiss those Brahmins,
having honored them according to the rule, followed them for a short distance, and saluted them.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, on the Śrāddha rites, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy-Four

Then, on the Aṣṭakā days, having performed the Śrāddha preceded by the rites for the gods with vegetables, meat, and cakes; and on the Anvaṣṭakā days, having offered oblations into the fire as on the Aṣṭakā days; and having fed the Brahmins for the mother, paternal grandmother, and paternal great-grandmother—preceded by the rites for the gods—as before; and having honored them with sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), he should follow them and dismiss them. Then he should make six trenches (karṣū). Having established the fire at their base as before and having offered oblations, he should perform the offering of rice-balls (piṇḍa) at the base of each trench. There should be three trenches for the males and three for the females. He should fill the three trenches for the males with water mixed with food. He should fill the three trenches for the females with milk mixed with food. [He should fill them] respectively with curd, meat, and milk.
Having filled it, one should recite this: "May this be inexhaustible for you. ||8||
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, concerning the Aṣṭakā rites, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy-Five.

1. When the father is living, he who performs the *śrāddha* should perform it for those for whom his own father would perform it. 2. When both the father and the grandfather are living, [he should perform it] for those for whom his own grandfather would perform it. 3. When the father, the grandfather, and the great-grandfather are all living, he should not perform it at all. 4. He whose father is deceased should, having placed the *piṇḍa* for his father, give [the remaining two] to the two beyond the great-grandfather. 5. He whose father and grandfather are both deceased should, having placed the two *piṇḍas* for them, give [the third] to one beyond the great-grandfather. 6. He whose grandfather is deceased should, having placed the *piṇḍa* for him, give [the remaining two] to the two beyond the great-grandfather.
In this same manner, a wise person should perform the śrāddha for his maternal grandfathers as well;
for the remaining [ancestors], it should be done according to rule with the omission of the mantras, while for the others, it is performed without mantras.
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, on the Rules for Śrāddha, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy-Six:

The new moon day (amāvāsyā), the three Aṣṭakās, the three Anvaṣṭakās, the full moon day of Māgha, the full moon day of Prauṣṭhapada, the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight following [the full moon], and the times of the ripening of rice and barley. (1)
Prajāpati has declared these times for the Śrāddha to be obligatory;
one who does not perform the Śrāddha on these occasions falls into hell. ||2||
Thus ends the seventy-sixth chapter, concerning the Nityaśrāddha, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy-Seven: [The Occasions for Śrāddha]. 1.

The sun’s passage into a new zodiacal sign (saṃkrānti). 2. The two equinoxes (viṣuvat). 3. Especially the two solstices (ayana). 4. The Vyatīpāta yoga. 5. One's own birth-star (janmarkṣa). 6. And occasions of prosperity (abhyudaya).
Prajāpati has indeed declared these to be the optional times for the śrāddha;
whatever śrāddha is offered during these occasions conduces to infinity.
Indeed, a wise person should not perform a Śrāddha during the two twilights or at night;
however, it may be performed even during those times if there is an eclipse of the moon.
For a Śrāddha offering given at the sight of Rāhu remains as long as the moon and stars endure; endowed with all virtues, it fulfills every desire for the ancestors.
Thus ends the seventy-seventh chapter, concerning the Śrāddha for Specific Desires, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy-Eight.

One who constantly performs the *śrāddha* on Sunday attains health; on Monday, good fortune; on Tuesday, victory in battle; on Wednesday, all desires; on Thursday, the desired knowledge; on Friday, wealth; on Saturday, long life; under the *Kṛttikā* asterism, heaven; under *Rohiṇī*, offspring; under *Mṛgaśiras*, spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*); under *Ārdrā*, success in undertakings; under *Punarvasu*, land; under *Puṣya*, nourishment; under *Āśleṣā*, prosperity; under *Maghā*, all desires; under *Pūrvaphalgunī*, good fortune; under *Uttaraphalgunī*, wealth; under *Hasta*, preeminence among one’s kin; under *Citrā*, handsome sons; under *Svāti*, success in trade; under *Viśākhā*, gold; under *Anurādhā*, friends; under *Jyeṣṭhā*, sovereignty; under *Mūla*, agriculture; under *Pūrvāṣāḍhā*, success in sea-voyages; under *Uttarāṣāḍhā*, all desires; under *Abhijit*, preeminence; under *Śravaṇa*, all desires; under *Dhaniṣṭhā*, strength; under *Śatabhiṣaj*, health; under *Pūrvabhādrapadā*, base metals; under *Uttarabhādrapadā*, a house; under *Revatī*, cattle; under *Aśvinī*, horses; under *Bharaṇī*, long life. On the first lunar day (*pratipad*), beautiful women come to one’s house; on the second, excellent daughters-in-law; on the third, all desires; on the fourth, fame; on the fifth, prosperity; on the sixth, victory at dice; on the seventh, nourishment; on the eighth, trade; on the ninth, livestock; on the tenth, swift horses; on the eleventh, sons endowed with spiritual luster; on the twelfth, gold and silver; on the thirteenth, good fortune; on the fifteenth, all desires. For the *śrāddha* rite of those slain by weapons, the fourteenth day is recommended. There are also two verses sung by the ancestors: [The verses follow.]
"May there be born in our family some supreme among men, who, being composed, [attains this] on the thirteenth day of the dark fortnight during the rainy season. (52)

He who performs a śrāddha with honey-abundant milk-rice (pāyasa) throughout the entire month of Kārttika, or at the time when the shadow of an elephant falls toward the east, [attains the highest merit].
Thus ends the seventy-eighth chapter, concerning the specific Śrāddhas for particular desires, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Seventy-Nine.

Now, one should not perform a *śrāddha* with water taken at night. (1) In the absence of *kuśa* grass, one should offer *kāśa* or *dūrvā* grass in its place. (2) For the purpose of clothing, one may use threads of cotton or wool. (3) One should avoid fringes, even if they are from unwashed cloth. (4) Flowers that have a pungent odor, those that are odorless, those grown on thorny plants, and those that are red should be avoided. (5) One should offer white flowers that are fragrant, even if grown on thorny plants; likewise, those born in water, even if red. (6) One should not offer fat, marrow, or similar substances for the purpose of a lamp. (7) One should offer oil or clarified butter (*ghṛta*). (8) Nothing derived from living beings should be offered for the purpose of incense. (9) One should offer *guggulu* resin mixed with honey and clarified butter. (10) Sandalwood, saffron, camphor, aloe-wood, and *padmaka* wood are for the purpose of unguents. (11) One should not offer salt directly by hand. (12) Nor should one offer clarified butter, side-dishes, and so forth with the hand. (13) One should offer vessels made of metal. (14) Especially those made of silver. (15) One should offer a woollen blanket, a black antelope skin, sesame seeds, white mustard, and unbroken grains; these are purifying and destroyers of demons. (16) One should avoid long pepper, *sṛmuka*, *bhūstṛṇa*, *asurasa*, mustard, *surasa*, *kūṣmāṇḍa*, *alābu*, eggplant, *pālakyā*, *taṇḍulīyaka*, safflower, *piṇḍamūlaka*, and buffalo milk. (17) One should also avoid kidney beans, lentils, stale food, and prepared salt. (18) One should avoid anger. (19) One should not shed tears. (20) One should not act with haste. (21) For the offering of clarified butter and other items, vessels made of metal, vessels of rhinoceros horn, or vessels of *phalgu* wood are recommended. (22) And on this matter, there is a verse: (23)
A gift given with a sword made of gold or silver, or one made of udumbara wood,
or even with a vessel of phalgu wood, attains imperishability.
Thus ends the seventy-ninth chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.

Chapter Eighty: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices. Part One. Thus have I heard: At one time the Bhagavat was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas, all of whom were great beings who had attained mastery over the dharmas of the Mahāyāna. Among them were the bodhisattva mahāsattvas Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, Akṣayamati, Anantamati, Ratnamati, Gaganagañja, Sarvanīvaraṇaviṣkambhin, Samantabhadra, and others. At that time, the venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, placed his right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him: “Bhagavat, I have heard from the mouth of the Tathāgata that there are five kinds of people who do not attain parinirvāṇa even after a hundred thousand kalpas. What are these five? First, those who harbor malice toward the Three Jewels; second, those who slander the true Dharma; third, those who commit the five heinous crimes; fourth, those who break the precepts; and fifth, those who are arrogant and conceited. These five types of people do not attain parinirvāṇa even after a hundred thousand kalpas. Now, Bhagavat, you have already taught us how to eliminate these five faults. However, I have not yet heard how a person may cultivate the roots of goodness to transcend birth and death and quickly attain parinirvāṇa. May the Bhagavat, out of compassion for us, explain this in detail. The Buddha told Ānanda: “Excellent, excellent! You have asked well. Listen attentively and reflect deeply; I shall now explain it for you. Ānanda replied: “I am listening with all my attention; may the Bhagavat speak. The Buddha said: “Ānanda, if there is a person who wishes to transcend birth and death and quickly attain parinirvāṇa, they should practice the ten virtuous paths of action, the four immeasurable minds, the four bases of miraculous power, the four dhyānas, the four formless absorptions, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the six perfections, the three gates of liberation, the eight liberations, the nine successive absorptions, the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four unhindered knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the eighty-four thousand dharmas of the Great Vehicle. Furthermore, they should uphold the precepts purely, practice meditation and wisdom, and cultivate the various samādhis. They should also generate the mind of great compassion, vow to save all sentient beings, and never abandon the aspiration for supreme perfect enlightenment. By practicing these dharmas, they will transcend birth and death and quickly attain parinirvāṇa. At that time, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha: “Bhagavat, if there is a person who has committed the five heinous crimes or slandered the true Dharma, can they still attain parinirvāṇa by cultivating these roots of goodness? The Buddha told Ānanda: “Even if such a person has committed these grave offenses, if they encounter a good friend, hear the profound Dharma, and give rise to a heart of repentance, they can indeed transcend birth and death and attain parinirvāṇa. Why is this? Because the nature of the Dharma is empty and non-arising; all karmic obstacles are like illusions and dreams. If one realizes this, one is liberated from all suffering. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha: “Bhagavat, what is the name of this teaching? How should we uphold it? The Buddha told Ānanda: “This teaching is called ‘The Method for Transcending Birth and Death and Attaining Parinirvāṇa through Cultivating Roots of Goodness. You should uphold it thus. When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the venerable Ānanda and the entire great assembly, having heard the Buddha’s words, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. Thus ends the first part of the eighty-first chapter of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, titled “The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra’s Vows and Practices. (Note: This title reflects the traditional Chinese structural division; the content corresponds to the initial portion of Chapter 80 in the Sanskrit tradition.)

With sesame, rice, barley, beans, water, roots, fruits, vegetables, *priyaṅgu*, wild rice (*nīvāra*), mung beans, and wheat, they are satisfied for one month. (1) For two months with the flesh of fish. (2) For three months with the meat of the spotted deer (*hāriṇa*). (3) For four months with the meat of a sheep (*aurabhra*). (4) For five months with the meat of birds (*śākuna*). (5) For six months with the meat of a goat (*chāga*). (6) For seven months with the meat of a red deer (*raurava*). (7) For eight months with the meat of the *pārṣata* deer. (8) For nine months with the meat of a gayal (*gāvaya*). (9) For ten months with the meat of a buffalo (*māhiṣa*). (10) For eleven months with the meat of a hornless goat (*tūpara*). (11) For a full year with cow's milk or its derivatives. (12) Black pot-herbs (*kālaśāka*), large-scaled fish (*mahāśalka*), and the meat of the *vārdhrīṇasa* (a type of rhinoceros) are for the satisfaction of the ancestors until the destruction of time (*pitṛkṣaya*). (13) In this regard, there is a verse sung by the ancestors:
We shall eat black potherbs, large-scaled fish, the flesh of the Vārdhrīṇasa crane, and rhinoceroses that are devoid of horns, until the sun sets. (14)
Thus ends the eightieth chapter, concerning the Praise of Meat, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eighty-One.

One should not place food upon a seat. (1) One should not touch it with the foot. (2) One should not spit upon it. (3) One should drive away the *yātudhānas* with sesame or mustard seeds. (4) And one should perform the *śrāddha* in an enclosed space. (5) One should not look at a menstruating woman. (6) Nor a dog. (7) Nor a village pig. (8) Nor a village cock. (9) One should diligently show the *śrāddha* to a goat. (10) The Brahmins should eat while maintaining silence. (11) Not those with their heads wrapped. (12) Not those wearing sandals. (13) Not those with their feet placed upon a stool. (14) Those with missing or extra limbs should not look upon the *śrāddha*. (15) Nor Śūdras. (16) Nor outcasts (*patitas*). (17) Nor those suffering from major diseases. (18) At that time, with the permission of the Brahmins, one should honor a Brahmin or a mendicant. (19) Even when asked by the donor, the Brahmins should not speak of the qualities of the sacrificial offerings (*havirguṇas*). (20)
As long as there is warmth in the food, as long as they eat with speech restrained,
so long do the ancestors eat, until the qualities of the sacrificial offerings have been described.
Having collected food of all kinds and sprinkled it with water,
he should scatter it on the ground in front of those who have eaten.

The leavings on the *darbha* grass and whatever food is scattered there shall be the portion for those who have attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), for those who have died, and for the women of the family who have renounced worldly life.
They declare that the food remaining on the ground after the meal belongs as a share to the group of servants who are upright and free from deceit during the ancestral rite.
Thus ends the eighty-first chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eighty-Two.

In rites for the gods (*daiva-karma*), one should not examine a Brāhmaṇa [for defects]. (1) In rites for the ancestors (*pitrya*), one should examine him with great care. (2) One should avoid those who have missing or extra limbs. (3) And those who persist in forbidden acts (*vikarmastha*). (4) Those who act like cats (*baiḍālavratika*). (5) Those who wear religious marks in vain (*vṛthāliṅgin*). (6) Those who live by astrology (*nakṣatra-jīvin*). (7) Temple-priests (*devalaka*). (8) Physicians. (9) Sons of unmarried women. (10) Sons of such sons. (11) Those who officiate at sacrifices for many people (*bahuyājin*). (12) Those who officiate as priests for an entire village (*grāmayājin*). (13) Those who officiate for Śūdras. (14) Those who officiate for those for whom one should not officiate (*ayājya-yājin*). (15) Outcastes (*vrātya*). (16) Those who officiate for them. (17) Those who work on festive occasions (*parvakāra*). (18) Informers (*sūcaka*). (19) Teachers for a fee (*bhṛtakādhyāpaka*). (20) Those taught by teachers for a fee (*bhṛtakādhyāpita*). (21) Those nourished by the food of Śūdras. (22) Those associated with outcasts (*patita*). (23) Those who do not study the Vedas. (24) Those who have fallen away from the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyopāsana*). (25) Servants of kings. (26) Those of fierce temperament (*ugra*). (27) Those who quarrel with their fathers. (28) And those who have abandoned their father, mother, teacher, sacred fire, or Vedic study. (29)
For these are outcasts among Brahmins, fallen and defilers of the row;
a wise man should avoid them with effort during the performance of a śrāddha rite. (30)
Thus ends the eighty-second chapter, concerning those who defile the assembly, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eighty-three.

Now, those who sanctify the company (paṅktipāvana): one who has thrice kindled the Nāciketa fire; one who maintains the five fires; one who chants the Jyeṣṭha Sāman; one who has mastered the Vedas; one who has mastered even a single auxiliary of the Veda (vedāṅga); one who has mastered the Purāṇas, Itihāsas, and Grammar; one who has mastered even a single treatise on Dharma (dharmaśāstra); one purified by sacrifice; one purified by visiting sacred fords (tīrtha); one purified by austerity; one purified by truth; one purified by charity; one purified by mantras; one devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī; one whose lineage consists of those who have given away their daughters in marriage according to the Brahma rite; one who knows the Trisuparṇa hymn; a son-in-law; and a daughter's son—these are the sanctifiers. Especially so are the practitioners of Yoga (yogins). Regarding this, there is a verse sung by the ancestors:
There may be such a being in a family who would diligently feed a yogi at a śrāddha ceremony; by him we are satisfied. (21)
Thus ends the eighty-third chapter, on those who purify the company, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eighty-Four:

One should not perform a *śrāddha* rite in a land of barbarians (*mleccha*). (1) One should not go to a land of barbarians. (2) By drinking water at the wells of others [in such a land], one attains equality with them. (3)
One should know that country as a land of Mlecchas in which the established order of the four castes does not exist; beyond that is Āryāvarta. ||4||
Thus ends the eighty-fourth chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eighty-Five.

Now, at Puṣkara, the Śrāddha is inexhaustible; so too are recitations, oblations, and ascetic penances. (1–2) Merely by bathing at Puṣkara, one becomes purified from all sins. (3) It is exactly the same at Gayāśīrṣa, (4) at the Vaṭa tree, (5) on Mount Amarakaṇṭaka, (6) on Mount Varāha, (7) anywhere on the banks of the Narmadā, (8) on the banks of the Yamunā, (9) especially at the Gaṅgā, (10) at Gaṅgādvāra, (11) and at Prayāga, (12) at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean, (13) at Kuśāvarta, (14) at Bilvaka, (15) on Mount Nīla, (16) at Kanakhala, (17) at Kubjāmra, (18) at Bhṛgutuṅga, (19) at Kedāra, (20) at Mahālaya, (21) at Lāḍatikā, (22) at Sugandhā, (23) at Śākambharī, (24) at Phalgutīrtha, (25) at Mahāgaṅgā, (26) at Taṇḍulikāśrama, (27) at Kumāradhārā, (28) at Prabhāsa, (29) and anywhere on the Sarasvatī, especially so, (30) constantly in the Naimiṣa forest, (31) especially at Vārāṇasī, (32) at Agastyāśrama, (33) at Kaṇvāśrama, (34) at the Kauśikī, (35) on the banks of the Sarayū, (36) at the confluence of the Śoṇa and the Jyotīrathyā, (37) at Śrīparvata, (38) at Kālodaka, (39) at Uttaramānasa, (40) at Vaḍavā, (41) at Mataṅgavāpī, (42) at Saptārṣa, (43) at Viṣṇupada, (44) at Svargamārgaprada, (45) at the Godāvarī, (46) at the Gomatī, (47) at the Vetravatī, (48) at the Vipāśā, (49) at the Vitastā, (50) on the banks of the Śatadrū, (51) at the Candrabhāgā, (52) at the Irāvatī, (53) on the banks of the Sindhu, (54) in the southern Pañcanada, (55) at Auṣaja, (56) and in other such holy places (tīrthas), (57) in the best of rivers, (58) at their confluences and sources, (59) on sandbanks, (60) at springs, (61) on mountains, (62) in groves, (63) in forests, (64) in parks, (65) in houses smeared with cow dung, (66) and in charming spots. (67) Regarding this, there are verses sung by the ancestors: (68)
May that being be born in our family who would offer us handfuls of water in rivers with abundant waters, especially those that are cool. (69)
"May there be born in our family some supreme among men who, with a concentrated mind, shall perform for us the śrāddha ceremony at the Banyan Tree of Gayāśīrṣa. (70)
One should desire many sons, so that even one among them might go to Gayā,
or perform an Aśvamedha sacrifice, or release a dark-colored bull.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, the Section on Sacred Fords (Tīrtha-prakaraṇa), in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eighty-Six.

Now follows the rite of the release of a bull (*vṛṣotsarga*). [1] It should be performed on the full moon day of either Kārttika or Āśvayuja. [2] At the very beginning of that ceremony, one should examine a bull. [3] It should be the calf of a cow that has living calves and is full of milk. [4] It must possess all the auspicious marks. [5] It should be blue, [6] or red, with its face, tail, and feet entirely white, or half-white. [7] It should also be one that protects the herd. [8] Then, having strewn grass around a well-kindled fire in the midst of the cows, and having cooked a sacrificial pap (*caru*) for Pūṣan, one should offer oblations with the verses "May Pūṣan follow our cows" and "May there be delight here," and have the blacksmith brand the bull. [9] On one side [he should brand it] with a discus, and on the other with a trident. [10] Once branded, he should bathe it with the four verses beginning with "The golden steed" (*hiraṇyavarṇa*) and with the verse "Be gracious to us, O goddesses" (*śaṃ no devīḥ*). [11] Having brought the bathed and adorned bull together with four bathed and adorned young heifers, he should recite the Rudra hymns, the *Puruṣasūkta*, and the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras there. [12] And he should whisper the mantra "Thou art the father, O calf" (*pitā vatse*) into the right ear of the bull. [13] And this [following verse]: [14]
For the Blessed Lord Dharma is proclaimed to be a bull with four feet;
I choose him with devotion; may he protect me on all sides. (15)
I give this young man to you as a husband; sport with him, your beloved,
and do not be parted from offspring nor from our own bodies.
O King Soma, may we not be delivered over to our enemy. 16.
One should have a bull yoked with a heifer placed in the northeastern direction;
one should give a pair of garments, gold, and even bell-metal to the Hotṛ priest.
The blacksmith should be given wages according to his heart's desire;
one should provide him with food containing abundant ghee and feed the Brahmins there as well. ||18||
In whatever reservoir a bull that has been released drinks, that entire reservoir serves his ancestors. (19)
Wherever a proud bull scratches the earth with its horn, that constitutes an abundant offering of food for the ancestors. (20)
Thus ends the eighty-sixth chapter, concerning the Release of the Bull, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eighty-Seven.

Then, on the full moon day of Vaiśākha, having prepared a black antelope skin complete with its hooves and horns—its horns adorned with gold and its hooves with silver, and its tail decorated with pearls—one should spread it out upon a stretched woolen cloth. (1) One should also provide a golden navel for it. (2) Then one should cover it with sesame seeds. (3) [One should cover it] with a pair of new, unwashed garments. (4) One should adorn it with all kinds of perfumes and jewels. (5) Having placed four metallic vessels filled with milk, curd, honey, and clarified butter in the four directions, one should give [the gift] to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires, who is well-adorned, and covered with a pair of garments. (6) And regarding this, there are these verses: (7)
But he who should give a black antelope skin, complete with hooves and horns, covered with sesame seeds and cloths, and adorned with all kinds of jewels; ||8||
By him, the earth with its oceans, caves, mountains, forests, and groves—extending to its four boundaries—would have been given; of this there is no doubt. (9)
He who places sesame seeds, gold, honey, and clarified butter upon a black antelope skin and gives them to a Brahmin overcomes all evil deeds.
Thus ends the eighty-seventh chapter, the section on the black antelope skin, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Eighty-Eight:

Now, a cow that is about to give birth becomes the earth. By giving her, adorned with ornaments, to a Brāhmaṇa, one obtains the fruit of a gift of the earth. Regarding this, there is a verse: [Verse 3]
Having given a cow with its calf facing both ways, one who is faithful and composed attains heaven for as many ages as there are hairs on its body. (4)

Thus ends the eighty-eighth chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra. Chapter Eighty-Nine: The month of Kārttika has Agni as its presiding deity, and Agni is the deity of all the gods. (1) Agni is the mouth of all the gods. (2) Therefore, one should bathe outdoors during the month of Kārttika; by being devoted to the recitation of the Gāyatrī and eating sacrificial food once [a day], one becomes purified from the sins committed throughout the year. (3) On this subject, there is a verse: (4)

One who bathes in the morning throughout the entire month of Kārttika, with senses subdued, reciting [mantras], eating sacrificial food (haviṣya), and remaining tranquil, is liberated from all sins. ||5||
Thus ends the eighty-ninth chapter, concerning the Kārttika vow, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.

On the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of Mārgaśīrṣa, when it is joined with the asterism Mṛgaśīrṣa, one should present at moonrise a prastha of powdered salt with a golden center to a Brāhmaṇa. By this rite, one is born endowed with beauty and good fortune. If the full moon of Pauṣa should be joined with Puṣya, on that day one whose body has been rubbed with a paste of white mustard seeds, who has been sprinkled with a jar full of cow’s ghee, and who has bathed with all medicinal herbs, all perfumes, and all seeds, should bathe the Blessed Vāsudeva with ghee, worship him with flowers, perfumes, food offerings, and so forth, offer oblations into the fire with Vaiṣṇava, Śakra, and Bārhaspatya mantras, feed the Brāhmaṇas with ghee mixed with gold, and cause them to pronounce blessings. One should also give a pair of garments to the officiant. By this rite, one prospers. If the full moon of Māgha should be joined with Maghā, by performing a *śrāddha* with sesame seeds on that day, one becomes purified. If the full moon of Phālguna should be joined with Phalgunī, by offering a well-prepared bed with a fine mattress to a Brāhmaṇa on that day, one obtains a beautiful wife who is virtuous and wealthy. A woman likewise obtains a husband. If the full moon of Caitra should be joined with Citrā, by the gift of variegated garments on that day, one obtains good fortune. On the full moon of Vaiśākha, having gratified seven Brāhmaṇas with sesame seeds mixed with honey and having pleased Dharmarāja, one becomes purified from sins. If the full moon of Jyaiṣṭha should be joined with Jyeṣṭhā, by the gift of an umbrella and sandals on that day, one attains lordship over a city. On the full moon of Āṣāḍha, when it is joined with Āṣāḍhā, by the gift of food and drink, one obtains that very same reward in an inexhaustible form. On the full moon of Śrāvaṇa, when it is joined with Śravaṇa, by giving a water-cow (a vessel for water) accompanied by food and covered with a pair of garments, one attains the heavenly world. On the full moon of Prauṣṭhapada, when it is joined with that asterism, by the gift of a cow, one becomes liberated from all sins. On the full moon of Āśvayuja, when the moon is in the asterism Aśvinī, by giving a vessel full of ghee along with gold to a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes possessed of a radiant digestive fire. If the full moon of Kārttika should be joined with Kṛttikā, by giving on the rising of the moon a white bull or one of another color, equipped with all kinds of grain, gems, and perfumes, in the midst of lamps to a Brāhmaṇa, one does not experience fear in the wilderness. Having fasted on the third day of the month of Vaiśākha, one who worships Vāsudeva with unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), offers them as oblations, and gives them away, becomes purified from all sins. Whatever one bestows on that day, that becomes inexhaustible. When the full moon of Pauṣa has passed, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, one who has fasted and bathed with sesame seeds, having offered sesame-water, worshipped Vāsudeva with sesame seeds, offered oblations of them, and given and eaten them, becomes purified from sins. When the full moon of Māgha has passed, having reached the twelfth day of the dark fortnight joined with Śravaṇa, one should place two lamps before Vāsudeva using two large wicks. On the right side, one should give a balance of ghee weighing eight [units] more, with a complete garment dyed with saffron; on the left side, one should give a balance of oil weighing eight [units] more, with a complete white garment. Having done this, in whatever kingdom, country, or family one is born, one becomes resplendent there. By giving ghee daily to Brāhmaṇas throughout the entire month of Āśvina and pleasing the two Aśvins, one becomes a possessor of beauty. In that same month, by feeding Brāhmaṇas daily with cow's products (milk, curds, etc.), one becomes a possessor of health. Every month, when the moon is in Revatī, by feeding Brāhmaṇas with *paramānna* (rice-pudding) mixed with curds, honey, and ghee, and pleasing Revatī, one becomes a possessor of beauty. In the month of Māgha, by offering oblations of sesame seeds into the fire daily and feeding Brāhmaṇas with boiled pulse (*kulmāṣa*) mixed with ghee, one becomes possessed of a radiant digestive fire. By bathing in river water on every fourteenth day and pleasing Dharmarāja, one becomes purified from all sins.
He who desires vast enjoyments comparable to the sun, the moon, and the planets should always bathe in the morning for two months: Māgha and Phālguna. (29)
Thus ends the ninetieth chapter, concerning the rules for giving, in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Ninety-One.

Now, when water has begun to flow from a well dug by someone, half of that person's evil deeds perishes. (1) The maker of a pond enjoys the world of Varuṇa, being eternally satisfied. (2) The giver of water is always satisfied. (3) For one who plants trees, the trees become sons in the next world. (4) The trees of one who gives a tree gratify the gods with their blossoms, (5) guests with their fruits, (6) and travelers with their shade. (7) When it rains, they gratify the ancestors with water. (8) The builder of a bridge attains heaven. (9) The builder of a temple for a deity attains the very world of that deity. (10) By whitewashing [a temple] with lime, one shines with glory. (11) By painting it, one attains the world of the Gandharvas. (12) By the gift of flowers, one becomes prosperous. (13) By the gift of ointments, one becomes famous. (14) By the gift of lamps, one becomes possessed of keen vision and radiant everywhere. (15) By the gift of food, one becomes strong. (16) By removing the faded garlands from a deity, one obtains the fruit of giving a cow. (17) This also applies to sweeping the temple, smearing it [with cow dung], cleaning the remnants of a Brahmin’s meal, washing his feet, and attending to those who are ill. (18)
One who performs restorative repairs on wells, groves, ponds, and temples obtains the same fundamental merit as the original builder. (19)
Thus ends the ninety-first chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Ninety-Two.

The gift of fearlessness (*abhaya*) is superior to all other gifts. (1) By giving that, one attains the desired world. (2) And by the gift of land. (3) Having given even a piece of ground the size of a cow-hide (*gocarma*), one becomes purified from all sins. (4) By the gift of a cow, one attains heaven. (5) One who gives ten cows attains the World of Cows (*goloka*). (6) And one who gives a hundred attains the World of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). (7) Having given a cow with horns tipped in gold, hooves in silver, a tail adorned with pearls, a bronze milking vessel, and a cloth as a covering, one attains the heavenly world for as many years as there are hairs on the cow's body. (8) This is especially true for a tawny (*kapila*) cow. (9) By giving a well-trained ox capable of bearing the yoke, one becomes as one who has given ten cows. (10) The giver of a horse attains the same world as the Sun (*sūryasālokya*). (11) The giver of clothing attains the same world as the Moon. (12) The giver of gold attains the same world as Fire. (13) By the gift of silver, one obtains beauty. (14) By the gift of vessels made of precious metals, one becomes a recipient of all desires. (15) By the gift of honey, clarified butter, and oil, one obtains health. (16) And by the gift of medicine. (17) By the gift of salt, one obtains charm (*lāvaṇya*). (18) By the gift of grain, one obtains satisfaction. (19) And by the gift of crops. (20) By the gift of food, one obtains everything. (21) By the gift of beverages, one obtains good fortune. (22) The giver of sesame seeds obtains desired offspring. (23) By the gift of fuel, one possesses a blazing fire. (24) And in battle, one always obtains victory. (25) By the gift of a seat, one obtains a place. (26) By the gift of a bed, one obtains a wife. (27) By the gift of sandals, one obtains a chariot yoked with mules. (28) By the gift of an umbrella, one attains heaven. (29) By the gift of a palm-leaf fan and a fly-whisk, one obtains freedom from suffering. (30) By the gift of a building site, one obtains lordship over a city. (31)
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is beloved in the home—that very thing should be given to one possessed of virtue by him who desires that it become inexhaustible. (32)
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra. Chapter Ninety-Three:

What is given to one who is not a Brāhmaṇa yields an equal reward in the world hereafter. (1) To one who merely calls himself a Brāhmaṇa, it yields a twofold reward. (2) To one who has studied [the Vedas], it yields a thousandfold reward. (3) To one who has mastered the Vedas, it yields an infinite reward. (4) The domestic priest is indeed a worthy recipient for oneself alone. (5) So too are one’s sister, daughter, son, and son-in-law. (6)
A knower of dharma should not give even water to a twice-born who follows the "cat-vow," nor to one who follows the "heron-vow" and is sinful, nor to one who is ignorant of the Vedas. (7)

One who carries the banner of Dharma while being always greedy, deceitful, and hypocritical toward the world; one who is violent and a deceiver of all—such a person should be known as a "cat-vowed" ascetic (baiḍālavratika). ||8||
With downward gaze, deceitful, intent on achieving his own ends, crafty, and falsely humble—such is the twice-born who practices the "heron-vow. (9)
