Those in the world who practice the vow of the crane and those who bear the mark of the cat fall into the Andhatāmisra hell because of that sinful action.
Having committed a sin, one should not perform a vow under the pretext of dharma;
for by concealing the sin with a vow, one practices deception upon women and Śūdras. (11)
Such a Brahmin is censured by those who discourse on the Veda, both in this world and after death; and whatever vow is practiced through hypocrisy goes to the Rākṣasas. (12)
He who, being without the marks, subsists by the livelihood of one wearing the marks, takes upon himself the sin of those who bear the marks and is born among the animal species. ||13||
One should not give a gift for the sake of fame, nor out of fear, nor to a benefactor, nor to those devoted to dancing and singing; such is the certainty regarding the purpose of Dharma. (14)
Thus ends the ninety-third chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Ninety-Four.

A householder should retire to the forest upon seeing his hair grow grey and wrinkles appear; ||1|| or upon seeing the offspring of his offspring; ||2|| or having entrusted his wife to his sons, he may go accompanied by her. ||3|| There too, he should maintain the sacred fires. ||4|| He should not neglect the five sacrifices with food that is not produced by plowing. ||5|| And he should not abandon the private recitation of the Veda. ||6|| He should observe celibacy. ||7|| He should wear garments of skin or bark. ||8|| He should let his matted hair, beard, body hair, and nails grow. ||9|| He should bathe at the three periods of the day. ||10|| He should subsist like a pigeon, accumulating provisions for a month or for a year. ||11|| One who accumulates for a year should discard what was previously stored on the full moon day of Āśvayuja. ||12||
Living in the forest, he should eat eight mouthfuls after bringing them from the village,
receiving them either in the hollow of his hand, in a leaf-cup, or in a wooden bowl.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Ninety-Five.

The forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) should wither his body through austerity (*tapas*). (1) In summer, he should practice the "five-heat" penance (*pañcatapas*). (2) In winter, he should wear wet clothes. (3) In the rainy season, he should sleep under the open sky. (4) Or he may eat only at night. (5) Or he may eat at every other mealtime, every second mealtime, or every third mealtime. (6) He may subsist on flowers. (7) On fruits. (8) On roots. (8) On vegetables. (9) Or on leaves. (10) Or he may eat a single portion of barley-gruel once at the end of each fortnight. (11) Or he may live according to the *cāndrāyaṇa* fasts. (12) He may grind [his food] with stones. (13) Or he may use his teeth as a mortar. (14)
This entire world of gods and humans has austerity as its root;
it has austerity as its middle and austerity as its end, and it is likewise sustained by austerity. (15)

Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to accomplish—all that can be achieved through austerity, for austerity is indeed insurmountable. 16.
Thus ends the ninety-fifth chapter in the Viṣṇu-smṛti.
Chapter Ninety-Six.

Now, one whose passions (*kaṣāya*) have matured through the three stages of life (*āśrama*) should perform the *Prājāpatya* sacrifice, giving away all his possessions as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and become a member of the Brahma-stage (*brahmāśramī*). (1) Having consigned the sacred fires into himself, he should enter the village for the sake of alms. (2) He should accept alms from seven houses. (3) If he receives nothing, he should not be distressed. (4) He should not beg after another beggar. (5) He should accept alms when people have finished eating and the vessels have been removed. (6) He should use a vessel made of clay, a gourd, or wood. (7) Their purification is by means of water. (8) He should shrink from receiving honors. (9) His dwelling should be in an empty house. (10) Or he may dwell at the foot of a tree. (11) He should not stay in a village for a second night. (12) He should wear only enough clothing to cover his private parts. (13) He should place his foot down purified by sight. (14) He should drink water purified by a cloth. (15) He should speak words purified by truth. (16) He should act purified by his mind. (17) He should desire neither death nor life. (18) He should endure insults. (19) He should not despise anyone. (20) He should be free from expectations. (21) He should be free from salutations. (22) Whether someone hacks off one of his arms with an axe or anoints the other with sandalwood paste, he should think neither ill of the former nor well of the latter. (23) He should be constant in self-restraint (*yama*), observances (*niyama*), breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*), withdrawal of the senses (*pratyāhāra*), concentration (*dhāraṇā*), and meditation (*dhyāna*). (24) He should perceive the impermanence of the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). (25) The impurity of the body. (26) The transformation of form due to old age. (27) The affliction caused by physical, mental, and external diseases. (28) And those born of nature. (29) Dwelling in the womb, which is eternally dark. (30) There, in the midst of excrement. (31) And there, the experience of the suffering of cold and heat. (32) At the time of birth, the experience of great suffering from passing through the narrowness of the birth canal. (33) In childhood, delusion and dependence on teachers. (34) The hardship of study and acquisition. (35) In youth, falling into hell through the failure to obtain sense objects, or through obtaining them by improper means, or through indulgence in sense objects. (36) Dwelling with those who are unpleasant and separation from those who are dear. (37) Great suffering in hell. (38) And in the migrations of the cycle of existence among the animal wombs. (39) Thus, in this ever-moving cycle of existence, there is no happiness whatsoever. (40) Even that which is designated as "happiness" only in comparison to suffering is impermanent. (41) When one is unable to indulge in it or when it is lost, there is great suffering. (42) He should view this body as consisting of seven constituents (*dhātu*). (43) It consists of chyle, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen. (44) It is covered with skin. (45) It is foul-smelling. (46) It is a repository of filth. (47) Though surrounded by hundreds of pleasures, it is subject to change. (48) Though maintained with effort, it is perishable. (49) It is the seat of lust, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and envy. (50) It is composed of earth, water, fire, air, and ether. (51) It is joined with bones, veins, arteries, and sinews. (52) It is full of passion (*rajas*). (53) It has six layers of skin. (54) It is supported by three hundred and sixty bones. (55) The division of these is as follows: including the minute ones, there are sixty-four teeth. (57) Twenty nails. (58) And the long bones of the hands and feet. (59) Sixty phalanges of the fingers and toes. (60) Two in the heels. (61) Four in the ankles. (62) Four in the forearms. (63) Four in the shanks. (64) Two each in the knees and cheeks. (65) And two each in the thighs and shoulders. (66) And in the collarbones and the palate; likewise in the hip-blades. (67) The bone of the pelvis is one. (68) The backbone consists of forty-five segments. (69) The neck has fifteen bones. (70) The collarbone is one. (71) And the jaw. (72) And two at its base. (73) Two each in the forehead, eyes, and cheeks. (74) The nose consists of solid bone. (75) Together with the *arbuda* and *sthālaka* bones, there are seventy-two ribs. (76) The chest has seventeen bones. (77) Two *śaṅkhaka* bones. (78) And four cranial plates of the head. (79) In this body, there are seven hundred veins (*śirā*). (80) Nine hundred sinews (*snāyu*). (81) Two hundred arteries (*dhamanī*). (82) Five hundred muscles (*peśī*). (83) There are twenty-nine lakhs, nine hundred, and fifty-six minor arteries. (84) There are three lakhs of pores for hair and beard. (85) One hundred and seven vital spots (*marman*). (86) Two hundred joints (*saṃdhi*). (87) Fifty-four crores and sixty-seven lakhs of hairs. (88) The navel, the heart, the anus, semen, blood, the two *śaṅkhakas*, the head, the throat, and the heart are the seats of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). (89) The two arms, the two legs, the trunk, and the head are the six limbs. (90) Fat, membrane, the stomach, the navel, the *kloma*, liver, spleen, small intestine, kidneys, bladder, rectum, stomach, heart, large intestine, anus, abdomen, and the pelvic cavity are the internal organs. (91) The pupils, the eye-sockets, the ear-canal, the ears, the earlobes, the cheeks, the eyebrows, the temples, the gums, the lips, the pits of the loins, the groins, the testicles, the kidneys, the phlegm-glands, the breasts, the uvula, the buttocks, the arms, the shanks, the thighs, the calves, the sole of the foot, the abdomen, the top of the bladder, the chin, the tonsils, and the nape of the neck—these are the locations in this body. (92) Sound, touch, form, taste, and smell are the objects of the senses (*viṣaya*). (93) The nose, eyes, tongue, skin, and ears are the organs of perception (*buddhīndriya*). (94) The hands, feet, anus, genitals, and tongue are the organs of action (*karmendriya*). (95) Mind (*manas*), intellect (*buddhi*), self (*ātman*), and the unmanifest (*avyakta*) are beyond the senses. (96)
"O Earth, this body is designated as the 'field' (kṣetra);
those who know this call him who understands it the 'knower of the field' (kṣetrajña). (97)
Know Me also as the Knower of the Field in all fields, O beautiful lady;
the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field is that which must be known eternally by one who desires liberation. 98.
Thus ends the ninety-sixth chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Ninety-Seven.

With his feet placed upward on his thighs, having laid his left hand upon his right, with his tongue motionless against the palate, not touching his teeth with his teeth, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking toward the quarters, fearless and with a tranquil mind, he should contemplate that which transcends the twenty-four principles (tattvas). [He should contemplate] that which is eternal, beyond the senses, devoid of qualities, transcending sound, touch, taste, form, and smell; which abides in all, yet is exceedingly vast; [2] which pervades all, yet is exceedingly subtle; [3] which has hands and feet everywhere, eyes, heads, and faces everywhere, and the power of all the senses everywhere; [4] thus one should meditate. [5] For one devoted to meditation, the manifestation of Yoga occurs within a year. [6] Now, if one is unable to fix the mind (lakṣabandha) upon the formless, then, having first meditated upon each preceding element among earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, self, the unmanifest, and the Puruṣa, and having attained a fixed point (lakṣa) therein, one should abandon that and meditate upon the next. [7] In this way, one should ascend to the meditation upon the Puruṣa. [8] If one is incapable even of that, one should meditate upon the Puruṣa like a lamp in the center of the downward-facing lotus of the heart. [9] If one is incapable even of that, one should meditate upon the Blessed Vāsudeva, wearing a crown, earrings, and armlets, his chest adorned with a forest garland, of gentle form, four-armed, bearing the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, with the earth situated between his feet. [10] "Whatever one meditates upon, that one attains"—this is the secret of meditation. [11] Therefore, having abandoned everything perishable, one should meditate only upon the imperishable (akṣara). [12] And there is nothing imperishable whatsoever apart from the Puruṣa. [13] Having attained Him, one becomes liberated. [14]
Because the Great Lord, having pervaded the entire city [of the body], lies within it, he is therefore called "Puruṣa" by those who contemplate reality. ||15||
In the early and late watches of the night, the yogi, ever vigilant,
should meditate upon the Person Viṣṇu, who is beyond the qualities and the twenty-fifth principle.
He is the self of reality, unapproachable, and devoid of all principles;
he is unattached yet the sustainer of all, free from qualities yet the enjoyer of qualities.
It is outside and within all beings; it is both the unmoving and the moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, yet it is near.
It is undivided, yet it exists as if divided;
it is the form of the past, the future, and the present; it is both the devourer and the progenitor.
That is said to be the light of even the lights, beyond darkness;
it is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge, seated in the heart of all.
Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been described in brief.
Having understood this, my devotee attains to My own state of being. (21)
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Chapter Ninety-Eight.

Having been addressed thus, Vasumatī prostrated herself with her head and knees and said: “O Blessed One, here in your presence the four great elements have made their permanent abode: space in the form of the conch, wind in the form of the discus, fire in the form of the mace, and water in the form of the lotus. I too wish to remain in this very form, revolving at the feet of the Blessed One. Having been addressed thus, the Blessed One said, “So be it. Vasumatī, having obtained her desire, acted accordingly and praised the God of Gods: “Homage be to you! O God of Gods! Vāsudeva! Ādideva! Kāmadeva! Kāmapāla! Mahīpāla! Puṇḍarīkākṣa! Nārāyaṇa! Parāyaṇa! Jagatparāyaṇa! Homage, homage!”
Having thus praised her with a serene mind, the goddess Earth, having obtained her desire, then spoke face-to-face to the Queen. 102.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
Having beheld the splendor of Viṣṇu, the God of gods—
Having grasped her feet, the goddess Earth, filled with joy, questioned that lady who was blazing with ascetic power and possessed a beautiful complexion like well-refined gold.
To the one with hands as beautiful as blooming red lotuses, the most excellent one whose feet are held by a navel like a blooming red lotus,
who eternally dwells in a palace like a blooming red lotus—
Possessing a complexion equal to the center of a fully blossomed red lotus. ||2||
O you with eyes like blue lotuses, golden-hued, clad in white garments, your limbs adorned with jewels;
O moon-faced one, possessing a radiance equal to the sun!
Possessing great power, the foremost in the world. ||3||
You alone are the primary sleep of the world,
as well as Lakṣmī, Dhṛti, Śrī, Virati, Jayā, Kānti, Prabhā, Kīrti, and Vibhūti.
Sarasvatī is speech and also the purifier. ||4||
Svadhā, Titikṣā, Vasudhā, Pratiṣṭhā, Sthiti, Sudīkṣā, as well as Sunīti,
Viśālā, and Anasūyā.
And Svāhā, and Medhā, and likewise Buddhi. ||5||
O dark-eyed one, just as this best of gods stands having pervaded the entire three worlds,
so too do you stand, O giver of boons.
I ask you about the dwelling of your splendor.
Having been addressed in this way, Lakṣmī, standing then before the best of gods, spoke to the Earth:
"I am always established in Madhusūdana."
Beside the god, [there was] one with the color of refined gold. ||7||
By his command, whomsoever I remember in my mind,
the virtuous declare him to be endowed with prosperity;
and furthermore, in my recollection, wherever I am—
Listen, O Sustainer of the World, for she is eternally present there. ||8||
I dwell in the sun and in the moon, in the cloudless sky rich with hosts of stars,
and likewise in the cloud that holds abundant rain.
And [he was] richly adorned with Indra’s weapon (the rainbow) and radiant with lightning. ||9||
Likewise, upon pure gold and silver,
upon jewels and stainless garments on the ground,
and upon rows of white palaces;
In temples adorned with banners. ||10||
When cow dung has been freshly applied, when a lordly elephant is in rut, when a horse is exultant,
and likewise when a bull is filled with pride.
Likewise, toward a Brahmin who is endowed with the study [of the Vedas]. ||11||
Upon a lion throne, an āmalaka fruit, a bilva fruit, a parasol, a conch shell, and likewise a lotus;
upon a blazing fire and a stainless sword.
And I am always present in the mirror-image. ||12||
In full water-pots accompanied by fly-whisks and palm-leaf fans,
and in beautiful ornamental vessels and ewers.
And I am situated in the clay that has just been dug up. ||13||
Likewise in milk, in clarified butter, in a grassy meadow, in honey, in curd,
on the body of a virtuous woman, and in the bodies of the gods.
In the bodies of ascetics and those who have offered oblations in sacrifice. ||14||
I remained here when my hero had departed from the battle— whether he were dead and gone to dwell in heaven,
or amidst the sound of Vedic chanting and the blast of conchs.
And when there is the sound of "an auspicious day" (puṇyāha) and the sound of musical instruments. ||15||
At a royal consecration, as well as at a wedding, a sacrifice, or a bridegroom’s reception, when the head is wet and not yet dry,
and among white flowers and mountains.
Among delightful fruits and the best of rivers. ||16||
In lakes full [of water], likewise among white lotuses, on ground covered with young grass, and amidst clusters of lotuses;
and when the young calf and the infant were delighted.
In a virtuous man who is devoted to righteousness. ||17||
One who is devoted to right conduct, constant in the study of the scriptures, modest in dress, well-attired,
with perfectly clean teeth, and free from impurities.
And [he is] one who eats choice food and honors guests. ||18||
Content with his own wife, devoted to dharma, preeminent among beings, free from overeating,
always possessing flowers and fragrant limbs.
And she was constantly anointed and adorned. ||19||
Established in truth, devoted to the welfare of beings,
endowed with patience, and free from anger;
with senses well-restrained, he was skilled in the affairs of others.
And always disciplined with a virtuous mind. ||20||
Among women who are always well-adorned, devoted to their husbands, speaking kindly,
generous with their hands, and blessed with offspring.
In those who keep their vessels well-concealed and who are fond of offerings. ||21||
In women whose dwellings are well-swept, who have conquered their senses, who are free from malice, who are not greedy,
who regard righteousness, and who are endowed with compassion;
I am eternally established as the creator of the world.
By the mere act of being remembered, I always remain with a body of earth at the side of Madhusūdana;
yet, for even the duration of a single blink of an eye, I am made absent.
He never stands still with the Supreme among Men. ||23||
Thus ends the ninety-ninth section in the Dharmaśāstra of Viṣṇu.
This excellent Dharmaśāstra was spoken by the Lord himself.
For those twice-born ones who shall uphold it, their course in dharma is certain. ||1||
This is purifying, auspicious, most excellent, and indeed life-prolonging; it destroys demons, brings glory, and increases strength and good fortune. (2)
It should always be studied, retained, grasped, and heard, and it should be proclaimed to those who possess faith by men desiring prosperity. (3)
Thus ends the hundredth section in the Vaiṣṇava Dharmaśāstra.
